  • resolve_stack(stack_dir) -> Path — the resolved stack root, or raise if it is not a generated stack (see STACK_MARKERS).
  • resolve_assets(assets_dir) -> Path — validate and return the skill-bundle assets/ dir (room template + snippet).
  • compose_project_name(stack) -> str / default_room_id(stack) -> str — the compose project name, and the default about_<project> room id.
  • has_local_gitea(stack) -> bool — whether docker-compose.yml defines a local gitea service (by name or a gitea/gitea* image). When true (and not --no-local-gitea), main defaults the room's owner/repo to LOCAL_GITEA_OWNER / LOCAL_GITEA_REPO.

Edits — pure (text, …) -> (new_text, action) functions, so --dry-run is just "compute, don't write"; action is ADDED or UNCHANGED:

  • add_pyproject_dep(text, pin=None, with_truststore=False) — add the soliplex-concierge dependency to backend/pyproject.toml.
  • add_requirements_dep(text, pin=None, with_truststore=False) — add it to backend/requirements.txt, which a stack built on a soliplex release image installs its extra packages from.
  • add_dockerfile_dep(text, pin=None, with_truststore=False) — add it to the backend/Dockerfile uv add block, in an older stack without backend/requirements.txt.
  • merge_installation(text, *, confirm_skill_allow_list=False) -> (new_text, {target: action}) — surgically merge the installation.yaml entries: the three meta.tool_configs classes, environment, secrets, and the two filesystem skill_configs (room_paths is wired by install_room). The skill_configs targets come back COVERED on a permissive stack; on one with an explicit allow-list they are added only when confirm_skill_allow_list is true, and otherwise it raises SkillAllowListActive.
  • update_env(text, host, token) — add the GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN lines.
  • stack_gitea_script(pin=None, with_truststore=False) -> str — render the stack's scripts/gitea_issues.py admin shim text.

File installs — mutate the stack, returning ADDED / UNCHANGED:

  • install_room(assets, stack, opts) — copy and rewire the about-room template.
  • install_skill(name, skill_src, stack, opts) — copy a skill tree into the stack and defang it (via soliplex_skills.install.defang_skill).
  • install_gitea_script(stack, opts) — write the admin gitea_issues.py CLI.

Constants — ADDED / UNCHANGED (action strings); SKILL_NAME and STACK_MARKERS; the wiring constants DIST, TOOL_CONFIG, GITEA_TOOL, GITEA_HOST, GITEA_TOKEN_SECRET, ASSET_ROOM; DEFAULT_GITEA_HOST / DEFAULT_GITEA_TOKEN; LOCAL_GITEA_OWNER / LOCAL_GITEA_REPO (the service account and repo soliplex-template's init_gitea.py provisions, defaulted into the room when a local Gitea is detected); and GITEA_ADMIN_MIN (the soliplex-concierge version floor pinned into the generated gitea_issues.py when --version is omitted).

items.title: Command-line scripts
items.text: The repo ships two runnable CLI scripts, each bundled with a skill. Both are PEP 723 scripts: run them with uv run, which provisions their dependencies from the inline metadata — no install step. (Each skill also bundles a skill_versions.py; that one is documented with the soliplex-skills versions CLI, not here.)

items.title: install_concierge.py — install the extension
items.text:
skills/soliplex-concierge-installer/scripts/install_concierge.py wires the extension into a soliplex-template-generated stack, idempotently. See Setup for the full walkthrough; this is the option summary.

uv run scripts/install_concierge.py --stack-dir /path/to/stack \
    --owner <gitea-owner> --repo <gitea-repo> [options]

The same logic is also installed as the install-concierge console script (uv tool install soliplex-concierge, or run it once without installing via uvx --from soliplex-concierge install-concierge …). It takes the options below, but — because the installed package does not ship the room template — the skill bundle's assets/ directory is a required leading positional argument:

install-concierge /path/to/soliplex-concierge-installer/assets \
    --stack-dir /path/to/stack --owner <gitea-owner> --repo <gitea-repo>

The uv run scripts/install_concierge.py shim supplies that path from its own bundle automatically, so you never pass it there.

Option Purpose --stack-dir stack root (default: current directory) --owner / --repo Gitea owner and repository for filed issues --gitea-host / --gitea-token fill real .env values instead of placeholders --no-local-gitea skip local-Gitea auto-detection; keep the external-Gitea defaults --version <X.Y> pin the soliplex-concierge dependency added to the stack (latest for newest; omitted warns about skew) --with-truststore install the [truststore] extra (verify TLS against the OS trust store; issue #46) --room-skill-version / --docs-skill-version published tag to install for the room / docs skill --room-skill-dir / --docs-skill-dir install the room / docs skill from a local directory --room-id room id to create (default about_<compose-project-name>) --force overwrite an existing room/skill --dry-run report changes without writing

items.title: gitea_issues.py — triage and resolve requests
items.text:
skills/soliplex-concierge-admin/scripts/gitea_issues.py is a thin shim over soliplex_concierge.gitea_admin. The installer drops an identical copy into the stack at scripts/gitea_issues.py. See Administering requests for the workflow; this is the subcommand summary.

Every subcommand takes the connection options --host / --token (falling back to GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN) and the required --owner / --repo.

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py <command> --owner <owner> --repo <repo> [...]
Command Purpose init create the request labels on the repository list list request issues (--state open\|closed\|all, repeatable --label, --created-by <login>) search filter by --type new-room\|room-access, --decision approved\|denied, --state, --label, --created-by <login> show <number> print one issue's labels and metadata, the requester's profile (--profile-name for a non-default attachment name), and its body comment <number> --body <text> add a comment close <number> [--body <text>] optionally comment, then close approve <number> [--body <text>] label approved, record the decision, and close deny <number> [--body <text>] label denied, record the decision, and close

Behind an enterprise / internal CA, add --with truststore to the uv run invocation so TLS verifies against the OS trust store (issue #46).

items.title: Provisioner REST API
items.text:
A room provisioner creates a private RAG room on a requesting user's behalf. The concierge's request_room and check_room_request tools are its client. Each deployment serves the API with an implementation of its own, because what creating a room involves depends on the stack: a soliplex-template stack's soliplex-provisioner service is one such implementation.

This page specifies the HTTP endpoints every implementation serves. The models and constants it names live in soliplex_concierge.provisioner.api (see the Python API). To check an implementation against this contract, see Implementing a provisioner.

items.title: Credentials
items.text: Every request to /rooms carries a Bearer soliplex service token. The token holds the requesting user's claims and is signed with the installation's URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET (api.SERVICE_TOKEN_SECRET): the caller mints it with soliplex.token_mint, and the service validates it with the same secret. A missing or invalid token gets 401, with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header.

items.title: Admission
items.text:
The service admits a requester who is either of these:

  • an admin of the installation
  • a holder of WRITE on the reserved room id __provision__ (api.ADMISSION_ROOM_ID)

It answers any other requester 403.

items.title: POST /rooms
items.text:
The body is a RoomRequest:

{"name": "Q3 Plans", "description": "Plans for Q3", "slug": "q3-plans"}

description and slug are optional, and no other field is allowed. The new room's id is <owner><separator><slug>, the separator being the deployment's (by default --, as in alice--q3-plans). The owner part derives from one of the requester's claims: lowercased by default, with any separator in it replaced and any trailing ., _ or - stripped. The slug derives from the request's name, unless the request asks for a specific slug; one that does not fit (including one containing the separator) is a 400, and the caller may retry with another.

An admin may make someone other than themselves the room's owner with the optional owner, a RoomOwner. owner.owner is the room id's owner part, normalized as a claimed one is (lowercased by default, any separator replaced, any trailing ., _ or - stripped). Whom the room is granted to is given in one of two forms:

  • a claim and its exact value, for one person:

    {"name": "Q3 Plans",
 "owner": {"owner": "bharney", "claim": "email",
           "value": "bharney@example.com"}}

  • a predicate the installation registers under meta.jsonpath_functions, applied to a user's claims as a whole, for everyone it recognizes:

    {"name": "Quarry Notes",
 "owner": {"owner": "foremen", "predicate": "is_foreman"}}

The service builds the access rule (a soliplex ACL JSONPath) from the form; no caller writes one, and an owner with a json_path is a 422. The requester is still the one who asked, and may see the request.

Status Body Meaning 202 Accepted: room_id, issue_url Admitted; the room is created in the background 400 Error: detail The name, slug or named owner yields no usable room id, the owner's predicate is not registered, or the deployment's own check finds the request unacceptable 401 Error No service token, or one that is not valid 403 Error The requester is not admitted, or names an owner without being an admin 409 Refusal: detail, room_id The room exists, a request for it is in flight, or resources named for it exist already 409 Error The deployment's own check finds the room's name conflicts with something it knows of 422 The body is not a RoomRequest (including an owner in neither form, or both) 429 Error The deployment's own check refuses the request as one too many (a rate limit, or a quota of rooms); a Retry-After header, when present, says when to ask again 503 Error The provisioner is busy with other rooms; a Retry-After header says when to ask again

The deployment's own check may answer with any status; those above are the ones the concierge's room tool understands. | 500 | Error | The service failed |

The service refuses in this order, cheapest first: 401 for the token, 400 for the request's own form, 409 for a request already in flight, then the deployment's own check, if it has one, then 403 for a caller it does not admit (a check that may cost the backend a call). The in-flight check comes before the deployment's, so a retry of a request that got through is answered as in flight, never refused by a rate limit counting it again. So a caller it would not admit still gets 400 for a malformed request. Whether an admin's named predicate is registered (a 400 listing the registered ones) is checked only after the 403s, and a room that exists already (a 409) only once the caller is admitted.

The service's own 409s name the room they refuse (a Refusal); a deployment's never does (a plain Error). A 409 names the room it refuses, because the caller cannot work the room id out for itself. The concierge relies on this when it retries a request that timed out: a 409 naming the room means the first attempt got through.

items.title: GET /rooms/{room_id}
items.text:
The room id is quoted as one path segment (api.room_path); the default -- separator needs no quoting, and a legacy : is left as is.

Status Body Meaning 200 RequestState The request's state 401 Error As for POST /rooms 404 Error No extant request for that room, or one the caller may not see 500 Error As for POST /rooms

Only a request's requester and admins may see it. Anyone else gets 404, as if there were no such request.

A RequestState carries:

  • room_id
  • state: one of the states below
  • issue_url: the request's tracking issue, if any
  • incomplete: the steps an admin must finish
  • error: why the room was not created

An admin sees incomplete and error in full. A requester who is not one gets a fixed sentence for each instead (an administrator must finish setting the room up; creating it failed, and an administrator has the details), since both can name the stack's hosts, paths and storage.

The states:

  • pending: the room is being created
  • live: the room is ready
  • incomplete: the room exists, but an admin must finish the steps in incomplete
  • failed: the room was not created; error says why

items.title: GET /ok
items.text:
For health checks; it needs no token.

Status Body Meaning 200 OK (plain text) The service can create rooms 503 plain text, saying why It cannot yet: for instance, the backend does not admit the provisioner itself

items.title: Versions
items.text:
Every response carries the header X-Soliplex-Provisioner-API (api.API_VERSION_HEADER), with the version of the API the service implements (api.API_VERSION, currently 1).

The concierge's tools fail with IncompatibleService when a service names another version. They take an answer without the header to be version 1's, because the services that predate the header implement it.

items.title: Skills
items.text:
The concierge is delivered as three Agent Skills, each published as a release artifact and installed either into a coding agent or into a Soliplex room. Each page below covers what the skill is for, where to find it, and where and how to install it:

  • soliplex-concierge-installer — wires the extension into a stack; runs in a coding agent.
  • soliplex-concierge-room — the in-room request formatter; installed into a room's configuration.
  • soliplex-concierge-admin — resolves the filed requests; runs in a coding agent.

items.title: Related skills
items.text:
The concierge works alongside two skills published by sibling repositories. Their own documentation covers installing and using them:

  • soliplex-template — generate and configure a Soliplex stack, create rooms, and build RAG databases. The installer skill uses it to stand up a stack, and the admin user uses it to provision the rooms requests ask for.

  • soliplex-docs — the full Soliplex documentation as a skill. The installer wires it into the about-room so the concierge can answer "how do I …" questions about Soliplex, and the admin consults it for room, access, and RAG configuration.

Like the installed copy of the soliplex-concierge-room skill, the installer strips the skill_versions.py helper from the copy of the soliplex-docs skill it installs. To update an installed copy, re-run the installer's install_concierge.py (with --force) against the stack from a coding agent.

items.title: soliplex-concierge-admin
items.text:
Function. Helps an administrator work through the request issues the concierge files: it lists and reads them, and drafts the change each asks for (a new room's configuration, or the commands granting access) for the administrator to review and apply through their deployment's own process. It never applies a change itself. Once the administrator has acted, it records the outcome and closes the issue. Its gitea_issues.py CLI and workflow are documented under Administering requests.

Where to find it. Published as a release artifact of soliplex/soliplex-concierge: the admin-skill-latest pointer tracks the newest build (the asset is soliplex-concierge-admin-skill.tar.gz), and tagged software releases (v*) attach the same tarball pinned to that version.

Where to install it. Into an external coding agent (e.g. Claude Code) — the admin works against the Gitea repository and the deployed stack from there, not inside the Soliplex server. (The installer separately drops a copy of the gitea_issues.py CLI into the stack at scripts/gitea_issues.py, so the same commands can be run from the stack directory.)

How to install it. Download and extract the release tarball into your coding agent's skills directory (where it discovers Agent Skills); the soliplex-skills installation guide covers fetching a published skill.

Keeping it current. Each published copy bundles scripts/skill_versions.py, which can list, diff, and upgrade the installed skill against the published builds — see the soliplex-skills versions CLI docs.

items.title: soliplex-concierge-installer
items.text:
Function. Wires the concierge into a target Soliplex stack — creating the about-room, installing the room and docs skills, merging the installation.yaml entries, and dropping in the admin CLI. It is the convenient path described in Setup.

Where to find it. Published as a release artifact of soliplex/soliplex-concierge: the installer-skill-latest pointer always tracks the newest build (the asset is soliplex-concierge-installer-skill.tar.gz), and every tagged software release (v*) attaches the same tarball pinned to that version.

Where to install it. Into an external coding agent (e.g. Claude Code) — the skill runs there to operate on your stack, not inside the Soliplex server.

How to install it. Download and extract the release tarball into your coding agent's skills directory (where it discovers Agent Skills); the soliplex-skills installation guide covers fetching a published skill. Once the agent has the skill, run its bundled scripts/install_concierge.py as shown in Setup.

Keeping it current. Each published copy bundles scripts/skill_versions.py, which can list, diff, and upgrade the installed skill against the published builds — see the soliplex-skills versions CLI docs.

items.title: soliplex-concierge-room
items.text:
Function. The in-room request formatter: it turns a user's new-room or room-access request into a ready-to-file tracking-issue draft that the about-room's create_gitea_issue tool files. See The concierge for how it fits the request flow.

Where to find it. Published as a release artifact of soliplex/soliplex-concierge: the room-skill-latest pointer tracks the newest build (the asset is soliplex-concierge-room-skill.tar.gz), and tagged software releases (v*) attach the same tarball pinned to that version.

Where to install it. Into a Soliplex installation, as a filesystem skill enabled in the about-room's configuration — not into a coding agent. It runs as a sub-agent of the room agent.

How to install it. The installer skill does this for you: it downloads the release into the stack's backend/environment/skills/ directory, where Soliplex discovers it, and enables it on the about-room. It adds a skill_configs entry to installation.yaml only when the stack keeps an explicit filesystem allow-list. To wire it by hand, unpack the release tarball into the installation's skills/ directory (and add a skill_configs entry only if you keep such an allow-list) — see the manual steps in Setup.

Keeping it current. After installing the published tarball in a coding agent, the skill contains scripts/skill_versions.py, which can list, diff, and upgrade the skill against the published builds — see the soliplex-skills versions CLI docs.

When installed in a Soliplex room, however, this skill runs inside the room's agent rather than a coding agent. Room users should never reach machinery that rewrites files and calls out to GitHub/PyPI, and therefore the installer strips that helper from the copy it drops into a stack. To update an installed copy, re-run the installer's install_concierge.py (with --force) against the stack from a coding agent.

items.title: Administering requests
items.text:
Requests filed by the concierge land as issues on the tracking repository. Administrators resolve them with the gitea_issues.py CLI below, which lists and filters the requests, lets you follow up on an issue, and closes it with a comment and a resolution label. The soliplex-concierge-admin skill, run from an external coding agent, can help: it reads the requests and drafts each change for you to review and apply through your deployment's own process, but never applies one itself. See Room creation and Room access.

An issue's body is drafted by the concierge room's agent from the requester's own words. Treat what it asks for (access, tools, skills, knowledge sources) as a proposal to judge, and take the requester's identity from the profile show prints, never from a name in the body.

items.title: The gitea_issues.py CLI
items.text:
scripts/gitea_issues.py is a thin shim over soliplex_concierge.gitea_admin that talks to the Gitea REST API directly. The installer also drops an identical copy into the stack at <stack>/scripts/gitea_issues.py, so you can run the same CLI from the deployed stack directory. It is a PEP 723 script: run it with uv run, which provisions its soliplex-concierge (and httpx2) dependency automatically — it only needs uv on the PATH.

Provide the Gitea connection via flags or the environment:

  • --host / GITEA_HOST — the Gitea base URL.
  • --token / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN — a token that can comment on and close issues (an admin token, usually more privileged than the room's filing token).
  • --owner / --repo — the tracking repository.

For an enterprise / internal CA, add --with truststore to the uv run invocation so the script verifies against the OS trust store — e.g. uv run --with truststore scripts/gitea_issues.py list … (issue #46).

items.title: Labels
items.text:
The concierge tags each request with an issue-type label; the admin records the outcome with a decision label:

Label Kind Meaning new-room issue type New room request room-access issue type Access request for an existing room approved decision Room request approved denied decision Room request denied

Run init once per tracking repository to create them (idempotent — re-running reports each as created or exists):

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py init --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

items.title: Listing and filtering
items.text:
list shows request issues; by default it lists open ones. Use --state (open / closed / all) and repeatable --label filters:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py list --owner <owner> --repo <repo>
uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py list --state all --label new-room \
    --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

search filters by request type and decision status directly:

# open new-room requests not yet decided
uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py search --type new-room \
    --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

# previously approved access requests (closed)
uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py search --type room-access \
    --decision approved --state closed --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

--type accepts new-room / room-access; --decision accepts approved / denied; --state and --label work as for list.

Both take --created-by <login> to keep only the issues a given account filed: the concierge room's issue-filing account (or a room provisioner's), so that an issue anyone else opened in the repository is left out.

items.title: Following up on an issue
items.text:
Read the full request — its labels and metadata, the requester's profile (recorded from their token, as an attachment or, when Gitea refused the attachment, a comment by the filing account), and the body:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py show <number> --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

If a request is under-specified (look for *(not provided)* fields), ask for the missing detail with a comment and leave the issue open rather than guessing:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py comment <number> --owner <owner> \
    --repo <repo> --body "Which existing room should this draw its docs from?"

items.title: Closing a request
items.text:
Carry out the operation (see Room creation / Room access), then close the issue. A plain close records a comment without a decision label:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py close <number> --owner <owner> \
    --repo <repo> --body "Done — room 'marketing' is live."

For room-access requests, prefer the approve / deny subcommands, which also apply the approved / denied decision label — see Room access.

Only close once the operation is actually complete. Never close a request you could not fulfil — comment what is blocking it and leave it open.

items.title: Resolving a room-access request
items.text: A room-access request (the room-access label) asks for an existing private room to be opened to a specific user. Resolving it means understanding who wants access to which room, then granting it with the soliplex-cli room-authz command set. The soliplex-concierge-admin skill helps you read the request and records the decision with the approved / denied label.

items.title: 1. Understand the request
items.text:
Find the open access requests and read one:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py search --type room-access \
    --owner <owner> --repo <repo>
uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py show <number> --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

The body (the room-skill's room-access template) gives the room and the justification. The requester's identity, though, comes from the attached user profile, not the body: when the concierge filed the issue, create_gitea_issue attached the signed-in user's profile as a YAML file (user-profile.yaml by default). It holds the OIDC claims Soliplex knows about the user — typically their email and preferred_username — which are exactly the discriminators you grant against below.

show prints the profile's claims, ahead of the body. If Gitea refused the attachment, they come from the comment the filing account posted instead, as a YAML block; a look-alike block in the body, or in another account's comment, is ignored. If the installation names the attachment differently, pass --profile-name <name> to show. If the issue carries no profile, the request cannot be attributed: don't take an identity from the body. (An installation may set exclude_claims on the tool to keep selected fields — e.g. email — out of the tracking repo; if the discriminator you need was excluded, fall back to the other, or ask the requester.)

items.title: 2. Grant access
items.text:
Granting access mutates the running stack's authorization database, so run the soliplex-cli room-authz commands against the stack through a one-off backend container, from the stack directory:

# Make the room private if it isn't already — add-acl-entry needs a RoomPolicy.
docker compose run --rm backend \
  /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli room-authz make-private /environment <room_id>

# Allow the requesting user, matched by an OIDC claim from their profile.
docker compose run --rm backend \
  /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
    --allow --permission read --email <user-email> /environment <room_id>

Notes:

  • /environment is the in-container installation path.
  • --permission is required. read is what using the room needs; a write- or admin-scoped entry grants only that permission and does not let the user into a private room.
  • Match the user with the discriminator that fits their profile: --email <email> or --preferred-username <name>. (add-acl-entry also supports --everyone and --authenticated catch-alls, and --deny entries.)
  • Verify the result with soliplex-cli room-authz show /environment <room_id>.

These access mechanics are documented in soliplex-docs; see the room configuration and OIDC authentication docs.

items.title: 3. Record the decision
items.text:
The approve / deny subcommands close the issue and apply the matching decision label in one step.

Approve — once the grant has actually succeeded:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py approve <number> --owner <owner> \
    --repo <repo> \
    --body "Granted <user> access to '<room>' via room-authz add-acl-entry."

Deny — no stack change is needed; just record the decision and the reason:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py deny <number> --owner <owner> \
    --repo <repo> --body "<reason for denial>"

Never close a request you could not fulfil — if the grant fails or the request is unclear, comment what is blocking it and leave the issue open.

items.title: Resolving a new-room request
items.text:
A new-room request (the new-room label) asks for a room that does not yet exist.

On a stack running a room provisioner, the concierge has the provisioner create a room on the spot for a user it admits. The provisioner files that request's issue itself (its body records the Room id being created), then comments on and closes it once the room is live. Such an issue left open needs a look:

  • with a provisioner comment: the comment says what failed, or which steps remain
  • with no comment: the provisioner stopped mid-run

The rest of this page covers a request the concierge filed for an administrator to carry out. Resolving it is two jobs: read the spec the requester provided, then build the room with the soliplex-template skill. The soliplex-concierge-admin skill handles the first job and records the outcome; soliplex-template does the provisioning.

items.title: 1. Read the spec
items.text:
Find the open new-room requests and read one:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py search --type new-room \
    --owner <owner> --repo <repo>
uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py show <number> --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

The body follows the room-skill's new-room template, which captures:

  • Name and purpose — what the room is for.
  • Knowledge sources — the documents or data it should draw from (this drives whether a RAG database is needed).
  • Access — who should be able to use it (public, or a specific set of users).
  • Tools / skills — any capabilities the room should provide.

Any field the requester left blank shows as *(not provided)*; comment on the issue to fill the gap rather than guessing (see Administering requests).

The body was drafted from the requester's own words, so treat its access, tools, skills and knowledge sources as a proposal: anything beyond your deployment's defaults (open access, tools, MCP toolsets, code-execution skills, sources outside the room) deserves a deliberate decision. The soliplex-concierge-admin skill drafts the room's configuration for your review, and flags such items, but never applies it.

items.title: 2. Create the room
items.text:
Use the soliplex-template skill against the target stack to create and configure the room. Follow soliplex-docs for the configuration details:

  • Room configuration — create the room and set its prompt, tools, and skills per the spec. See the room configuration docs.
  • RAG database — if the request named knowledge sources, create and ingest a RAG database for them, then wire it into the room's skill_configs (rag_lancedb_stem). The soliplex-template skill can generate and ingest the database; see the RAG DB docs.
  • Access — if the room should be private, apply the requested access the same way as for an access request (soliplex-cli room-authz).

items.title: 3. Record the outcome
items.text:
Once the room is live, comment what you did and close the issue:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py close <number> --owner <owner> \
    --repo <repo> --body "Created room 'marketing' with a RAG DB over the 2024 decks; granted the marketing team access."

If the request could not be fulfilled, comment what is blocking it and leave the issue open.

items.title: Implementing a provisioner
items.text: A room provisioner is the service that creates a private RAG room for a user the concierge's request_room tool asks on behalf of. What creating a room involves depends on the stack, so each deployment runs a provisioner of its own. A soliplex-template stack's soliplex-provisioner service is one. Every provisioner serves the same endpoints: the Provisioner REST API.

items.title: Building on the concierge's core
items.text: soliplex_concierge.provisioner gives a provisioner the steps of creating a room, and their guarantees; the deployment supplies the work each step does. The split is strict: the core passes data (the request, the tracking issue, each step's outcome) and writes no files and no prose of its own. Every room config, REQUEST.md, issue body, ingester registration and piece of advice to an operator comes from the deployment's adapters, in its own words.

items.title: What the core does
items.text:
provision.provision_room runs three phases; each also runs on its own (plan_room, admit_room, create_room), which is how a service answers a request before the room exists.

  • Planning works out the room's owner and id, changing nothing.
  • Admission checks that the backend admits the provisioner, then, holding the store, refuses a room whose id anything uses already and files the tracking issue.
  • Creation, holding the store again, checks again, then writes the room's files, creates its uploads area, registers its database, makes it private to its owner, audits the installation's rooms, commits and publishes. Without the store, it then has the backend load the room and resolves the issue.

The guarantees:

  • every refusal comes before anything is created
  • a failure before the commit undoes what this run created, and only that, newest first, then reports on the tracking issue, which stays open
  • after the commit the room stands: a step that fails is reported, with how to finish it, rather than undone

items.title: What your adapters do
items.text:
A provision.Provisioner gathers one adapter for each part of the stack. The interfaces are in soliplex_concierge.provisioner.interfaces:

  • RoomStore: where the room's own files live, and their history
  • DatabaseRegistrar: the room's database, and how it is filled
  • UploadsArea: where the room's documents are uploaded
  • Authz: who may use the room
  • Backend: the Soliplex backend that serves the room
  • IssueTracker (optional): the request's tracking issue

They share these conventions:

  • clashes(request) describes, in the adapter's words, each thing named for the room that exists already. It changes nothing, and may raise to refuse the request outright.
  • A step that creates something returns the Undo that removes it again, or None when it created nothing.
  • A step after the commit (publish, reload_rooms, resolve) returns what remains to do, each a sentence saying how to finish it.
  • RoomStore.locked() raises interfaces.StoreBusy on entering, rather than wait without limit, when another run keeps the store too long (landing_clone.locked raises CloneBusy, which is one). During admission the service answers it with a 503 and a Retry-After; while creating an admitted room, the core tries again after each of the Provisioner's busy_retry_delays (by default 30 and 60 seconds), then gives up, reporting on the tracking issue. Admission waits for the store within the requester's POST /rooms, so keep the wait shorter than the concierge's request_timeout (120 seconds by default).

items.title: The owner and the requester
items.text:
A RoomRequest keeps who asked (requester_claims) apart from whom the room belongs to (owner, a room_ids.RoomOwner). The owner pairs the room id's owner part with its access rule, a soliplex ACL JSONPath over a user's claims:

  • by default, plan_room derives the requester's own owner from one of their claims (Provisioner.owner_claim), with a rule matching that claim's raw value
  • given owner=provisioner.scheme.named_owner(...), it makes someone else the owner, for instance everyone a predicate recognizes; whether the requester may do that is for the caller to decide

Either way, the owner part follows the provisioner's scheme, a room_ids.RoomIdScheme: flattened when its flatten_owner is set (a claimed owner only), lowercased unless its lowercase_owner is false, with any separator replaced and any trailing ., _ or - stripped. Both parts of an id start and end with a letter or digit, and a separator holds neither, so a room id splits into owner and slug one way only; a requested slug containing the separator is refused instead.

To work out a room's id without planning a request, use provisioner.scheme.make_room_id(owner, slug), and provisioner.scheme.parse_room_id(room_id) to split one.

Build a named owner's rule with access_rules, never by hand: claim_rule(claim, value) for one person, or predicate_rule(name) for a predicate the installation registers under meta.jsonpath_functions. A service built with service.create_app does this itself, from the request's owner, and refuses a predicate your Authz.predicates() does not list.

For example, with a provisioner built as in The toolkit and its defaults, a user asking for a room for themselves gives it a title; the slug derives from that, and the owner part from their preferred_username, lowercased:

request = provision.plan_room(
    {"preferred_username": "Alice.Smith"},
    name="Q3 Plans & Budget",
    provisioner=provisioner,
)
request.room          # 'alice.smith--q3-plans-budget'
request.owner         # RoomOwner(owner='alice.smith',
                      #   json_path='$[?$.preferred_username == "Alice.Smith"]')

The access rule matches the raw claim value, Alice.Smith, so the lowercasing never costs Alice her room.

An admin creating a room for a group names its owner, identified by a predicate the installation registers (here is_foreman); the owner part is normalized the same way, and the admin stays the requester:

foremen = provisioner.scheme.named_owner(
    "Foremen", access_rules.predicate_rule("is_foreman")
)
request = provision.plan_room(
    admin_claims,
    name="Quarry Notes",
    provisioner=provisioner,
    owner=foremen,
)
request.room          # 'foremen--quarry-notes'
request.owner         # RoomOwner(owner='foremen',
                      #   json_path='$[?is_foreman($)]')
request.requester_claims is admin_claims   # True

Authz.grant_owner grants the room to request.owner.json_path, whoever that is.

items.title: The toolkit
items.text:
Adapters can build on these modules, which do the mechanical work and leave the wording to you:

  • landing_clone: a git clone of rooms, with its writer's lock, committing a room with its requester as author, and pushing
  • ingester: reading a haiku.rag serve ingester's config and its databases_include fragments, and asking it to reload
  • soliplex_cli: running soliplex-cli (or a CLI offering the same commands) for room policies and audits
  • soliplex_api: reading the signing secret, minting service tokens, and calling the backend's installation API
  • the concierge's own Gitea calls, tools.gitea.create_gitea_issue_sync and gitea_admin, for an issue tracker on Gitea — gitea_admin.label_issue tags one with the named labels a deployment's tracker decides on, among those defined on the repository

The core calls your adapters while it holds the store, so a call that never returns stops every later request. Every blocking call in the toolkit is bounded, by a timeout= defaulting to one in timeouts: CLI_TIMEOUT for a soliplex-cli command, GIT_TIMEOUT for a local git command (its hooks and signing included), PUSH_TIMEOUT for a push, LOCK_TIMEOUT (their sum) for waiting on the clone's lock, and HTTP_TIMEOUT for each socket operation of an HTTP call. When a command runs out of time, it is killed with everything it started, and the module raises soliplex_cli.CliTimedOut (a CliFailed), landing_clone.GitTimedOut or PushTimedOut; a lock that stays taken raises landing_clone.CloneBusy, naming its holder. Pass other values at your call sites, and bound your own adapters' blocking calls the same way.

For example, an uploads area on a local directory:

import dataclasses
import pathlib
import shutil

from soliplex_concierge.provisioner import interfaces


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class LocalUploads:
    root: pathlib.Path

    def clashes(self, request):
        directory = self.root / request.room
        if directory.is_dir() and any(directory.iterdir()):
            return [f"documents already uploaded to {directory}"]
        return []

    def create(self, request):
        directory = self.root / request.room
        if directory.exists():
            return None
        directory.mkdir(parents=True)
        return interfaces.Undo(
            description=f"remove the uploads directory {directory}",
            run=lambda: shutil.rmtree(directory, ignore_errors=True),
        )

With an adapter for each part, provisioning a room is one call:

from soliplex_concierge.provisioner import provision

provisioner = provision.Provisioner(
    store=store,
    registrar=registrar,
    uploads=LocalUploads(pathlib.Path("/uploads/rooms")),
    authz=authz,
    backend=backend,
    tracker=tracker,  # or None
    # scheme=room_ids.RoomIdScheme(separator=":"),  # to change id rules
)
provisioned = provision.provision_room(
    requester_claims, name="Q3 Plans", provisioner=provisioner
)

provisioned.unfinished lists what remains to do once the room is committed; it is empty when the room is fully live.

items.title: Serving it
items.text:
soliplex_concierge.provisioner.service.create_app(provisioner, admission) builds a FastAPI application serving the Provisioner REST API over your adapters. Besides the Provisioner, it takes an interfaces.Admission, which decides who is asking and whether they may:

  • claims(token): the claims of the caller's service token, raising interfaces.InvalidToken (or a subclass) when it is not valid
  • is_admitted(token): whether its holder may request rooms (an admin, or WRITE on __provision__)
  • is_admin(token): whether its holder is an admin, who may name a room's owner and see anyone's requests

The toolkit has the pieces for a soliplex installation: soliplex_api.validate_service_token (its InvalidServiceToken is an InvalidToken), and soliplex_cli.is_admin and soliplex_cli.may, the admin-users check and room-authz check verdicts.

The application's lifespan starts a watcher that calls your Backend.check_access until the backend admits the provisioner; until then, GET /ok answers 503 with the reason. Raise interfaces.AccessRefused (or a subclass, such as soliplex_api.AccessDenied) when the backend refuses the provisioner: the watcher logs it as an error and checks again every service.ACCESS_RETRY seconds. Any other error counts as the backend being unreachable: a warning, checked again every service.BACKEND_RETRY seconds.

items.title: Refusing requests yourself
items.text:
To refuse some requests before the provisioner does any work (a rate limit per requester, a quota of rooms per owner, limits on a name's or a description's length), give the Provisioner a check_request. The service calls it with the requester's claims and the planned RoomRequest, once a request proves well-formed and not already in flight, and before admitting its requester:

def check_request(requester_claims, request):
    if len(request.description) > 500:
        raise provision.RequestRefused(
            400, "the description must be at most 500 characters"
        )
    if limiter.exhausted(request.owner.owner):
        raise provision.RequestRefused(
            429, "too many room requests", retry_after=limiter.wait()
        )


provisioner = provision.Provisioner(..., check_request=check_request)

The service answers a RequestRefused with its status and detail, as a plain error, and with a Retry-After header when it gives retry_after (seconds). The status is yours to choose; the concierge's room tool understands these:

  • 400: the request itself is unacceptable; the user is asked to correct what the detail says
  • 409: the room's name conflicts with something you know of (a reserved name, say); the user is asked for another
  • 429: one too many (a rate limit, or a quota of rooms); the user is told the detail, and when they may ask again

Any other status reads to it as the service failing, and the agent offers to file the request as an issue instead. The check runs for each well-formed request, admitted or not, so keep it cheap. Your own routes to admit_room (a retry, say) should call provision.check_request(provisioner, claims, request) too, so that every route applies the same checks.

Your wiring module builds the adapters, and a factory returns the application:

from soliplex_concierge.provisioner import provision
from soliplex_concierge.provisioner import service


def create_app():
    provisioner = provision.Provisioner(...)  # your adapters
    return service.create_app(provisioner, MyAdmission(...))

uvicorn --factory my_deployment.provisioner:create_app --port 8090

Run one worker: the service keeps its requests' state in memory. A restart loses it, and the tracking issue remains the record. It forgets a finished request a day after it finished (service.REQUEST_TTL); pass create_app(..., request_ttl=...) for another span (seconds), or None to keep every request until the next restart.

The service writes an audit trail to soliplex's soliplex-audit logger, under the scope room-provisioning: each service token it refuses, each request it admits, refuses (denied) or fails on (error, with the cause a requester is not told), each read of a request (by its requester, or by an admin) and each it hides, and how creating each room ended. Each record names the user by their token's claims. Configure that logger as for soliplex itself, and your own adapters' records join the same trail.

items.title: Checking an implementation against the contract
items.text: soliplex_concierge.provisioner.contract checks that an implementation keeps the contract. It drives the implementation's ASGI application in-process and raises ContractViolation, saying what the application answered, when the application breaks the contract.

items.title: Supply a harness
items.text:
A Harness is any object with these attributes:

  • app: the ASGI application, ready to admit requests (its GET /ok answers 200)
  • admitted_token: a valid service token for a requester the application admits, who is not an admin
  • other_token: a valid service token for another such requester, whose rooms get another owner part
  • admin_token: a valid service token for an admin
  • not_admitted_token: a valid service token for a requester the application does not admit
  • occupy(name): make the room that admitted_token's requester would get for a request named name exist already
  • optionally, room_id_separator: the separator in the room ids the application composes (by default room_ids.DEFAULT_SEPARATOR, --)

items.title: Run the checks
items.text:
Await the checks from your implementation's own tests:

import pytest

from soliplex_concierge.provisioner import contract


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_keeps_the_provisioner_contract(harness):
    await contract.check_all(harness)

check_all runs every check in contract.ALL_CHECKS and stops at the first failure. Each check_* function also runs on its own, which helps when you are working on one part of the contract.

Keep these in mind when you write the harness:

  • The checks request rooms with fresh, unique names, so they do not depend on one another. A check that requests a room may leave it created, so point the harness at a disposable stack or fakes.
  • The checks drive the application through httpx2.ASGITransport, which does not run its lifespan: anything the lifespan would start (such as a readiness watcher) must already be in place. For an application from service.create_app, call app.state.access.update(True) in the harness.

items.title: The self-serve concierge
items.text:
The concierge is a single Soliplex room — the about-room (created as about_<project> by default) — that users chat with to request changes to the installation. It answers two kinds of need:

  • Questions about Soliplex — grounded in the soliplex-docs skill (and optionally this installation's own RAG database).
  • Room requests — a new room, or access to an existing private room. A new room is created on the spot for a user the stack's room provisioner admits (see New rooms on request); every other request is filed as a tracking issue for an administrator to resolve.

Filing a request is a collaboration between three actors, all behind the single chat the user sees:

Actor What it is Role Room agent the about-room's chat agent talks to the user, gathers details, files the issue soliplex-concierge-room skill a filesystem skill, run as a sub-agent formats the gathered details into an issue draft create_gitea_issue tool a Python tool bound to the room files the draft on the fixed tracking repository request_room / check_room_request tools Python tools bound to the room ask the stack's room provisioner to create a room, and check on it

items.title: New rooms on request
items.text:
A soliplex-template stack runs a room provisioner service, soliplex-provisioner, which creates a private room for a requester in one step and files its tracking issue itself. For a new room, the room agent first asks for the room's name and purpose, then calls request_room:

  • Accepted (or already requested, when an earlier attempt of the same request reached the provisioner) — the room is being created, private to the user. The agent reports its id and tracking issue, and checks on it with check_room_request when asked: pending, live (refresh the room list), incomplete (an administrator must finish some steps) or failed.
  • Not admitted — the provisioner admits only admins, and users granted WRITE on the reserved room id __provision__. For anyone else, the agent files the request as an issue, as below.
  • For someone else — an admin may ask for a room owned by another person, or by everyone a predicate the installation registers recognizes (a role, say). The agent settles whom with them, as a claim and its exact value (email is bharney@example.com) or a predicate's name, plus the room id's owner part, and asks them to confirm before requesting it; it never writes an access rule itself. Anyone else who names an owner gets owner not permitted, and the agent offers the room as their own, or files the request as an issue naming whom it is for.
  • Failed — a name already taken sends the agent back to the user for another; when the provisioner cannot take the request at all (for example, a stack without the service), the agent files it as an issue.
  • No answer — the tool waits up to request_timeout seconds (120 by default), then asks once more. When the provisioner still does not answer, the room may yet be created, so the agent tells the user to look for it shortly, and files no issue.

The tools act as the user: each call carries a short-lived service token holding the user's claims, signed with the installation's URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET.

items.title: The request flow
items.text:
Every request the provisioner does not take is filed as an issue:

  1. The user asks for a new room or for access to a private one.

  2. The room agent gathers the details with follow-up questions:

  3. New room — proposed name and purpose, the documents or knowledge sources it should draw from, who should have access, and any tools or skills it should provide.

  4. Access request — which room, and why access is needed.

  5. The room agent delegates formatting to the soliplex-concierge-room skill via the execute_skill tool. The skill runs in isolation, so the agent passes it everything it gathered. The skill picks the matching template (new-room or room-access), fills every placeholder — writing *(not provided)* for anything missing so the reviewer knows to follow up — and returns a draft in a fixed shape:

TYPE: <new-room | room-access>
TITLE: <one-line title>

<issue body, in Markdown>

The skill only drafts; it does not file anything itself.

  1. The room agent files the draft by calling create_gitea_issue exactly once, passing the skill's TITLE as title, its body as body, and its TYPE as request_type. The target repository is fixed by the room's tool configuration, so the agent cannot file against an arbitrary repo. The tool:
  2. ensures the request-type label (new-room / room-access) exists, creating it if needed, and tags the issue with it;
  3. attaches the requesting user's profile to the issue as a YAML file (user-profile.yaml by default), so the requester's identity is recorded without the agent transcribing it — see Room access. If Gitea refuses the attachment (e.g. its [attachment] ALLOWED_TYPES lacks .yaml), the profile goes into a comment on the issue instead;

  4. returns the issue number and URL.

  5. The room agent reports the issue number and link back to the user. If the tool returns an error, the agent tells the user plainly that it could not file the request and shows the drafted title and body for manual submission — it never claims to have filed an issue it did not create.

items.title: Things to know
items.text:
• Authentication is required. The tool attributes every request to the signed-in user; an anonymous run is refused (AnonymousUser). Configure an OIDC provider so users are identified.
  • The Gitea account needs Write access. Gitea lets a Read-only account open issues but silently drops their labels; the tool detects the missing label and raises rather than filing an untagged request that would slip past triage (see issue #59). Setup covers the token requirements.
  • The repository is fixed by the room config, not chosen by the agent — the concierge can only file against the tracking repo you configured.

To stand up the about-room in an installation, see Setup.

items.title: Setting up the concierge
items.text:
Adding the concierge to an installation means creating the about-room, wiring in the soliplex-concierge-room and soliplex-docs skills, registering the create_gitea_issue, request_room and check_room_request tools, and declaring the Gitea connection. This page covers:

  • installing it with the soliplex-concierge-installer skill, which does all of this for you on a soliplex-template-generated stack
  • installing it by hand, on any other installation
  • configuring the about-room, however it was installed: what it needs to create rooms on request, bringing an older about-room up to date, and what it answers questions from

Either way you install it, you will need a Gitea repository to file requests against, and an access token whose account has Write access to it — not just Read. Gitea lets a Read-only account open issues but silently drops their labels, so requests would be filed untagged and slip past triage (issue #59). A fine-grained token additionally needs the write:issue and read:repository scopes.

items.title: The installer skill (recommended)
items.text:
Run the soliplex-concierge-installer skill from an external coding agent (e.g. Claude Code). It runs its bundled scripts/install_concierge.py with uv run — a thin shim that provisions soliplex-concierge from its PEP 723 header (so no install step is needed) and delegates to the soliplex_concierge.installer module — applying every change idempotently.

Preview first with --dry-run, then apply:

# dry run — report changes without writing
uv run scripts/install_concierge.py --stack-dir /path/to/stack \
    --owner <gitea-owner> --repo <gitea-repo> --dry-run

# apply, pinning the dependency version
uv run scripts/install_concierge.py --stack-dir /path/to/stack \
    --owner <gitea-owner> --repo <gitea-repo> --version <X.Y>

items.title: What it changes
items.text:
It applies these idempotent edits to the stack:

  • Adds soliplex-concierge to backend/pyproject.toml, and to the list of packages the backend image installs: backend/requirements.txt in a stack built on a soliplex release image, or the backend/Dockerfile uv add block in an older stack (whose Dockerfile ignores the pyproject.toml deps).
  • Merges its entries into backend/environment/installation.yaml: meta.tool_configs (the three tool-config classes), environment, secrets, and room_paths. On a stack with an explicit filesystem skill_configs allow-list, it also adds the two skills there, but only with --confirm-skill-allow-list; otherwise it stops with an error.
  • Copies the about-room into backend/environment/rooms/<room-id>/ (about_<compose-project-name> by default; override with --room-id).
  • Downloads and installs the soliplex-concierge-room and soliplex-docs filesystem skills into backend/environment/skills/.
  • Appends the GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN placeholders to .env — unless the stack ships a local Gitea service (see below), in which case .env is left for that service's own scripts/init_gitea.py to populate.
  • Writes the admin scripts/gitea_issues.py CLI (see Admin).

items.title: Useful flags
items.text:
• --version <X.Y> — pin the dependency added to the stack; omitting it warns about version skew, --version latest opts into the newest release.
  • --room-id — room id to create (default about_<compose-project-name>).
  • --gitea-host / --gitea-token — fill real .env values instead of placeholders.
  • --no-local-gitea — skip local-Gitea auto-detection (see below) and keep the external-Gitea defaults (placeholder .env values and room owner/repo).
  • --with-truststore — install the soliplex-concierge[truststore] extra so the tool verifies TLS against the OS trust store rather than certifi's bundle; use when the Gitea host's certificate chains to an enterprise / internal CA (issue #46).
  • --room-skill-dir / --docs-skill-dir (or --room-skill-version / --docs-skill-version) — install the skills from a local copy or a pinned tag instead of downloading the latest.
  • --force — overwrite an existing room/skill.

Afterwards, set the real Gitea values in .env and rebuild: docker compose build backend && docker compose up -d. Confirm both skills are present under backend/environment/skills/ and that uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py --help works.

items.title: Local Gitea service
items.text:
When the target stack was generated by soliplex-template with include_gitea, its docker-compose.yml defines a gitea service (backed by Postgres) and the stack ships a scripts/init_gitea.py shim that provisions it. The installer detects that service and, instead of emitting dead placeholders:

  • wires the room's create_gitea_issue tool to soliplex-admin/soliplex-requests — the service account and repository init_gitea.py creates, and
  • leaves .env untouched, since init_gitea.py writes GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN itself.

The order is then: run the installer → docker compose up -d → uv run scripts/init_gitea.py (mints the token, creates the repo, populates .env) → docker compose up -d backend to pick up the new .env. Pass --owner / --repo to override the defaults, or --no-local-gitea to opt out of detection entirely (for an external Gitea).

items.title: Manual wiring
items.text:
For a non-generated installation, do the same steps by hand.

  1. Install the package into the environment that runs Soliplex (it depends on soliplex). In a containerized stack, add soliplex-concierge to whatever the backend image installs from — backend/requirements.txt, or the uv add block in an older stack's backend/Dockerfile — and rebuild the image. For an environment managed directly:
# a uv-managed project
uv add soliplex-concierge
# an existing virtual environment
uv pip install soliplex-concierge

For an enterprise / internal CA, install soliplex-concierge[truststore] instead so the tool verifies TLS against the OS trust store (issue #46).

  1. Merge the installation.yaml entries from the bundled installation-snippet.yaml. They:
  2. register the tool-config classes via meta.tool_configs (Soliplex resolves each tool by its dotted tool_name; no core edit is needed),
  3. add the directories of the two filesystem skills the about-room uses (soliplex-concierge-room and soliplex-docs) to filesystem_skills_paths, and enable both under skill_configs, and

  4. declare the GITEA_HOST environment variable and GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN secret the tool reads to call the Gitea REST API (no MCP server or external binary is required).

  5. Copy the about-room template from rooms/about_soliplex/ into your installation's rooms/ directory, editing the owner / repo on the create_gitea_issue tool to point at your tracking repository. (Either may be a literal value or a Soliplex interpolation string such as env:GITEA_OWNER.)

  6. Set the Gitea connection — GITEA_HOST and the GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN secret (see the .env lines at the bottom of the snippet), using a token with Write access as noted above.

items.title: Configuring the about-room
items.text:
The request_room and check_room_request tools (see New rooms on request) need:

  • the address of the stack's room provisioner service: each tool's service_url, which defaults to http://soliplex-provisioner:8090, a soliplex-template stack's service
  • the installation's URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET secret, to sign their requests (a soliplex-template stack declares it)

Whether a user may create rooms is the provisioner's call: it admits admins, and users granted WRITE on the reserved room id __provision__ (the provisioner's docs show how to write that policy).

An about-room installed before these tools existed lacks them: re-run the installer with --force to replace the room (which also replaces any edits made to it), or add the two tool entries from the bundled room_config.yaml and the new prompt.txt by hand.

The about-room answers questions from the bundled soliplex-docs skill, so no RAG database is required. To also answer from this installation's own ingested content, uncomment the skill_configs block in the room's room_config.yaml, pointing rag_lancedb_stem at a database under rag/db/. The soliplex-template skill can generate and ingest one (see the RAG DB docs).

items.title: The audit trail
items.text: The room tools record what they do on a user's behalf to soliplex's soliplex-audit logger, under the scope room-requests, alongside soliplex's own audit records: each service token minted for the user (and for which call), each room requested or checked on, and each Gitea issue filed, with how its profile was recorded. Each record names the user by their claims, less any exclude_claims the create_gitea_issue tool sets, and the room, thread and run it came from.

items.title: exquisite
items.text:
exquisite labels evaluation question sets with the documents that answer them, so that a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system can be scored on retrieval as well as on its answers.

A question set cites its sources the way people do, in prose such as ISO 9001 Sec 4. A RAG database stores documents under URIs such as file:///data/standards/iso-9001-2015.pdf. Something has to connect the two, and has to keep doing so when the database is rebuilt. exquisite does that:

  1. it describes each ingestion of a corpus in a manifest;
  2. it generates a worksheet in which a person who knows the corpus records which documents each citation means;
  3. it binds the question set to one ingestion, writing the documents' current URIs into each question as metadata.relevant_uris;
  4. it checks that a RAG database's searches return those documents.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
• Installation
  • The data repository: how a repository of question sets and corpora is laid out
  • Question sets: what exquisite reads from them
  • Ingestion manifests: describing one ingestion of a corpus
  • Worksheets: recording which documents each citation means
  • Binding: labelling a question set for one ingestion
  • Checking retrieval: searching a database for each question, and checking for its documents
  • Normalization rules: how citations are grouped, and how to extend the rules
  • Development

The name comes from the exquisite corpse, a drawing made by several people, each adding a part without seeing the whole.

items.title: Binding
items.text:
Binding writes a question set out with relevant_uris filled in from one ingestion:

exquisite bind --corpus standards --questions quality-basics > labelled.json
exquisite bind --corpus standards --questions quality-basics --out labelled.json

The labelled set goes to stdout, or to the --out file. Diagnostics always go to stderr, so a redirect yields a usable dataset and a readable report at once. Each case's metadata gains the URIs its documents have in this ingestion:

{
  "uuid": "a1",
  "reference": "ISO 9001 Sec 4",
  "relevant_uris": ["file:///data/standards/iso-9001-2015.pdf"]
}

bind refuses a worksheet that is not finished, listing every problem:

quality-basics.yaml is not ready to bind:
  'ISO 9001': provisional answer not yet confirmed -- check it, then delete its `provisional:` line
  'NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5': documents not filled in

Binding half a worksheet would be indistinguishable from someone having decided those documents do not exist. Each document is found by its sha256, falling back to its source_url:

  • changed: the hash misses but the source_url hits. The file at that location is no longer the one that was approved, so look at it again.
  • unbound: both miss. The document is not in this ingestion.

bind exits with status 1 when a reference has no apply key or a document is unbound. A bound set is never stored: it goes stale as soon as its ingestion is replaced, so produce it when it is wanted.

items.title: Checking retrieval
items.text:
A validated worksheet says which documents answer each question. check-retrieval checks that a RAG database actually returns them: it binds the question set to one ingestion, as bind does, then runs one search per question against a haiku-rag database, and looks for the bound documents among the results.

There is no answering model and no judge, so a run is fast, and its scores are stable from run to run. That's what checking a freshly ingested database needs. It checks documents, not passages: a hit means a chunk of a relevant document came back, not that the chunk holds the answer.

items.title: Running a check
items.text:
exquisite check-retrieval --root data/nist-sp-800 --corpus sp800 \
    --questions sp800 --ingestion sp800 \
    --db sp800.lancedb --config haiku.rag.yaml
  • --db is the database to search: a local path, or a URI haiku-rag accepts. It is opened read-only. A local path with nothing there is refused, never opened, since opening it would create an empty database.
  • --config is the haiku-rag configuration the database was ingested with, so the searches use the same embedder. Any databases it names are set aside in favour of --db, and the command says so.
  • --top-k is how many results each search returns (default 30). It is deliberately more than a chat agent's search limit: a newly ingested document relevant to a question can push a labelled one out of a short list without anything being broken.
  • -v / --verbose shows each question's result, as well as the summary.
  • --out saves the results to a file, to compare a later run against. An existing file is refused, before any searching, unless --force is passed too. Without --out, nothing is written.

Binding problems are reported on stderr, as bind reports them. A worksheet that isn't ready to bind is refused.

items.title: What counts as a hit
items.text:
A question is a hit when any of its bound documents is among the results, and a miss when none is. Each question is scored by retrieval_mrr, the reciprocal rank of its first relevant document: 1.0 at rank 1, 0.5 at rank 2, and 0.0 for a miss. Questions with no bound documents (unresolved, or citing nothing) are ineligible: counted, not checked.

Results are matched to the manifest the way bind matches documents: by the sha256 the database records for each document, then its source_url, and only failing both by URI. So a database whose documents sit at different paths from the manifest's is still checked correctly.

20/20 questions passed;  mean retrieval_mrr 0.975

With --verbose, each question gets a line first, in question-set order: the rank of its first relevant document, its retrieval_mrr, and the question. Below a question not at rank 1 are the documents that came ahead of it. Below a miss are the first few that came back instead:

rank  mrr    question
   1  1.000  What are the steps of a risk assessment?
   ...
   2  0.500  What levels of potential impact are used to categorize information and systems?
             after: NIST.SP.800-53r4.pdf
   ...
20/20 questions passed;  mean retrieval_mrr 0.975

Documents are shown by name; the results file has their full URIs.

items.title: Comparing with an earlier run
items.text:
--compare names the results of an earlier run. Against it, a question fails when it loses: the earlier run hit, and this one misses. The rest is reported, but never fails:

  • RANK: the first relevant document ranks lower than before. The embedder and reranker can reorder near-tied results between two runs on the same database.
  • DROPPED: a relevant document dropped out while another still hits.
  • the mean retrieval_mrr over the questions both runs scored fell by more than --mrr-tolerance (default 0.02).

A question the earlier run doesn't have is checked for a miss instead.

The earlier run is refused, before any searching, when its searches differ by design: a different configured embedder, reranker or top K, or a database stored with a different embedder. So is one that asked a different question under some case's key, the question's metadata.uuid. Different versions of exquisite or haiku-rag only warn: a check across an upgrade is meant to span them.

Any run saved with --out can be a reference, including one that failed: read its report, then compare the next run against it.

items.title: Exit status
items.text:
check-retrieval exits with status 0 when every eligible question passes. It exits with status 1 when:

  • a question misses, or loses against --compare;
  • no question is eligible;
  • the worksheet isn't ready to bind;
  • the database is missing, or haiku-rag won't search it as it stands (it needs migrating to the installed haiku-rag, say);
  • the --compare file isn't a results file, or is refused;
  • the --out file exists, and --force wasn't passed.

items.title: The results file
items.text:
With --out, a run that searches saves its results, whatever its outcome:

{
  "format": "exquisite check-retrieval 1",
  "question_set": "questions/sp800.yaml",
  "corpus": "sp800",
  "ingestion": "sp800",
  "settings": {
    "embedder": "vllm:nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-vl-1b-v2 (dim 2048)",
    "reranker": null,
    "top_k": 30,
    "config_hash": "5f8a9bfe…"
  },
  "database": {
    "location": "sp800.lancedb",
    "embedder": "vllm:nvidia/llama-nemotron-embed-vl-1b-v2 (dim 2048)",
    "documents": 8,
    "chunks": 5502,
    "written_at": "2026-10-03T01:54:08.941536",
    "version": "0.89.0"
  },
  "substrate": {"exquisite": "0.2", "haiku-rag-slim": "0.89.0"},
  "started": "2026-10-03T08:58:41",
  "finished": "2026-10-03T08:58:45",
  "cases": [
    {
      "key": "33e57977-…",
      "question": "What levels of potential impact are used to categorize information and systems?",
      "relevant": ["file:///data/nist-sp-800/nistspecialpublication800-60v1r1.pdf"],
      "retrieved": [
        "file:///data/nist-sp-800/NIST.SP.800-53r4.pdf",
        "file:///data/nist-sp-800/nistspecialpublication800-60v1r1.pdf"
      ],
      "score": 0.5
    }
  ]
}
  • settings: how the searches were made. config_hash is a SHA-256 of the whole haiku-rag configuration.
  • database: what the database held: the embedder it was stored with, its size, when it was last written, and its haiku-rag version.
  • substrate: the installed versions of exquisite and haiku-rag.
  • cases: one per question. retrieved lists one entry per distinct document, in rank order: its manifest URI when the manifest holds it, else the database's own. score is null for an ineligible question.

It is the file --compare reads.

items.title: The data repository
items.text:
exquisite is installed separately from the data it manages. It works on a data repository: a directory, usually under version control, laid out like this:

exquisite.yaml                     normalization rules (optional)
questions/
  quality-basics.yaml              a question set
  quality-basics_pruned.yaml       a subset of it
corpus/
  standards/                       one corpus
    ingestion/
      standards.csv                one ingestion's documents
      standards.yaml               what that ingestion is
    worksheet/
      quality-basics.yaml          which documents the set cites

Every command takes --root; without it, the root is $EXQUISITE_ROOT, or else the working directory. A root lacking questions/ or corpus/ is refused.

A few rules shape the layout:

  • A question set belongs to no corpus. Two databases built from different documents can be scored with the same questions, so a set lives once, under questions/.
  • A corpus directory is named for its documents, not for a database. Re-ingesting the same documents under a new database name adds a manifest to ingestion/, rather than starting a new directory.
  • A worksheet's existence declares the pairing. Nothing derives that a question set should be scored against a corpus; someone decided it, and creating the worksheet records the decision.

items.title: Development
items.text:
uv sync --group dev
uv run pytest            # unit tests, with a 100% branch-coverage gate
uv run ruff check
uv run ruff format --check
uv run pre-commit install    # optional:  run the same checks on commit
uv run --group docs zensical serve    # preview these docs locally

The coverage gate applies to every pytest run, so pass --no-cov when running a subset, e.g. uv run pytest --no-cov tests/unit/test_rules.py.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
exquisite needs Python 3.13 or later. Install the command with uv:

uv tool install exquisite

or with pip install exquisite.

exquisite --help lists the commands; exquisite <command> --help describes each one.

items.title: Ingestion manifests
items.text: A manifest describes one ingestion of one corpus, as two files sharing a stem: a CSV listing its documents, and a YAML sidecar describing the ingestion as a whole.

items.title: The CSV
items.text:
One row per document, with every field quoted, so that an empty column reads as "" rather than being inferred from delimiters:

"uri","sha256","source_url","document_identifier","identifier_source","identifier_certainty"
"file:///data/standards/iso-9001-2015.pdf","3f1c…","https://example.org/iso-9001-2015.pdf","ISO 9001","llm","5"
"file:///data/standards/sp800-53r5.pdf","9a2e…","","NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5","llm","3"
Column Meaning uri Where this ingestion stored the document. sha256 The document's content hash. source_url Where the document was fetched from. document_identifier The publication's designator, e.g. ISO 9001. identifier_source llm (inferred at ingestion), override (mapped by hand), unrecorded, or empty when there is no identifier. identifier_certainty The inference's 0–5 score, for llm identifiers: 5 means the identifier appears verbatim in the text.

uri is the only column that is not durable: re-ingesting under a different source root rewrites every URI. sha256 and source_url survive that, so worksheets record those instead. Neither is always populated, but every document needs at least one of them.

An identifier is trusted when its source is override, or llm with a certainty of 4 or 5. Only trusted identifiers produce provisional answers and cross-references between worksheet groups. An unrecorded identifier is shown and matched, but not trusted.

items.title: The sidecar
items.text:
database: standards
database_path: /lancedb/standards.lancedb
extracted_at: 2026-10-02T12:00:00+00:00
documents: 3
chunks: 4210
substrate:
  embeddings: {provider: ollama, name: example-embedder, vector_dim: 1024}
  processing: {chunk_size: 256, converter: docling}
  • database names the database; when absent, the manifest's stem is used.
  • documents, when present, must equal the CSV's row count, or the manifest is refused: a truncated extraction would otherwise look exactly like a corpus that shrank.
  • substrate records how the corpus was ingested: the embedding model and the chunking. It matters as much as the document list, since the same documents ingested with a different embedder or chunk size make a different database. Worksheets record a digest of it.

The other keys are for people reading the file.

items.title: Producing a manifest
items.text:
Build the CSV from each document's URI and metadata, as the RAG database stores them. exquisite.manifest.from_metadata applies the provenance rule for the identifier columns, so every extraction applies it the same way:

import json
import pathlib

from exquisite import manifest

# One {"uri": ..., "metadata": {...}} object per line, dumped from wherever
# the database is reachable.
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in open("standards.jsonl")]
manifest.write(
    pathlib.Path("corpus/standards/ingestion/standards.csv"),
    [manifest.from_metadata(row["uri"], row["metadata"]) for row in rows],
)

Write the sidecar alongside it, from the database's own settings and row counts.

items.title: Question sets
items.text:
A question set is a pydantic-evals dataset, stored under questions/ as YAML (<name>.yaml) or JSON (<name>.json). Should both exist for one name, the YAML file is used. exquisite reads two keys from each case's metadata:

cases:
- inputs: What does clause 4 of ISO 9001 cover?
  expected_output: Context of the organization
  metadata:
    uuid: a1
    reference: ISO 9001 Sec 4

Every case must have metadata: without it there is nothing to tie the question to a worksheet, so a set holding such a case is refused when it is loaded.

  • reference is the source citation as written. exquisite never modifies it: it is the provenance, and what a worksheet is regenerated from when a corpus is rebuilt. A reference may also be a document URI, for a set whose author picked the files directly (see references that are already URIs).
  • uuid identifies the case. A pruned set, whose name ends in _pruned, is a subset of the set it is named for. It needs no worksheet of its own: binding labels it from its parent's worksheet, matching cases by uuid.

The question set itself is never written to. Binding produces a labelled copy on demand (see Binding).

items.title: Normalization rules
items.text:
Question sets cite documents in prose (ISO 9001 Sec 4.2), and the same publication is spelled many ways. exquisite reduces each citation to a designator (ISO 9001) and groups designators by a collapsed key (iso9001), so spelling variants of one document land together.

The built-in rules cover only conventions that hold across publishers:

  • dashes of every kind read as -;
  • Vol 3 / Volume 3 read as v3;
  • Supplement / Suppl / Sup read as supp;
  • the location half of a citation begins at a comma, semicolon, or a word such as Sec, Chapter, Para, Page, Table or Figure;
  • an empty reference, or [To Be Filled Out], is no reference at all.

A corpus following a publisher's own scheme adds its own rules in an exquisite.yaml at the root of the data repository, beside questions/ and corpus/. Pass --rules PATH to use another file. With no file, only the built-ins apply.

designators:
  # Regex -> replacement, applied in order to the lower-cased designator,
  # before the built-in folding.  Here:  "Std. 12" and "12" are one key.
  rewrite:
    - {pattern: '^\s*std\.?\s+', replace: ''}
    - {pattern: '\baddendum\b', replace: 'supplement'}
  # A series renamed over time:  the canonical name, then its aliases.
  # Filenames beginning with an alias are searched as the canonical series.
  series:
    handbook: [manual, guide]
  # Extra words that begin the location half of a citation.
  location_words: [clause, annex]
references:
  # Extra values that stand where a reference belongs but are none,
  # compared exactly (after trimming whitespace), like the built-in one.
  placeholders: ["TBD", "n/a", "N/A"]
# Extra kinds of extension.  Each pattern is matched against what a
