Each revision is listed as its id followed by the message naming the release it belongs to (e.g. a1c7d3e90b42 soliplex-v0.80).

A database which cannot be migrated as it stands is reported as a single ERROR: line in place of its revision lists.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — every database in scope could be migrated as it stands, whatever is pending.
  • 1 — at least one could not: it did not open, it holds tables with no alembic_version row (see #1367), or it is stamped at a revision this release does not have, which means the code was rolled back without downgrading its databases first.

items.title: database upgrade
items.text:
Migrate the databases forward.

soliplex-cli database upgrade [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Options
items.text:
• -d NAME / --database NAME — limit the run to one database. Both move by default.
  • -r REV / --revision REV — the revision to migrate to; head by default. With --sql, Alembic's <from>:<to> range form is accepted too.
  • --sql — write the SQL to <database>.sql in the current directory instead of running it, for a deployment whose DDL somebody else applies. Each file covers that database's own pending range, read from its stamp, so the output is the delta rather than a replay from base. Passing an explicit <from>:<to> range skips reading the stamp, which is the only form that works when the databases cannot be reached from wherever the command runs.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• All or nothing. Both databases move in one Alembic run, committing together, and the whole run is refused if any target cannot be moved: its policy is disabled, it did not open, it is unstamped, or it is stamped by a newer release. --database narrows the run, which is what a configuration giving the two databases different policies needs.
  • Refusals are messages, not tracebacks. A revision name the tree does not have, a database that will not open, a role the database refuses the DDL to: each is reported under a Cannot upgrade rule.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — every database in scope reached the requested revision, or its SQL was written.
  • 1 — the run was refused, or Alembic failed.

items.title: database downgrade
items.text:
Migrate the databases back to an explicit revision. For the deployment whose code is about to be rolled back: downgrade first, from the version which still has these revisions, with every writer stopped.

soliplex-cli database downgrade [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH REVISION

items.title: Positional Arguments
items.text:
• INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — as above.
  • REVISION — the revision to migrate back to. Required: there is no sensible default for going backwards.

items.title: Options
items.text: -d / --database and --sql, both as for database upgrade. There is no --revision: the revision is the positional argument above, and under --sql it accepts the same <from>:<to> range form -- which is what lets a rollback be planned from somewhere that cannot reach the databases.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text: As for database upgrade, with refusals reported under a Cannot downgrade rule.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
See what an upgrade would do, without doing it:

soliplex-cli database status /environment

Migrate both databases to the revision this release expects:

soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment

Migrate only the authorization database, where the two stanzas configure different policies:

soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment --database authz

Hand the DDL to somebody else instead of applying it:

soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment --sql

Do the same where the databases cannot be reached from here, naming the revision they stand at:

soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment --sql --revision 63edaa5987f6:head

Roll back to a previous release's head before rolling back the code:

soliplex-cli database downgrade /environment 63edaa5987f6

items.title: admin-users
items.text:
The admin-users group manages the installation's admin-user table. Each admin entry is an RFC 9535 JSONPath query stored in the installation's authorization database; a user whose OIDC token matches any admin entry's query is granted administrator privileges by the Soliplex authorization policy engine. The common case — an admin keyed by email — is stored as $[?$.email == "..."], mirroring how room-authz ACL entries store their discriminators. The subcommands below read from and modify that table directly, and check a user against it.

This group replaces the flat list-admin-users / add-admin-user / clear-admin-users commands; see Renamed Commands.

These subcommands only make sense against a persistent authorization database (configured via authorization_db in the installation YAML). When the installation uses the default in-memory SQLite DB (sqlite://), each command detects the RAM-based URI, prints a note that the operation would be a no-op, and exits with status 1 without touching the database. There is no override.

All seven commands share the following conventions (except where check notes otherwise):

  • Positional argument INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.
  • On completion, the current admin-user list is dumped as a single JSON object on stdout (emitted via plain print(...), not Rich, so the output pipes cleanly into jq or other tooling). Email-keyed admins surface as their email; an admin added with a non-email --json-path query surfaces as the raw query string:
{"admin_users": ["alice@example.com", "$[?$.role == \"admin\"]"]}
  • The -v / --verbose and -q / --quiet flags at the group level (soliplex-cli admin-users -v <subcommand> …) toggle between the default JSON dump and a human-focused, Rich-rendered summary. Resolution: --quiet always forces JSON; --verbose (without --quiet) forces the human summary; with neither, the per-deployment default applies (currently JSON, set via _DEFAULT_VERBOSE in cli/admin_users.py). --quiet is intended as the override for scripts in a deployment that has flipped the default to verbose. Example verbose output:
─── Admin users ───
Admin users (2):
  1. alice@example.com
  2. bob@example.com

  • The group-level --cli-log-config PATH option (also read from the SOLIPLEX_CLI_LOG_CONFIG environment variable) enables CLI audit logging by applying the named Python logging-config YAML; without it, the audit records these commands emit are suppressed so they don't intermingle with the JSON / human output. See CLI Audit Logging.

  • Exit status is 0 on success, or 1 when the RAM-DB guard fires or any per-command precondition fails: for admin-users add, when the discriminator selection is invalid or the resolved entry is already an admin; for admin-users delete, when the discriminator selection is invalid or no admin matches the resolved query; for admin-users from-yaml, when an entry fails its discriminator check.

items.title: admin-users list
items.text:
Dump the current set of admin users from the installation's authorization database without changing anything.

soliplex-cli admin-users list [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Examples
items.text:
List admin users for a full installation:

soliplex-cli admin-users list example/installation.yaml

Extract just the emails with jq:

soliplex-cli admin-users list example/installation.yaml \
  | jq -r '.admin_users[]'

items.title: admin-users check
items.text:
Check whether the user identified by a service token is an admin user: that is, whether any admin entry's query matches the token's claims. Nothing in the authorization database is changed.

soliplex-cli admin-users check [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Options
items.text: • -i PATH / --input PATH — file from which the token is read. If omitted, or -, the token is read from stdin. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored.

items.title: Output
items.text:
Instead of the admin-user list, the command prints the outcome of the check as a single JSON object on stdout:

{"sub": "ops", "is_admin": true}

With the group-level --verbose flag, it prints a human-focused summary instead, e.g.:

─── Admin user ───
Subject: ops

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• The token is validated first, as by service-token validate: the command exits with status 1, printing the reason on stderr and nothing on stdout, if the token's signature does not verify, it holds no exp, or it has expired, or if URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source.
  • The check is not audited. Unlike the server's checks at the point of a privileged operation, it emits no admin-access audit record.
  • A stale admin entry never matches. If an admin entry's stored json_path no longer compiles (e.g., it references a meta-config filter function that is no longer registered), the check skips it, as the server does, logging a warning on the soliplex.authz logger. Find such entries with audit admin-users, and remove them with admin-users delete --allow-invalid-json-path. With --verbose, a "not an admin user" result suggests running the audit.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — the token's user is an admin user.
  • 1 — the token's user is not an admin user, the token is not valid, URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source, or the RAM-DB guard fires.
  • 2 — a usage error, e.g. the input file does not exist.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Check that a token kept in a file belongs to an admin user:

soliplex-cli admin-users check example/installation.yaml \
  --input ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token

Gate a script on admin access, using a freshly-minted token:

soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --claims '{"email": "alice@example.com"}' --expires-in 5m --quiet |
  soliplex-cli admin-users check example/installation.yaml > /dev/null &&
  echo "alice is an admin user"

items.title: admin-users add
items.text:
Insert a new admin entry into the installation's authorization database and then dump the resulting list.

soliplex-cli admin-users add [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH [EMAIL]

Exactly one discriminator must be supplied, naming which user token(s) the entry grants admin to: the positional EMAIL (shorthand for the common case), --preferred-username USERNAME, or --json-path QUERY. Each is stored as an RFC 9535 JSONPath query — EMAIL and --preferred-username as $[?$.email == "..."] / $[?$.preferred_username == "..."], and --json-path verbatim (after validation). check_admin_access admits a user when their token matches any stored query, so --json-path can grant admin by an arbitrary claim (e.g. group membership).

items.title: Positional Arguments
items.text:
• INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — as described above.
  • EMAIL — optional; the email address to grant admin privileges, matched against the authenticated user's OIDC-asserted email claim. No format validation is performed by the CLI. Mutually exclusive with --preferred-username and --json-path.

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --preferred-username USERNAME — grant admin by OIDC preferred_username claim. Mutually exclusive with EMAIL and --json-path.
  • --json-path QUERY — grant admin to any user token matched by this RFC 9535 JSONPath query. The query is validated against the currently-loaded JSONPath environment (so meta-config-registered filter functions are usable); a malformed query is reported and the command exits non-zero. Mutually exclusive with EMAIL and --preferred-username.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Exactly one discriminator. Supplying none — or more than one — of EMAIL / --preferred-username / --json-path is reported and the command exits with status 1 without touching the table.
  • Rejects duplicates. Before inserting, the command checks whether the resolved query is already an admin. If it is, the command prints a note and exits with status 1 without touching the table — the AdminUser.json_path column is unique, so a blind second insert would otherwise fail with a backend-specific IntegrityError. Re-adding an already-present admin is thus a safe, non-destructive no-op, signalled by the non-zero exit code; run admin-users list to see the current set.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Grant admin privileges to a new operator by email:

soliplex-cli admin-users add example/installation.yaml alice@example.com

Grant admin by preferred_username, or by an arbitrary claim:

soliplex-cli admin-users add example/installation.yaml \
  --preferred-username alice
soliplex-cli admin-users add example/installation.yaml \
  --json-path '$[?$.groups[?@ == "admins"]]'

items.title: admin-users delete
items.text:
Remove a single admin entry from the installation's authorization database and then dump the resulting list. The entry is identified by the same parameter shape as admin-users add: exactly one of the positional EMAIL, --preferred-username, or --json-path discriminator. The match is by string equality against the stored AdminUser.json_path, so the same discriminator that inserted the entry will remove it.

soliplex-cli admin-users delete [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH [EMAIL]

items.title: Positional Arguments
items.text:
• INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — as described above.
  • EMAIL — optional; the email address to revoke admin from. Mutually exclusive with --preferred-username and --json-path.

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --preferred-username USERNAME — revoke admin by OIDC preferred_username claim. Mutually exclusive with EMAIL and --json-path.
  • --json-path QUERY — revoke admin from any user token matched by this RFC 9535 JSONPath query. By default the query is validated against the currently-loaded JSONPath environment; pass --allow-invalid-json-path to skip that check. Mutually exclusive with EMAIL and --preferred-username.
  • --allow-invalid-json-path — skip JSONPath compile-validation of --json-path so a stored entry whose json_path no longer compiles (e.g. because the meta-config filter function it referenced has been removed) can still be matched and removed. Use the value reported by audit admin-users verbatim.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Exactly one discriminator. Same rule as admin-users add: supplying none — or more than one — is reported and the command exits with status 1 without touching the table.
  • No match is an error. If no admin row matches the resolved query, the command prints <descriptor> is not an admin and exits with status 1 so the operator can tell that the delete was a no-op.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Revoke admin from a single user by email:

soliplex-cli admin-users delete example/installation.yaml alice@example.com

Remove a stale entry reported by audit admin-users:

soliplex-cli admin-users delete \
  --json-path '$[?stale_filter_func($.email)]' \
  --allow-invalid-json-path \
  example/installation.yaml

items.title: admin-users clear
items.text:
Remove every row from the installation's admin-user table, then dump the (now empty) list.

soliplex-cli admin-users clear [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Destructive. This command is unconditional: there is no per-email filter, no confirmation prompt, and no backup is taken. Use admin-users delete to remove a single admin without wiping the rest, or admin-users from-yaml to replace the entire admin set atomically.
  • Follow-up required. After clearing, no user is an admin. If the installation relies on admin privileges for its bootstrap flow (e.g. to configure rooms or seed authorization), re-run admin-users add before restarting serve.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Drop all admins from a production-style installation:

soliplex-cli admin-users clear example/installation.yaml

Wipe-and-seed — start from a known state, then add a single admin:

soliplex-cli admin-users clear example/installation.yaml
soliplex-cli admin-users add example/installation.yaml alice@example.com

items.title: admin-users as-yaml
items.text:
Dump every admin user as a YAML document. This is the YAML counterpart of list (which emits JSON), and the inverse of from-yaml.

soliplex-cli admin-users as-yaml [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Options
items.text: • --output, -o PATH — write the YAML to this file path. If omitted, the YAML is written to standard output with no console or rule decoration, so it is safe to pipe or redirect.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Structured per-entry shape. Each admin row dumps as a dict with three discriminator slots (preferred_username, email, json_path); exactly one is non-null. An admin stored as the canonical $[?$.email == "..."] / $[?$.preferred_username == "..."] query is surfaced back under email / preferred_username; any other query is surfaced under json_path.
  • Empty table is empty list. An installation with no admin rows dumps as admin_users: [].
  • Invalid json_path entries are tolerated. A row whose stored query no longer compiles (e.g. it references a meta-config filter function that's no longer registered) is still emitted verbatim under json_path. The dump never raises.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Dump the admin set to standard output:

soliplex-cli admin-users as-yaml example/installation.yaml

Save the admin set to a file (e.g. to back it up or edit it):

soliplex-cli admin-users as-yaml \
  --output admins.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml

items.title: admin-users from-yaml
items.text:
Replace every admin entry with the rows in a YAML document. The YAML uses the same shape produced by as-yaml, so the two commands round-trip.

soliplex-cli admin-users from-yaml [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Options
items.text: • --input, -i PATH — read the YAML from this file path. If omitted, the YAML is read from standard input.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Whole-table replace. All existing admin rows are deleted; the rows in the YAML (if any) are then inserted.
  • null (or empty list) removes every admin. Importing a null document, an empty admin_users: [], or a document with no admin_users key truncates the table.
  • Per-entry discriminator check. Each entry must specify exactly one of email, preferred_username, or json_path; a malformed entry is reported and the command exits with status 1 without touching the table.
  • Stored json_path validity is enforced on insert. The storage layer's @validates hook rejects a json_path that no longer compiles against the currently-loaded JSONPath environment. To re-import a YAML that includes such a query, ensure the meta-config that registered its filter functions is in place first.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Round-trip the admin set through a file (export, then re-import):

soliplex-cli admin-users as-yaml \
  --output admins.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml
soliplex-cli admin-users from-yaml \
  --input admins.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml

Copy the admin set from one installation onto another:

soliplex-cli admin-users as-yaml example/installation.yaml \
  | soliplex-cli admin-users from-yaml staging/installation.yaml

Wipe every admin via an empty document:

echo 'admin_users: []' \
  | soliplex-cli admin-users from-yaml example/installation.yaml

items.title: room-authz
items.text:
The room-authz group manages per-room authorization policies. Room- level authorization lets the installation restrict which users can see and interact with a given room, on top of the admin-user mechanism described above. The subcommands below read from and modify the per-room authorization policy stored in the installation's authorization database.

This group replaces the flat show-room-authz command; see Renamed Commands.

items.title: The Model in One Paragraph
items.text:
Each room's authorization is captured by a RoomPolicy row plus zero or more ACLEntry rows attached to it. A RoomPolicy has a default_allow_deny flag (default: DENY) which governs read access. An ACLEntry has an allow_deny flag plus a discriminator — one of everyone, authenticated, preferred_username, email, or a free-form json_path — used to decide whether it matches the caller's token, plus a permission flag (read, write, or admin) scoping the entry to that permission. (The preferred_username and email discriminators are stored as equivalent json_path queries; the row layout has just everyone, authenticated, and json_path underneath.)

The first matching entry — scoped to the queried permission — wins. If no entry scoped to that permission matches, read access falls back to default_allow_deny, while write and admin access fall back to DENY: only an entry explicitly scoped to write or admin can grant it.

The critical distinction to keep in mind is between no policy row and an empty policy row:

  • A room with no RoomPolicy row at all is treated as public for read: every authenticated user is allowed in, but write and admin operations remain denied unless explicitly granted. This is the default state of every room on a fresh authz database.
  • A room with a RoomPolicy row and no matching ACL entries falls through for reads to default_allow_deny, which defaults to DENY — making the room effectively private. Write and admin access are denied unless an entry scoped to them grants it.

The nine commands below create, inspect, edit, and populate these rows, and check a user's access against them.

items.title: Shared Conventions
items.text:
All nine commands share the following (except where check notes otherwise):

  • Positional argument INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — as documented in the admin-users section. If omitted, falls back to SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH.
  • Positional argument ROOM_ID — the id of a configured room (the same identifier surfaced by audit rooms). The commands validate that ROOM_ID matches a room in the installation YAML; an unknown id prints an error (with the list of configured rooms, when any are defined) and exits with status 1 without touching the authorization database. The read-only show command supports an --allow-stale escape hatch for inspecting policies left behind by removed or renamed rooms; the other commands do not, so cleanup of stale rows still requires direct database tooling.
  • As with admin-users, when the installation's authorization_db is the in-memory default (sqlite://), each command detects the RAM-based URI, prints a note that the operation would be a no-op, and exits with status 1 without touching the database. There is no override.
  • On completion, the resulting RoomPolicy is dumped as a single JSON object on stdout (emitted via plain print(...), not Rich). If no policy row exists for the room, null is printed instead.

Example output:

{
  "room_id": "chat",
  "default_allow_deny": "DENY",
  "acl_entries": [
    {
      "allow_deny": "ALLOW",
      "permission": "READ",
      "everyone": false,
      "authenticated": false,
      "preferred_username": null,
      "email": "alice@example.com",
      "json_path": null
    }
  ]
}
  • The -v / --verbose and -q / --quiet flags at the group level (soliplex-cli room-authz -v <subcommand> …) toggle between the default JSON dump and a human-focused, Rich-rendered summary. Resolution: --quiet always forces JSON; --verbose (without --quiet) forces the human summary; with neither, the per-deployment default applies (currently JSON, set via _DEFAULT_VERBOSE in cli/room_authz.py). --quiet is intended as the override for scripts in a deployment that has flipped the default to verbose. Example verbose output:
─── Room policy: chat ───
Default: DENY READ (private -- denies callers that don't match an
ALLOW READ entry).
ACL entries (2):
  1. ALLOW READ  email=alice@example.com
  2. DENY READ   everyone

  • The group-level --cli-log-config PATH option (also read from the SOLIPLEX_CLI_LOG_CONFIG environment variable) enables CLI audit logging by applying the named Python logging-config YAML; without it, the audit records these commands emit are suppressed so they don't intermingle with the JSON / human output. See CLI Audit Logging.

  • Exit status is 0 on success (including when no policy row exists for the room), or 1 when the RAM-DB guard fires or ROOM_ID doesn't match a configured room.

items.title: room-authz show
items.text:
Dump the current RoomPolicy for a single room without changing it.

soliplex-cli room-authz show [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text: • --allow-stale — skip the configured-room check that the rest of the room-authz commands enforce. show will dump whatever policy row (if any) exists in the authorization database for the given ROOM_ID, even when the id isn't present in the installation's current YAML. Useful for inspecting stale policies left behind by a room rename or removal.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Inspect the policy for the chat room:

soliplex-cli room-authz show example/installation.yaml chat

Extract just the list of allowed emails with jq:

soliplex-cli room-authz show example/installation.yaml chat \
  | jq -r '.acl_entries[] | select(.allow_deny == "ALLOW") | .email'

A null response means no RoomPolicy row exists yet — i.e. the room is in its default public (for read) state, with writes and admin operations denied unless explicitly granted:

$ soliplex-cli room-authz show example/installation.yaml search
null

Entries whose stored json_path no longer compiles (e.g. it references a meta-config filter function that's no longer registered) are still dumped — the value comes back under json_path verbatim, so the dump itself never raises. Use audit room-authz to surface such entries, and delete-acl-entry --allow-invalid-json-path to remove them.

Inspect a stale policy for a room that has since been removed from the YAML — without --allow-stale this would exit with status 1:

soliplex-cli room-authz show --allow-stale \
  example/installation.yaml old-room-id

items.title: room-authz check
items.text:
Check whether the user identified by a service token has a permission on a room, as the room's policy decides it. Nothing in the authorization database is changed.

soliplex-cli room-authz check [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --permission PERMISSION — required. The permission to check: one of read, write, or admin.
  • -i PATH / --input PATH — file from which the token is read. If omitted, or -, the token is read from stdin. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored.

items.title: Output
items.text:
Instead of the room's policy, the command prints the outcome of the check as a single JSON object on stdout:

{"room_id": "chat", "permission": "write", "sub": "ops", "allowed": false}

With the group-level --verbose flag, it prints a human-focused summary instead, e.g.:

─── Denied: WRITE on chat ───
Subject: ops

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• The token is validated first, as by service-token validate: the command exits with status 1, printing the reason on stderr and nothing on stdout, if the token's signature does not verify, it holds no exp, or it has expired, or if URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source.
  • The check is the room policy's alone. It answers as the server's room-access checks do (see the model), without regard to whether the user is an admin user: some server operations (e.g., file uploads) also allow admin users write access to every room.
  • The check is not audited. Unlike the server's checks at the point of a gated operation, it emits no room-access audit record.
  • A stale ACL entry can only deny. If one of the room's ACL entries has a stored json_path which no longer compiles (e.g., it references a meta-config filter function that is no longer registered), the check treats it as the server does: a deny entry matches every token, and an allow entry matches none, logging a warning on the soliplex.authz logger. Find such entries with audit room-authz, and remove them with room-authz delete-acl-entry --allow-invalid-json-path. With --verbose, a "denied" result suggests running the audit.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — the room's policy allows the permission.
  • 1 — the room's policy denies the permission, the token is not valid, URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source, ROOM_ID doesn't match a configured room, or the RAM-DB guard fires.
  • 2 — a usage error, e.g. --permission is missing or not one of read, write, or admin, or the input file does not exist.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Check that a token kept in a file grants write access to the chat room:

soliplex-cli room-authz check example/installation.yaml chat \
  --permission write --input ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token

Gate a script on read access, using a freshly-minted token:

soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --claims '{"email": "alice@example.com"}' --expires-in 5m --quiet |
  soliplex-cli room-authz check example/installation.yaml chat \
    --permission read > /dev/null &&
  echo "alice may read chat"

items.title: room-authz as-yaml
items.text:
Dump a room's RoomPolicy and ACL entries as YAML. This is the YAML counterpart of show (which emits JSON), and the inverse of from-yaml.

soliplex-cli room-authz as-yaml [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --output, -o PATH — write the YAML to this file path. If omitted, the YAML is written to standard output with no console or rule decoration, so it is safe to pipe or redirect.
  • --allow-stale — skip the configured-room check, so a policy left behind by a removed or renamed room can still be dumped (same semantics as show).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Per-entry shape mirrors ACLEntry. Each entry dumps with the same fields as the public ACLEntry model, including the entry's permission scope (READ / WRITE / ADMIN): an entry stored as a preferred_username or email query is surfaced back under preferred_username / email (with json_path: null), and a general-purpose query is surfaced under json_path. The document re-loads cleanly via from-yaml.
  • No policy dumps as null. A room with no RoomPolicy row dumps as a null document.
  • Invalid json_path entries are tolerated. The YAML is built directly from the stored rows rather than via the pydantic model, so an entry whose query no longer compiles (e.g. it references a meta-config filter function that's no longer registered) is still emitted verbatim under json_path. The dump never raises. Such an entry will not survive a from-yaml re-import unless the meta-config that registered its filter functions is in place — the storage layer's @validates hook rejects it on insert.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success.
  • 1 when the ROOM_ID is not configured and --allow-stale was not passed, or when the RAM-DB guard fires.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Dump the chat policy to standard output:

soliplex-cli room-authz as-yaml example/installation.yaml chat

Save a policy to a file (e.g. to back it up or edit it):

soliplex-cli room-authz as-yaml \
  --output chat-policy.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: room-authz from-yaml
items.text:
Load a room's RoomPolicy and ACL entries from YAML, replacing any existing policy for the target room. The YAML uses the same shape produced by as-yaml, so the two commands round-trip.

soliplex-cli room-authz from-yaml [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH [ROOM_ID]

items.title: Arguments
items.text: • ROOM_ID (optional) — the target room. If omitted, the room_id recorded in the input YAML is used.

items.title: Options
items.text: • --input, -i PATH — read the YAML from this file path. If omitted, the YAML is read from standard input.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Target room resolution. When ROOM_ID is given it is authoritative — the policy is written for ROOM_ID regardless of the room_id recorded in the YAML (useful for copying one room's policy onto another). When ROOM_ID is omitted, the YAML's own room_id is used.
  • Whole-policy replace. Any existing policy for the target room (and all its ACL entries) is replaced by the imported one.
  • null removes the policy. Importing a null document deletes the target room's RoomPolicy entirely, returning it to the default public (for read) state.
  • Configured-room check. Unlike as-yaml, from-yaml always requires the target room to be configured in the installation's YAML; there is no --allow-stale escape hatch.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success.
  • 1 when no target room can be resolved (a null import with no ROOM_ID), when the target room is not configured, or when the RAM-DB guard fires.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Round-trip a policy through a file (export, then re-import):

soliplex-cli room-authz as-yaml \
  --output chat-policy.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz from-yaml \
  --input chat-policy.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Copy the chat policy onto the search room (the explicit ROOM_ID overrides the room_id in the piped YAML):

soliplex-cli room-authz as-yaml example/installation.yaml chat \
  | soliplex-cli room-authz from-yaml example/installation.yaml search

Apply a policy to whichever room its YAML names (omit ROOM_ID):

soliplex-cli room-authz from-yaml \
  --input chat-policy.yaml \
  example/installation.yaml

items.title: room-authz make-private
items.text:
Ensure a room is private by inserting an empty RoomPolicy row (default_allow_deny=DENY, no ACL entries) when none exists for the room. Idempotent for rooms that are already private; refuses to silently overwrite an existing public-by-policy room unless --update is passed.

This is the non-destructive counterpart to clear --make-room-private: no existing ACL entries are deleted by this command.

soliplex-cli room-authz make-private [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text: • --update — when an existing RoomPolicy row is found with default_allow_deny=ALLOW, flip it in place to DENY. ACL entries are preserved either way. Without this flag, encountering an ALLOW policy is treated as an error (see Exit Status below).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Non-destructive. ACL entries are never deleted. If a RoomPolicy already exists and is already private (default_allow_deny=DENY), the command is a no-op and the existing policy — including all its ACL entries — is dumped unchanged.
  • Public-no-row vs. public-by-policy. A room with no policy row at all is the default public (for read) state; this command transitions it directly to private (DENY, no entries) without needing --update. A room with an explicit policy whose default_allow_deny=ALLOW is a deliberately public-by-policy room — the command refuses to flip it without --update, so an operator who relied on the explicit ALLOW isn't silently overridden.
  • Pairs with add-acl-entry. Run make-private first to lock the room down, then use add-acl-entry to grant access to specific users.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success — policy created, already private, or successfully flipped to DENY under --update.
  • 1 when the existing policy has default_allow_deny=ALLOW and --update is not passed, or when the RAM-DB guard fires.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Make the chat room private as a fresh setup step:

soliplex-cli room-authz make-private example/installation.yaml chat

Re-run safely — the room is already private, so the command is a no-op and dumps the existing policy:

soliplex-cli room-authz make-private example/installation.yaml chat

Flip an explicitly public-by-policy room to private while preserving any existing ALLOW ACL entries (so previously-listed users keep access and everyone else is now denied):

soliplex-cli room-authz make-private --update \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Make-private then grant a single user explicit access:

soliplex-cli room-authz make-private example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: room-authz make-public
items.text:
Ensure a room is public for read (WRITE and ADMIN remain granted only by entries scoped to them). Inverse of make-private: a room with no RoomPolicy row is already public-to-all-authenticated-users, so the command is a no-op in that case; a room with an existing policy whose default_allow_deny=ALLOW is also already public-by-policy, again a no-op. The command refuses to silently flip a private room (default_allow_deny=DENY) to public unless --update is passed.

Existing ACL entries are preserved; the command only ever toggles default_allow_deny.

soliplex-cli room-authz make-public [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text: • --update — when an existing RoomPolicy row is found with default_allow_deny=DENY, flip it in place to ALLOW. ACL entries are preserved either way. Without this flag, encountering a DENY policy is treated as an error (see Exit Status below).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Non-destructive. ACL entries are never deleted. After --update, any existing ALLOW entries become redundant (everyone is now allowed by default) and any existing DENY entries continue to block their specific users; if that's not what you want, follow up with clear-acl and rebuild.
  • No row needed for "public." Unlike make-private, this command does not create a RoomPolicy row in the no-row case — the room is already in the default public (for read) state. As a result, the JSON dump may be null after a successful run.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success — already public, or successfully flipped to ALLOW under --update.
  • 1 when the existing policy has default_allow_deny=DENY and --update is not passed, or when the RAM-DB guard fires.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Confirm a room is public (no-op when already in the default state):

soliplex-cli room-authz make-public example/installation.yaml chat

Flip a previously-private room to public while preserving its ACL entries (so any DENY entries continue to block their specific users):

soliplex-cli room-authz make-public --update \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Open a room back up and drop its ACL entries — combine with clear-acl:

soliplex-cli room-authz make-public --update example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz clear-acl example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: room-authz add-acl-entry
items.text:
Add an ACLEntry to a room's RoomPolicy. The entry's allow/deny flag is selected with --allow or --deny; the entry's permission scope is selected with --permission; the entry's discriminator (what it matches against the caller's token) is selected with one of --everyone, --authenticated, --json-path, --preferred-username, or --email.

The room must already have a RoomPolicy row — run make-private or make-public first to establish the policy's default_allow_deny. This avoids silently flipping a public room to private as a side effect of adding the first entry.

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text:
Exactly one of:

  • --allow — the entry grants access.
  • --deny — the entry denies access.

Exactly one of (the discriminator — what the entry matches on):

  • --everyone — matches every request, regardless of token. Useful as a catch-all that sets effective behavior independent of the policy's default_allow_deny.
  • --authenticated — matches any caller with a valid OIDC token, regardless of identity.
  • --json-path TEXT — matches when the RFC 9535 JSONPath query TEXT selects at least one node from the caller's token. This is the underlying claim discriminator; the two options below are convenience aliases for the common equality case. The query is validated against the currently-loaded JSONPath environment (so meta-config-registered filter functions are usable); a malformed query is reported and the command exits non-zero.
  • --preferred-username TEXT — convenience alias matching a caller whose OIDC preferred_username claim equals TEXT. Stored as the equivalent --json-path query $[?$.preferred_username == "TEXT"].
  • --email TEXT — convenience alias matching a caller whose OIDC email claim equals TEXT. Stored as the equivalent --json-path query $[?$.email == "TEXT"].

Plus (the permission scope):

  • --permission read|write|admin — scope the entry to that permission. A write- or admin-scoped entry grants/denies that permission for matched callers without affecting read adjudication: reads always fall back to the policy's default_allow_deny, while write and admin access fall back to DENY — only an entry scoped to the same permission can grant them (see The Model in One Paragraph).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Existing policy required. If no RoomPolicy row exists for the room, the command prints an error and exits with status 1. Run make-private (or make-public) first.
  • Dedup is per-discriminator, per-permission. Adding an entry whose discriminator and permission match an existing entry on the policy deletes the existing entry before inserting the new one. Adding --allow --email alice@x.y replaces any prior read-scoped email=alice@x.y entry (whether previously ALLOW or DENY); adding --allow --permission write --email alice@x.y leaves any prior read-scoped entry for the same email in place. Entries keyed by other discriminators (--preferred-username alice, --email bob@x.y, etc.) are left alone.
  • First-match-wins, in insertion order. For each permission, the entries scoped to it are checked in their creation order at request time; the first one whose discriminator matches the caller wins (see ACLEntry.check_token). This means a --deny --email alice@x.y added after a --allow --everyone will still keep Alice out, because the email entry matches her token before the catch-all fires — but only if Alice's row was created before the --everyone row. When ordering matters, build the policy from most-specific to least-specific.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success.
  • 1 when --allow/--deny are both passed or both omitted; when no (or more than one) discriminator option is supplied; when no RoomPolicy exists for the room; or when the RAM-DB guard fires.
  • 2 when --permission is omitted or names an unknown permission (usage errors; the command is not run at all).

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Grant a single user access to a private room:

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Block a single user on a public-by-policy room:

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --deny \
  --permission read \
  --email mallory@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Open the room to every authenticated user, on top of an existing private policy (useful for temporarily widening access without flipping default_allow_deny):

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --authenticated \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Keyed by preferred_username instead of email:

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --preferred-username alice \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Catch-all DENY for a public-by-policy room, with selective ALLOW exceptions added beforehand (because earlier entries win):

soliplex-cli room-authz make-public example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --deny \
  --permission read \
  --everyone \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Grant a user write access (explicitly scoped, so who can read the room is unaffected, and the policy's default_allow_deny is not consulted for writes):

soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow --permission write --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: room-authz delete-acl-entry
items.text:
Delete a single ACLEntry from a room's RoomPolicy. The entry is identified by the same parameter shape as add-acl-entry: the combination of --allow/--deny, one discriminator option (--everyone, --authenticated, --json-path, --preferred-username, or --email), and a --permission scope.

The room must already have a RoomPolicy row with at least one ACL entry matching the supplied parameters. If no match is found, the command exits with status 1 so the operator can tell that the delete was a no-op.

soliplex-cli room-authz delete-acl-entry [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Options
items.text:
Exactly one of:

  • --allow — match an ALLOW entry.
  • --deny — match a DENY entry.

Exactly one of (the discriminator):

  • --everyone — match an everyone entry.
  • --authenticated — match an authenticated entry.
  • --json-path TEXT — match an entry whose JSONPath query equals TEXT. This is the underlying claim discriminator; the two options below are convenience aliases for the common equality case.
  • --preferred-username TEXT — convenience alias matching the entry stored as the equivalent --json-path query $[?$.preferred_username == "TEXT"].
  • --email TEXT — convenience alias matching the entry stored as the equivalent --json-path query $[?$.email == "TEXT"].

Plus (the permission scope):

  • --permission read|write|admin — match entries scoped to this permission. The match on permission is exact: a write-scoped entry is removed only by a delete carrying --permission write.

Optional:

  • --allow-invalid-json-path — skip JSONPath compile-validation of --json-path so a stored entry whose json_path no longer compiles (e.g. because the meta-config filter function it referenced has been removed) can still be matched and removed. Use the value reported by audit room-authz verbatim. Has no effect with any other discriminator (the canonical preferred_username / email forms always validate).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Exact match on (allow/deny, permission, discriminator). An entry with the same discriminator but the opposite allow/deny flag — or scoped to a different permission — is not a match. To swap an entry from DENY to ALLOW for the same discriminator and permission, just call add-acl-entry with the new flag — its per-discriminator dedup will replace the existing row.
  • Policy preserved. Only the matching ACL entries are removed; the RoomPolicy row remains. The room's default_allow_deny is unchanged.
  • Multiple matches. If the database somehow contains more than one entry matching the supplied parameters (which the CLI cannot produce on its own, but a seed YAML or direct DB write could), all matches are deleted.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 on success — at least one matching entry was deleted.
  • 1 when --allow/--deny are both passed or both omitted; when no (or more than one) discriminator option is supplied; when no RoomPolicy exists for the room; when no entry matches the supplied parameters; or when the RAM-DB guard fires.
  • 2 when --permission is omitted or names an unknown permission (usage errors; the command is not run at all).

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Revoke a single user's access:

soliplex-cli room-authz delete-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Remove a DENY blocking a specific user, so they fall back to the policy's default_allow_deny:

soliplex-cli room-authz delete-acl-entry \
  --deny \
  --permission read \
  --email mallory@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Lift a temporary --allow --authenticated catch-all that was added to widen access while keeping the policy private:

soliplex-cli room-authz delete-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --authenticated \
  example/installation.yaml chat

Remove a stale ACL entry reported by audit room-authz:

soliplex-cli room-authz delete-acl-entry \
  --allow \
  --permission read \
  --json-path '$[?stale_filter_func($.email)]' \
  --allow-invalid-json-path \
  example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: room-authz clear-acl
items.text:
Delete every ACLEntry attached to a room's RoomPolicy while leaving the policy itself in place. The room's default_allow_deny setting is preserved: a private room (DENY) stays private and now denies everyone (no ACL entries left to grant exceptions); a public-by-policy room (ALLOW) stays public-by-policy.

soliplex-cli room-authz clear-acl [OPTIONS] INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH ROOM_ID

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Policy preserved. The RoomPolicy row is not deleted, only its ACL entries; pair with make-private or make-public if you also need to change the room's default_allow_deny.
  • No-op on the no-row case. If no RoomPolicy exists for the room, the command makes no changes and dumps null. (There are no ACL entries to clear without a parent policy.)
  • Destructive and unconditional. There is no per-discriminator filter and no confirmation prompt — every ACL entry on the policy is removed in one call. If you want to revoke a single user, use your database tooling or rebuild the ACL with repeated add-acl-entry calls.
  • "Lock everyone out, then re-grant" primitive. Run clear-acl on a private room and the policy row stays in place with zero allowed users; follow up with add-acl-entry to re-grant access to a fresh set of users.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Strip every ACL entry from the chat room while keeping it private (no one can get in until add-acl-entry is run again):

soliplex-cli room-authz clear-acl example/installation.yaml chat

Reset-and-seed — clear all existing access without changing the room's privacy setting, then grant one user:

soliplex-cli room-authz clear-acl example/installation.yaml chat
soliplex-cli room-authz add-acl-entry \
  --allow --email alice@example.com \
  example/installation.yaml chat

items.title: service-token
items.text:
The service-token group mints and validates service tokens: bearer tokens which let a client (e.g., curl, or an operator's script) call the Soliplex API without an OIDC login. A service token carries the claims given when it was minted, plus its issue (iat) and expiry (exp) times, signed with the installation's URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET.

The server accepts a service token wherever it accepts an OIDC access token, as Authorization: Bearer <token>, and treats its claims as the user's: authorization (admin users, room ACLs) and thread ownership see them exactly as they would see the claims of an OIDC token. So give the token the claims those checks match on, typically preferred_username and / or email.

items.title: service-token mint
items.text:
Mint a service token, and write it to a file or to stdout.

soliplex-cli service-token mint [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Positional Argument
items.text: • INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file, or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.

items.title: Options
items.text:
• --claims JSON — the token's claims, as a JSON object, e.g. '{"preferred_username": "ops", "email": "ops@example.com"}'. If the object has no sub, the token's sub is a random UUID. It may not hold iat or exp: those are set when minting.
  • -i PATH / --input PATH — file from which the token's claims are read: as a YAML mapping if its extension is .yaml or .yml (in any case), and otherwise as a JSON object. As with --claims, a missing sub becomes a random UUID. Any iat or exp claims in the file are dropped (noted on stderr unless --quiet is given), so the file written by service-token validate can be used to mint a fresh token with the same claims.

Give exactly one of --claims or --input. - --expires-in DURATION — required. The token's lifetime: an integer followed by one of s, m, h, d, or w (e.g. 15m, 90d). - -o PATH / --output PATH — file to which the token is written. If omitted, or -, the token is written to stdout. - --force — replace the output file, if it exists. - -q / --quiet — report only errors.

items.title: Output
items.text:
The token is written, followed by a newline, to the output file or to stdout. A file is created readable only by its owner (mode 0600).

Everything else goes to stderr, so that a script can capture the token alone: unless --quiet is given, a summary showing the output file (if any), the token's sub, and its expiry time (UTC).

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Choosing a lifetime. Each token stays valid until it expires: Soliplex keeps no record of the tokens it mints, so a single token cannot be revoked. Give a token the shortest lifetime its use allows: minutes for a token a script mints at the point of use, weeks to months for one an operator keeps in a file for occasional scripting.
  • Revoking every token. Changing URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET invalidates every service token (and every MCP token) signed with the old value.
  • The secret must resolve to the same value for the CLI and the server. A random_chars source resolves differently in each process, so the command refuses to mint a token unless one of the sources ahead of any random_chars source resolves the secret; see URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET. The command cannot check that the server's environment resolves those sources to the same value.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — the token was minted and written.
  • 1 — URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source, the claims hold iat or exp, the lifetime is zero, or the output file exists and --force was not given.
  • 2 — a usage error: --claims is not a JSON object, the --input file is missing, does not parse, or does not hold a mapping / object, both or neither of --claims and --input are given, --expires-in is not a valid duration, or a required option is missing.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Mint a token for occasional scripting, valid for 90 days, into a file:

soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --claims '{"preferred_username": "ops", "email": "ops@example.com"}' \
  --expires-in 90d \
  --output ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token)" \
  http://localhost:8000/api/v1/rooms

Mint a token from claims kept in a YAML file, e.g. ops-claims.yaml holding:

preferred_username: ops
email: ops@example.com

soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --input ops-claims.yaml --expires-in 90d \
  --output ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token

Renew a token, keeping its claims (including its sub):

soliplex-cli service-token validate example/installation.yaml \
  --input ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token --output ops-claims.yaml --quiet
soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --input ops-claims.yaml --expires-in 90d --quiet \
  --output ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token --force

Mint a short-lived token at the point of use, capturing it from stdout:

TOKEN=$(soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --claims '{"preferred_username": "ci-bot"}' \
  --expires-in 5m --quiet)
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:8000/api/v1/rooms

items.title: service-token validate
items.text:
Validate a service token, and write its claims to a file or to stdout.

soliplex-cli service-token validate [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Positional Argument
items.text: • INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file, or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.

items.title: Options
items.text:
• -i PATH / --input PATH — file from which the token is read. If omitted, or -, the token is read from stdin. Leading and trailing whitespace (e.g., the newline written by service-token mint) is ignored.
  • -o PATH / --output PATH — file to which the claims are written: as YAML if its extension is .yaml or .yml (in any case), and otherwise as JSON. If omitted, or -, the claims are written to stdout, as JSON.
  • --force — replace the output file, if it exists.
  • -q / --quiet — report only errors.

items.title: Output
items.text:
The token's claims, including its iat and exp, are written as a JSON object to stdout, or to the output file as a JSON object or a YAML mapping, depending on its extension. A file is created readable only by its owner (mode 0600).

Everything else goes to stderr, so that a script can capture the claims alone: unless --quiet is given, a summary showing the output file (if any), the token's sub, and its expiry time (UTC). If the token is not valid, the reason: its signature does not verify, it holds no exp, or it has expired.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text: • The secret must resolve to the same value as when the token was minted. As with service-token mint, the command refuses to run unless one of the sources ahead of any random_chars source resolves URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET. A token which validates here validates on a server whose environment resolves the secret to the same value.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — the token is valid, and its claims were written.
  • 1 — URL_SAFE_TOKEN_SECRET resolves only from a random_chars source, the token is not valid, or the output file exists and --force was not given.
  • 2 — a usage error, e.g. the input file does not exist.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Check the claims of a token kept in a file:

soliplex-cli service-token validate example/installation.yaml \
  --input ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token

Save a token's claims as YAML, e.g. to edit them by hand:

soliplex-cli service-token validate example/installation.yaml \
  --input ~/.config/soliplex/ops.token --output ops-claims.yaml

Check a freshly-minted token, extracting a claim with jq:

soliplex-cli service-token mint example/installation.yaml \
  --claims '{"preferred_username": "ci-bot"}' --expires-in 5m --quiet |
  soliplex-cli service-token validate example/installation.yaml --quiet |
  jq -r .preferred_username

items.title: ollama
items.text:
The ollama group bundles subcommands that interact with Ollama servers referenced by the installation. Currently a single subcommand, ollama pull.

This group replaces the flat pull-models command; see Renamed Commands.

items.title: Group Options
items.text: • -q / --quiet — suppress human-readable console output and emit any errors as a single JSON document on stdout. The command still exits non-zero on failure (see each subcommand's Exit Status). Useful for piping into jq or for driving the command from automation. Belongs to the group, so it must appear before the subcommand name (e.g. soliplex-cli ollama -q pull example/installation.yaml).

items.title: ollama pull
items.text:
Scan the installation for every Ollama model referenced by its agents, completions, or tools, and pull each model onto the corresponding Ollama server via that server's REST API. Intended to preload a fresh Ollama deployment so that the first user-facing request against Soliplex doesn't have to wait for a cold-start model download.

soliplex-cli ollama pull [OPTIONS] [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Positional Argument
items.text: • INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file, or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.

items.title: Options
items.text:
• -u URL / --ollama-url URL — restrict the scan to one or more Ollama base URLs referenced by the installation. Repeatable: pass the flag once per URL (e.g. -u http://a.example.com -u http://b.example.com). If omitted, the command pulls models on every Ollama URL referenced by the installation (installations may point different rooms at different Ollama instances). Each supplied URL must already be referenced by the installation — see Behavior Notes.
  • -n / --dry-run — scan the installation and print the model list per URL without actually pulling. Useful for verifying what would happen before committing to potentially slow downloads.

items.title: Behavior
items.text:
For each Ollama URL in scope, the command:

  1. Reports the URL and the count of distinct models the installation references at it.
  2. Iterates the model names in sorted order, printing Pulling: <model_name> for each. Unless --dry-run is set, the model is then pulled via Ollama's REST API (stream=False — each pull blocks until complete, so no per-chunk progress is shown) and the final status line returned by Ollama is printed below the Pulling: line.
  3. Unless --dry-run is set, prints a summary in the form Pulled <success_count>/<total> model(s) successfully.

If a URL has no models referenced by the installation, a No Ollama models for URL: <url> line is printed and nothing is pulled for that URL.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Network-heavy and slow. Each pull downloads potentially many gigabytes per model. Use --dry-run first if you're unsure what the command will fetch.
  • Per-model errors are reported inline. Network failures (requests.RequestException) and missing-status responses are shown in red alongside the model name and counted against the success total, but do not abort the per-URL loop. Other models on the same URL will still be pulled. The command does exit non-zero at the end if any pull failed — see Exit Status.
  • --ollama-url is validated against the installation. Each supplied URL must already appear among the Ollama URLs the installation references. If any supplied URL is unknown, the command prints the list of configured Ollama URLs (or notes that there are none) and exits non-zero without pulling anything. The flag filters the existing set; it does not inject a new destination.
  • Non-Ollama providers are ignored. Models bound to OpenAI, Gemini, or any other non-Ollama provider are not considered here; this command deals strictly with the local-model case.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text:
• 0 — every requested pull succeeded, --dry-run was specified, or the in-scope URLs referenced no Ollama models.
  • 1 — at least one individual model pull failed, or one or more --ollama-url values were not referenced by the installation.

When the group's -q / --quiet flag is in effect, a 1 exit is accompanied by a single JSON document on stdout. The document is a mapping whose keys identify the failure mode:

  • unknown_ollama_urls: list of URLs supplied via --ollama-url that the installation does not reference.
  • pulls: mapping of Ollama URL → mapping of model name → error message, populated when individual pulls fail.

The two keys are mutually exclusive in practice: the unknown-URLs check fires before any pulls are attempted, so a run that fails on unknown URLs reports unknown_ollama_urls and skips the pull loop.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Preview which models would be pulled, without pulling anything:

soliplex-cli ollama pull example/installation.yaml --dry-run

Pull every Ollama model referenced by a full installation:

soliplex-cli ollama pull example/installation.yaml

Pull models only for a specific Ollama instance (useful when an installation references multiple Ollama URLs):

soliplex-cli ollama pull example/installation.yaml \
  --ollama-url http://ollama.internal:11434

Restrict the scan to several specific Ollama instances by repeating --ollama-url:

soliplex-cli ollama pull example/installation.yaml \
  --ollama-url http://ollama-a.internal:11434 \
  --ollama-url http://ollama-b.internal:11434

Drive the command from automation, suppressing the rule-decorated output and capturing any errors as JSON:

soliplex-cli ollama -q pull example/installation.yaml

items.title: config
items.text:
Dump the installation's fully-resolved declarative configuration as a single YAML document on stdout. Useful for debugging how nested config files and defaults combine, for diffing two installations, or for producing a flattened reference copy of a configuration that is normally split across many files.

soliplex-cli config [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Positional Argument
items.text: • INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file, or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.

items.title: Output
items.text:
The command prints a three-line banner comment followed by the YAML document:

#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Source: <installation_config_path>
#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
<yaml document>

Key ordering is preserved from the original declaration (the dump uses sort_keys=False), so the output tracks the structure of the hand-written YAML rather than reshuffling it alphabetically.

The YAML is the declarative form of the config: every secret appears as its configured source (kind + secret_name + source-specific arguments such as env_var_name, file_path, or command_line), not as the resolved value. Running config against an installation and feeding the output back into Soliplex should yield an equivalent installation.

items.title: Behavior Notes
items.text:
• Tolerant of unresolved secrets and environment variables. The command attempts to resolve both before dumping, but swallows SecretsNotFound and MissingEnvVars. This lets you export the declarative YAML even on a machine that is missing the credentials or environment needed to actually run the installation.
  • Redirect with care. Although resolved secret values are never printed, the dump does include operationally sensitive material: configured subprocess command lines used to fetch secrets, file paths on the host, server URLs, database URIs (which may themselves embed credentials), and OIDC client identifiers. Treat the output with the same care you would give the installation YAML itself.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text: • Always 0. Use audit all if you need a non-zero exit on configuration problems.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Dump the minimal example:

soliplex-cli config example/minimal.yaml

Snapshot a directory-style installation to a file:

soliplex-cli config example/ > snapshot.yaml

Diff two installations after normalizing both through config:

diff \
  <(soliplex-cli config example/minimal.yaml) \
  <(soliplex-cli config example/installation.yaml)

items.title: agui-feature-schemas
items.text:
Export the JSON Schemas for every AG-UI feature registered in the installation. An AG-UI "feature" is a contract — named by a key within the AG-UI protocol's state mapping — whose shape is defined by a Pydantic model. This command dumps each feature's schema alongside its source (client, server, or either), suitable for consumption by client-side code generators or schema-diffing tools.

soliplex-cli agui-feature-schemas [INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH]

items.title: Positional Argument
items.text: • INSTALLATION_CONFIG_PATH — path to the installation configuration. May be a YAML file, or a directory containing an installation.yaml. If omitted, falls back to the SOLIPLEX_INSTALLATION_PATH environment variable.

items.title: Output
items.text:
The command prints a single JSON object on stdout, mapping each feature's name to a two-field record:

{
  "<feature_name>": {
    "source": "<client|server|either>",
    "json_schema": { /* Pydantic-generated JSON Schema */ }
  }
}
  • source identifies which side of the AG-UI protocol is allowed to write this feature's slot of the state mapping. either means both client and server may write it.
  • json_schema is the Pydantic model's model_json_schema() output, suitable for feeding into any JSON-Schema-aware code generator.

The output is compact (json.dumps with no indent) and emitted on raw stdout — no banner, no rich formatting, no trailing commentary — so it pipes cleanly into jq, code generators, or file redirections.

items.title: Exit Status
items.text: • Always 0.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Dump the feature schemas from the minimal example and pretty-print with jq:

soliplex-cli agui-feature-schemas example/minimal.yaml | jq .

List just the registered feature names:

soliplex-cli agui-feature-schemas example/installation.yaml \
  | jq 'keys'

Snapshot the schemas to a file for client-side code generation:

soliplex-cli agui-feature-schemas example/ > agui-features.json

items.title: Renamed Commands
items.text:
Releases up to 0.62.x exposed each subcommand as a flat top-level name. Later releases kept those names as hidden aliases (absent from soliplex-cli --help) until 0.83, which removed all of them except check-config, which still works but prints a deprecation warning on stderr. A script still using a removed name fails with No such command; switch it to the grouped form.

Old name Use instead Status check-config audit (or audit all) hidden alias, deprecated list-secrets audit secrets removed list-environment audit environment removed list-oidc-auth-providers audit oidc removed list-rooms audit rooms removed list-completions audit completions removed list-skills audit skills removed list-admin-users admin-users list removed add-admin-user admin-users add removed clear-admin-users admin-users clear removed show-room-authz room-authz show removed pull-models ollama pull removed

The serve --add-admin-user option is unrelated to this rename: it has been removed, and passing it now fails with a non-zero exit pointing to admin-users add. Seed admins out of band with that subcommand instead.

items.title: Environment Variables
items.text:
Non-secret environment variables can and mostly should be configured directly in the installation.yaml file (e.g. example/installation.yaml, example/minimal.yaml, etc.).

Those files are checked into the Soliplex repository, and cannot know the URL of your Ollama server (if you use Ollama), They therefore declare the OLLAMA_BASE_URL variable without a value, meaning that the configuration expects the value to be present in the environments (see: https://soliplex.github.io/soliplex/config/environment/).

Those files also must not contain secrets (API keys, etc.): instead, they configure secret values to be found from the environment (see https://soliplex.github.io/soliplex/config/secrets/).

If your installation configures such values to be found from the OS environment, you can create a .env file which defines them, and arrange for the file to be sourced into your environment before startin the Soliplex application.

Copy .env.example to .env and edit it to configure your values:

cp .env.example .env

items.title: Database Migrations
items.text:
Soliplex keeps two SQLAlchemy databases -- one for AG-UI threads and runs, one for authorization data -- and drives both from a single Alembic revision tree. Their DBURIs come from the installation config rather than from Alembic's own settings (see SQLAlchemy DBURIs), so every alembic command has to be told which installation it is working on:

-x soliplex.installation_path=/path/to/installation.yaml

The revision tree lives inside the soliplex package, at src/soliplex/alembic_migrations/, so it ships in the wheel.

A deployment can therefore migrate from its own image, with no source checkout. env.py is a shim over soliplex.alembic_migrations, where that logic and its tests live.

Unless a migration_policy is configured otherwise, soliplex runs these revisions itself, on every writable open: this migration is how a database it creates ends up stamped.

items.title: Migrating a deployment
items.text:
soliplex-cli database drives the same revision tree, out of the installed package, so it works in a deployment image -- where the alembic CLI does not (see below).

A deployment which lets Soliplex migrate for itself needs none of these commands: the first writable open brings each database to head. They are for the deployment which has taken that job away from the application role (see migration_dburi / migration_policy), and for anyone who would rather migrate at a moment of their own choosing than at the next restart.

items.title: Reporting
items.text:
soliplex-cli database status <installation-path>

reports, for each of the two databases: the DBURI a migration would use (with its password masked), the policy in force, the revisions already applied, and those still pending. Nothing is created, migrated or stamped. It exits non-zero when a database cannot be migrated as it stands -- unreachable, unstamped, or stamped by a newer release -- so it is also the pre-flight for the two commands below.

This is not what soliplex-cli audit databases reports. That is one line per database inside a whole-installation audit, answering "is anything wrong?"; this answers "what would an upgrade do?".

items.title: Upgrading and downgrading
items.text:
soliplex-cli database upgrade <installation-path>
soliplex-cli database upgrade <installation-path> --revision <revision>
soliplex-cli database downgrade <installation-path> <revision>

Both databases move in one run, committing together, and the whole run is refused if any target cannot be moved: migration_policy: disabled, a database which will not open, one which is unstamped, or one stamped by a release newer than this one. --database agui / --database authz narrows a run to one of them, which is what a configuration giving the two databases different policies needs.

items.title: Emitting SQL instead
items.text:
soliplex-cli database upgrade <installation-path> --sql

writes agui.sql and authz.sql into the current directory and runs nothing, for a deployment whose DDL somebody else applies. Each file covers that database's own pending range, taken from its stamp, so the output is the delta rather than a replay from base.

Where the databases cannot be reached from wherever the command runs, name the range instead and nothing is connected to:

soliplex-cli database upgrade <path> --sql --revision <from>:head

items.title: Running alembic by hand
items.text:
This is mostly a development task -- writing the revision that goes with a schema change. The examples below presume the example/minimal.yaml installation, and this alx alias:

alias alx="alembic -x soliplex.installation_path=example/minimal.yaml"

They also presume a source checkout. Alembic reads script_location from [tool.alembic] in the project's pyproject.toml, which a deployment image does not carry, so running the alembic CLI there reports No 'script_location' key found in configuration. That is what soliplex-cli database is for.

items.title: Rolling a version back
items.text:
Migrating happens on the way up only. A database stamped by a newer Soliplex than the one now running is refused, naming the revision it carries: this release does not have the revisions between its own head and that stamp, so it cannot move the database in either direction.

Downgrade before rolling the code back, from the version that still has those revisions and with every writer stopped:

soliplex-cli database downgrade <path> <the older release's head revision>
alx downgrade <the older release's head revision>   # from a checkout

soliplex-cli database status and soliplex-cli audit databases both report the condition, so it surfaces there rather than at the next restart. Both load only the installation config, so either runs from a migration service holding a cut-down, migration-only configuration.

items.title: Cheat Sheet
items.text: See the Alembic docs for details.

items.title: Querying
items.text:
To see the history tree:

alx history

To discover if updates are required from the running schema to match the current soliplex schemae:

alx check

Nothing creates tables on the way in, so check compares the models against the migrated database. A difference means the revisions and the models disagree: either a revision is missing a change the models make, or a model changed without one. scripts/lint_alembic_chain.py fails CI for the same reason.

items.title: Snapshotting
items.text:
To create a new revison if needed:

alx revision --autogenerate

items.title: Upgrading
items.text:
To run a migration live to a given revision:

alx upgrade <revision hash>

To generate DDL for a migration to a given revision (generates agui.sql and authz.sql files in the CWD):

alx upgrade --sql <revision hash>

items.title: SSE Stream Resume
items.text: How Soliplex uses the AG-UI protocol and the run_event message store to let clients transparently reconnect to an in-flight run after a dropped network connection.

items.title: Why this exists
items.text:
AG-UI runs are long-lived, token-by-token SSE streams. A mobile radio flap, a proxy idle-timeout, or a sleeping laptop can tear the connection down mid-response. Without resume, the user sees a partial message and the run appears broken even though the agent is still running on the server. With resume, the agent keeps running, the client reconnects with a Last-Event-ID, and the UI catches up to the current state as if nothing happened.

The mechanism is the browser-standard SSE resume primitive (WHATWG spec) plus a persistent copy of every streamed event so the server can replay from an arbitrary point.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Three layers collaborate:

  1. Protocol layer — every data: frame on the wire carries an id: prefix of the form {run_id}:{event_index}. The client echoes the most recently seen id back on reconnect via the Last-Event-ID HTTP header.
  2. Storage layer — every event the agent emits is written to the run_event table (ordered by its autoincrement primary key) before being flushed to the live SSE stream. A separate finished timestamp on the run row tells reconnecting consumers when polling can stop.
  3. Client layer — the Flutter AgUiStreamClient tracks the last seen id, detects stream drops, reconnects with Last-Event-ID, and emits lifecycle CustomEvents (stream.reconnecting, stream.reconnected, stream.reconnect_failed) so the UI can show a toast.

items.title: Event identifier format
items.text:
id: {run_id}:{event_index}
data: {<json-encoded AG-UI event>}
  • run_id is the UUID of the Run row — identifies which stream this event belongs to when multiple runs overlap in the same thread.
  • event_index is a monotonically-increasing integer starting at 0, scoped to a single run. It is not a global sequence number; each run has its own. It is not stored as its own column — it is the position of the event within its run's events list, whose ordering is guaranteed by the autoincrement id_ primary key on run_event.
  • Keepalive comments (: keepalive …) and any non-data: frames pass through without an id: prefix — they do not consume an index and cannot be resumed against.

soliplex.views.streaming.add_sse_event_ids() is the only place ids are written; on reconnect it is re-entered with start_index = after_index + 1 so the replayed stream picks up exactly where the client left off.

items.title: Normal first-connect path
items.text:
POST /v1/rooms/{room_id}/agui/{thread_id}/{run_id} (no Last-Event-ID)

  1. Authorize the user for the room.
  2. Persist the RunAgentInput via add_run_input().
  3. Spawn a background task drive_llm_stream() that consumes the agent's event stream and:
  4. pushes each event onto an unbounded asyncio.Queue (for the live SSE consumer), and
  5. writes each event to run_event with its monotonic event_index via save_single_event().
