  6. When the agent completes (or errors), drive_llm_stream() puts a sentinel on the queue and calls finish_run() which stamps run.finished with the current time.
  7. The HTTP response streams events drained from the queue, encoded by the AG-UI adapter, tagged with ids by add_sse_event_ids(), wrapped with keepalives, and returned as a StreamingResponse.

Critical decoupling: drive_llm_stream() is a create_task() coroutine, not awaited inline. The queue is unbounded. Together this means a client disconnect cancels only the SSE response — the background task keeps draining the agent, persisting events, and marking the run finished. A reconnecting client can then pick up the full tail, including events written after it disconnected.

items.title: Reconnect path
items.text:
When the request carries a Last-Event-ID: {run_id}:{N} header, soliplex.views.agui.post_room_agui_thread_id_run_id takes a completely different path:

  1. parse_last_event_id() splits on the final : and extracts after_index = N. Malformed values are treated as if the header was absent (i.e. a fresh run is attempted).
  2. Authorize the user for the room (same check as first-connect).
  3. Skip add_run_input, skip the agent, skip drive_llm_stream — the run is already executing (or finished) somewhere else.
  4. Create a stream_from_db() generator scoped to (user_name, room_id, thread_id, run_id, after_index=N).
  5. Feed that generator through the normal AG-UI encoder and add_sse_event_ids(start_index=N+1) pipeline.
  6. Return the same StreamingResponse shape as first-connect; the client cannot tell the difference on the wire.

stream_from_db() loops: call list_run_events_after(after_index) (which loads run.events and returns the slice past after_index, paired with each row's position), yield everything it returns, update after_index to the last yielded index, then check is_run_finished(). If not finished, sleep SSE_RECONNECT_POLL_INTERVAL_SECS (0.2 s) and loop. If finished, do one final drain query (to catch events written between the last poll and the finished flag being set) and terminate.

items.title: Storage model
items.text:
run                       run_event
─────────                 ─────────
id_ (PK)           <──┐   id_ (PK, autoincrement) ← ordering key
user_name             └── run_id_ (FK → run.id_, ON DELETE CASCADE)
room_id                   data                    ← json-dumped AG-UI Event
thread_id_                created
...
finished (nullable)

See soliplex.agui.schema.Run and soliplex.agui.schema.RunEvent

Notes:

  • Retention is indefinite — no TTL. Events live until the parent run or thread row is deleted (both cascade).
  • event_index is not persisted; it is the position of the row within run.events (loaded in id_ order). On the write side, drive_llm_stream() keeps a local counter only for log/wire purposes. On the read side, list_run_events_after() slices run.events from after_index + 1 and pairs each row with its position.
  • run.finished is the single source of truth for "no more events coming". Crash-recovery after a process restart relies on it being unset — those runs are effectively stuck (stale events in run_event, no background task running) and will poll forever unless cleaned up administratively.
  • Events are persisted before they are counted as delivered — if the DB write fails, the error is logged but the event is still pushed to the live queue. The client sees it; a reconnect would not. This is a tradeoff in favor of live responsiveness.

items.title: Tracking the last seen id
items.text: AgUiStreamClient.runAgent() parses SSE via the ag_ui package's SseParser, which exposes SseMessage.id for every dispatched message. The client holds a local String? lastEventId and updates it on each non-empty id. The SseParser preserves _lastEventId across messages per the spec — individual data: frames do not need to repeat their own id.

items.title: When to resume
items.text:
Resume is triggered only by stream errors, not by clean EOF:

Termination condition Client action Normal close after RUN_FINISHED/RUN_ERROR Done, return. Clean EOF without a terminal event Done, return (log only). CancelledException (user cancel) Propagate, never resume. Initial-connect AuthException (401/403) Propagate. Initial-connect NetworkException Propagate (no id to resume against). Stream error mid-body, lastEventId != null Resume. NetworkException on reconnect attempt Retry, counts toward budget. 5xx ApiException on reconnect attempt Retry, counts toward budget. 4xx ApiException / AuthException on reconnect Synthesize terminal failure, stop.

A resume attempt reissues the same POST to the same URL with the same body — plus a Last-Event-ID header. The server routes it to stream_from_db. The client does not know, and does not need to know, whether the agent is still running or has already finished.

items.title: Retry policy
items.text:
Configured by ResumePolicy (defaults):

  • 5 attempts per drop, 500 ms → 8 s exponential backoff (×2), ±20 % jitter.
  • Attempt counter resets to zero after a successful resume — the budget is per-drop, not cumulative over the lifetime of the run.
  • On exhaustion, the client yields a CustomEvent(name: 'stream.reconnect_failed', …) followed by a synthetic RunErrorEvent(code: 'stream.resume_failed'), then returns cleanly. Downstream state machines see a terminal run via the normal RunErrorEvent path — no resume-specific branches needed in the UI state layer.

items.title: Surfacing the lifecycle to the UI
items.text:
The client emits three synthetic CustomEvents interleaved with the real run events:

name value stream.reconnecting {attempt, lastEventId, error} stream.reconnected {attempt} stream.reconnect_failed {attempts, error}

These are never sent by the server and never written to the run_event table — they exist only within a single client run instance. ReconnectStatus.tryParse() parses them into a typed sealed class; AgentSession exposes a reconnectStatus signal that drives the _ReconnectBanner toast above the chat thread.

items.title: Logging
items.text:
All client-side resume activity logs under the soliplex_client.agui_stream logger name:

  • Level 800 (info): attempt start and success.
  • Level 900 (warning): stream drop detected, will attempt resume.
  • Level 1000 (severe): final give-up after exhausted attempts.

Server-side activity is captured by logfire spans around drive_llm_stream() and the endpoint handler; reconnects surface as additional entries under the same endpoint span.

items.title: Sequence diagram
items.text:
Example: a run that starts normally, is interrupted mid-stream by a network drop, and resumes via Last-Event-ID.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant UI as Flutter UI
    participant C as AgUiStreamClient
    participant S as FastAPI<br/>(agui endpoint)
    participant T as drive_llm_stream<br/>(bg task)
    participant DB as run_event table
    participant A as Agent

    Note over UI,A: Initial connect
    UI->>C: runAgent(endpoint, input)
    C->>S: POST .../{thread}/{run}<br/>Accept: text/event-stream
    S->>DB: add_run_input
    S->>T: create_task(drive_llm_stream)
    S-->>C: 200 OK (stream opens)
    T->>A: consume llm_stream
    A-->>T: RunStarted
    T->>DB: save_single_event(index=0)
    T-->>S: queue.put(RunStarted)
    S-->>C: id: run-1:0\ndata: {RUN_STARTED}
    A-->>T: TextMessageContent("Hel")
    T->>DB: save_single_event(index=1)
    T-->>S: queue.put(...)
    S-->>C: id: run-1:1\ndata: {..."Hel"}
    C-->>UI: RunStartedEvent, TextMessageContentEvent

    Note over C,S: Network drop after id=run-1:1
    S-xC: TCP reset / proxy idle-close
    C->>C: lastEventId = "run-1:1"<br/>attempt = 1
    C-->>UI: CustomEvent(stream.reconnecting, attempt=1)
    UI->>UI: show "Reconnecting…" toast

    Note over T,DB: Agent keeps running in background
    A-->>T: TextMessageContent("lo")
    T->>DB: save_single_event(index=2)
    A-->>T: RunFinished
    T->>DB: save_single_event(index=3)
    T->>DB: finish_run() (sets run.finished)

    Note over UI,A: Resume (500ms backoff later)
    C->>S: POST .../{thread}/{run}<br/>Last-Event-ID: run-1:1
    S->>S: parse_last_event_id → after_index=1
    S->>S: authorize user for room
    S-->>C: 200 OK (stream_from_db path)
    loop until run.finished and drained
        S->>DB: list_run_events_after(after_index)
        DB-->>S: [(2, "lo"), (3, RunFinished)]
        S-->>C: id: run-1:2\ndata: {..."lo"}
        S-->>C: id: run-1:3\ndata: {RUN_FINISHED}
        S->>DB: is_run_finished?
        DB-->>S: true
    end
    S-->>C: stream closes

    C-->>UI: CustomEvent(stream.reconnected, attempt=1)
    UI->>UI: toast → "Reconnected." (auto-dismiss 3s)
    C-->>UI: TextMessageContentEvent("lo"),<br/>RunFinishedEvent
    C->>C: sawTerminalEvent = true, return

items.title: Backend
items.text: Concern File Symbols Endpoint dispatch & Last-Event-ID parse src/soliplex/views/agui.py parse_last_event_id, post_room_agui_thread_id_run_id Background event pump + DB writes src/soliplex/views/agui.py drive_llm_stream, save_single_event, finish_run SSE id injection & DB replay src/soliplex/views/streaming.py add_sse_event_ids, stream_from_db Event persistence API src/soliplex/agui/persistence.py ThreadStorage.save_single_event, list_run_events_after, is_run_finished, finish_run Storage schema src/soliplex/agui/schema.py Run, RunEvent Unit tests tests/unit/views/test_agui_views.py test_post_room_agui_reconnect End-to-end tests tests/functional/test_agui_thread.py test_sse_resume_with_last_event_id

items.title: Design notes and limits
items.text:
• Per-run, not per-thread. Last-Event-ID scopes to one run. Once a run ends, a new user turn creates a new run with a fresh event_index counter — a client's lastEventId from the previous run is not meaningful for the new one.
  • Authorization is re-checked on every reconnect. Revoked permissions mid-run terminate the resume cleanly (4xx → synthetic terminal event on the client).
  • Event persistence is best-effort. DB write failures during drive_llm_stream are logged but do not stop live delivery — the cost is that those specific events cannot be replayed. A reconnect after such a failure will skip them.
  • Polling cost. Reconnect readers poll every 200 ms. For long-lived resumes against a slow agent, this is cheap but non-zero; an event-driven notification would be more efficient at the cost of added complexity.
  • Crash recovery is partial. A server crash mid-run leaves run.finished unset. A reconnecting client will poll forever (modulo its own retry budget). There is no watchdog that force-finishes orphaned runs.
  • Synthetic client events never round-trip. stream.* CustomEvents are constructed in-memory by the Dart client; the server neither emits nor persists them, so they will not appear in a replay after a second drop.

items.title: Soliplex Docker Compose Template
items.text:
A Docker Compose template that assembles a running Soliplex stack:

  • nginx — serves the Flutter web frontend and reverse-proxies the API.
  • backend — the Soliplex server (soliplex-cli serve).
  • haiku-ingester — the document pipeline writer for the RAG vector store.
  • docling-serve — stateless document converter.
  • postgres — thread persistence and authorization policy.

This repository is configuration + Dockerfiles, not application source: the Soliplex backend is built on the published soliplex release image, the frontend is copied from the published soliplex/frontend web image, and haiku-rag / docling-serve use upstream images.

You don't run this repository directly. You generate your own stack from it with the bundled soliplex-template Agent Skill (or the generator script), then run and operate that generated project.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: Page What's there Generate a project Scaffold a tailored stack with the skill, or by running the generator directly.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
Hands-on walkthroughs that take a freshly generated stack from first launch through populating RAG and extending it:

Page What's there First steps Install the skill, generate a stack, bring it up, and try a demo room. Populate RAG Drop documents into the ingester and query them from a room. Add a custom tool Wire a Python tool into the backend and call it from an agent. Next steps Where to go after the core walkthroughs. Separate RAG database Create and wire in an additional RAG database. Work with Gitea Back the stack with a Gitea repo and push the initial commit. Concierge room Add and use the concierge room. Resolve room requests Administer concierge room requests.

items.title: Using a generated stack
items.text:
Documentation that ships inside a generated project — how to bring the stack up and operate it day to day:

Page What's there Installation Generate secrets, set OLLAMA_BASE_URL, bring the stack up. Service graph What each container does and how they connect. Backend configuration The backend/environment/ layout and the sandbox. Backend image & dependencies How the backend image is built and how to add dependencies. Secrets File-based vs env-var secret modes. RAG pipeline The vector store, the ingester, and adding documents. Ingester control plane The control-plane API and its auth token. Custom Python package The installable project under src/, wired into the backend.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Working on this repository rather than running a stack:

Page What's there Developing this template The repo → template derivation, the refresh workflow, and the documentation conventions.

items.title: Developing this template
items.text: This page is for working on the soliplex-template repository itself — not for running a generated stack. It is repo-only: it never ships into a generated project. To create a stack, see Generate a project.

items.title: What this repository is
items.text:
soliplex-template is configuration + Dockerfiles, not application source: the Soliplex backend is built on the published soliplex release image, the frontend on the published soliplex/frontend web image, and haiku-rag / docling-serve use upstream images.

The repository's stack files at the repo root (docker-compose.yml.mako, backend/environment/, nginx/, …) double as its own exemplar: the source the shipped template is derived from. The parameterized exemplars carry ${param} placeholders where per-stack values go, and the exemplar is render-source, not a runnable stack: runnable stacks exist only on the generation side (see Generate a project).

items.title: Repo → template
items.text:
The skill ships an embedded, parameterized copy of the stack under skills/soliplex-template/assets/template/. It is generated from the repo exemplars by scripts/refresh_skill_template.py:

  • most tracked files are copied verbatim (minus EXCLUDE_PATHSPECS);
  • the parameterized files are checked in as *.mako, already carrying the ${param} substitutions and the include_gitea / include_tui / enable_sandbox conditionals, and are copied as-is;
  • the shipped doc pages are copied from docs/users/, which carry the same placeholders (see below);
  • a few templates with no repo exemplar are written verbatim (AUTHORED, e.g. README.md.mako);
  • every *.mako the skill ships is render-checked with Mako against the generator's DEFAULTS, so a stale placeholder can't ship.

That generated tree is a build artifact, not source: it is gitignored and not committed. scripts/build_skill.py regenerates it before assembling the skill, and the functional tests regenerate it before they run, so it always reflects the current exemplars — there is nothing to keep in sync by hand.

items.title: Reviewing .mako diffs
items.text:
Reviewing a parameterized file's diff runs into two source spellings that read oddly against diff hunks:

  • <%text>…</%text> encloses text Mako must pass through untouched (shell / Docker ${...} expansions). A hunk showing a wrapper appear or disappear is an escaping change, not a content rewrite.
  • % if / % endif are the opt-in-service conditionals; the generated stack shows the branch resolved, the source shows both.

When in doubt, review the rendered output rather than the source: every shipped .mako is render-checked with the generator's DEFAULTS, and a generated stack shows the final shape. For rename-plus-templatize pairs, git diff --find-renames (and -M) keeps the edit attached to the rename.

So the workflow for changing the stack is just to edit the exemplar (the real files at the repo root). To preview the generated template, or to drive the generator from a checkout, regenerate it explicitly:

uv run scripts/refresh_skill_template.py   # (re)generate the embedded template

Build and validate the packaged skill (which refreshes first) with uv run scripts/build_skill.py.

items.title: Editing the documentation
items.text:
Documentation lives under docs/, split by audience:

  • docs/users/ documents a generated stack, and is the authoritative source of the shipped doc pages: the pages are checked in as *.md.mako, carrying their parameters as ${...} placeholders on top of the same conditional fences documented below. On this repo's site, the fences hide their conditional content and the placeholders render literally; in a generated project, the generator bakes the values and resolves the conditionals.
  • docs/contributing/ (this page) documents developing the template, and is repo-only.

Conditional content for an opt-in service is wrapped in HTML-comment fences. They are invisible on this site and become a Mako conditional in a generated project, so the block ships only when that service is included:

<!-- if:gitea -->
Shown only when the stack includes Gitea (likewise `if:tui`).
<!-- endif -->

To make a single list item conditional, indent the fences to the list's content column so the Markdown linter still sees one list:

- always shipped
  <!-- if:gitea -->
- shipped only with Gitea
  <!-- endif -->

Repo-site-only content — e.g. the "About this page" banner — is wrapped so it appears on this site but is stripped from the shipped docs entirely:

<!-- site-only -->
Shown only on this repo's docs site.
<!-- endsite-only -->

Parameters are written as ${param} placeholders, so the shipped value is whatever the generator's DEFAULTS resolve for that stack. A generated project's 9000 is only a value: the source spells it ${nginx_http}.

Pages that should not ship at all — the generator page and this contributing page — simply live outside docs/users/ (under docs/getting-started/ and docs/contributing/), so the copy step never touches them.

As with the stack files, the generated .mako are not committed — just edit the docs/users/ .md; the build and the functional tests regenerate the template from it.

For the working guide — the daily commands, the repository layout, and the release/backport procedure — see Development guide.

items.title: Development guide
items.text:
This guide is for developers working on the soliplex-template repository itself — the Docker Compose template, its generator, and the soliplex-template skill and Python package. If you only want to create a stack, see Generate a project; if you are operating one, see Using a generated stack.

Much of the repo→template machinery is documented in Developing this template; this page covers working on the repo day to day: the commands, the layout, and the release procedure.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
Prerequisites:

  • uv (used for everything — do not use pip)
  • Docker CLI and daemon (needed by the unit suite's docker-gated fixtures, and by every command under a stack directory)
  • Access to an Ollama server or other inference: at a minimum, run Ollama even on a machine without supported GPU, and pull tiny chat and embeddings models (e.g., qwen3.5:4b, qwen3-embedding:0.6b) for probing while generating.

Worktrees, following the container convention:

git worktree add [-b <branch>] ../<worktree-name>
cd ../<worktree-name>

# Install the project and its dev dependencies
uv sync --group dev

Run all Python commands through uv run so they use the project environment. If uv resolves a Python newer than the repo supports, set UV_PYTHON in your shell (the repo deliberately carries no .python-version pin; see below).

# Working on the template from a checkout of this repo
uv run scripts/refresh_skill_template.py     # regenerate the embedded template
uv run scripts/generate_soliplex_project.py  # drive the generator directly

items.title: Daily commands
items.text:
uv run pytest tests             # full suite: unit + functional, 100% coverage required
uv run pytest tests --no-cov    # skip the coverage gate when iterating
uv run pytest tests/unit/scripts/test_generate_soliplex_project.py  -q --no-cov
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format .
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
uv run zensical build --strict  # the docs site, repo-only pages included

scripts/refresh_skill_template.py is the load-bearing step: it regenerates the gitignored embedded template from the repo exemplars and render-checks every shipped .mako against the generator's DEFAULTS, so a stale placeholder cannot ship. Functional tests re-run it themselves.

items.title: Repository structure
items.text:
The repo-root stack files (docker-compose.yml.mako, nginx/, backend/, …) are the exemplar: the render-source the skill's template is assembled from. The repo is not a runnable stack; runnable stacks exist only on the generation side, and what ships is the assembled template copy under skills/soliplex-template/assets/template/ — never the repo files themselves. The non-obvious paths:

  • docs/users/ — the authoritative source of the shipped doc pages; everything ships, including the conditional fences
  • docs/getting-started/, docs/contributing/ — repo-only pages, never shipped (the contributing page documents the machinery)
  • skills/soliplex-template/ — the skill source; its assets/template/ is a gitignored build artifact, regenerated from the exemplars (never edit it directly)
  • scripts/ — the generator, the refresh/build tooling, and the per-stack helpers the generated stacks run (soliplex_config.py, rag_db.py, add_room.py, migrate_*.py, src_projects.py)
  • src/soliplex_template/ — the published Python package (the thin soliplex-plumber implementation behind the per-stack scripts)
  • tests/functional/ — generation end-to-end (some fixtures require docker); tests/unit/ — everything else

The generated stack's own files are parameterized copies: the ${param} placeholder spellings and the if:/ifp:/site-only fences live in the repo sources, and Developing this template documents how they resolve.

items.title: Documentation sites
items.text:
• This repo's site (zensical.toml) includes repo-only trees and is built with uv run zensical build --strict — part of the pre-release and pre-commit gates.
  • A generated stack ships its own parameterized site under docs/, built the same way from the generated pages.

items.title: Publishing
items.text: Changes to the exemplars, docs, or generator reach users by releasing the template. Releases are made from release branches, not main: vX.Y names the initial release of a minor line; vX.Y.Z names patch releases on that branch, normally cherry-picked from a squash-merged PR against main.

items.title: Cutting a minor release (vX.Y in the examples)
items.text:
1. Update main and open a new worktree for the release branch:
# from `main` worktree
git worktree add ../vX.Y
  1. Capturing the changelog draft — the container's release-notes/ directory (outside the repo) holds one draft per release:
cd ../vX.Y
git log vX.{Y-1}..HEAD > ../release-notes/soliplex-template-vX.Y.txt

Edit it down to a human-focused changelog; drop anything already released in the previous line's patch releases.

  1. Prepare the release on the branch: bump the package version in pyproject.toml from the X.Ydev dev spelling to X.Y, then:
uv sync --all-groups
git commit pyproject.toml uv.lock -m "chore: prep 'vX.Y' release"

  1. (optional, for changes which introduce significant changes to the structure / configuration of generated stacks) Add the release's rung to Upgrading an existing stack, walked with this tag's skill release: see Adding an upgrade rung.

  2. Tag and push:

git tag -s -F ../../release-notes/soliplex-template-vX.Y.txt vX.Y
git push origin vX.Y.x vX.Y
  1. Publish the GitHub release from the tag, pasting the changelog.

Publication triggers two releases via CI: - pypi.yaml publishes the soliplex-template wheel to PyPI using Trusted Publishing - build-skill.yaml cuts the release-stamped skill.

The stack's container images come from the other repos' releases; this release publishes no images.

  1. Sanity-check with uv run scripts/skill_versions.py list from any installed skill: the release build appears, and the rolling line still tracks main.

items.title: Smoke test before tagging
items.text: One full generate-walk from the release branch, both auth modes plus one *_port opt-in case, walking the rendered result the way Using a generated stack describes. The gates above cover the contract; the smoke test covers the experience.

items.title: Adding an upgrade rung
items.text:
A rung is the by-hand route from one generated-stack shape to the next, for stack owners who cannot regenerate. Each rung has:

  • A page under docs/upgrades/, named for what it does (move-to-…, serve-through-nginx.md), listed in the zensical.toml nav and in the Upgrade rungs list on Upgrading an existing stack. The page opens with "Part of Upgrading an existing stack" and the release to walk it with, as a skill_versions.py upgrade vX.Y command, then numbered steps ending in [**Check it**](index.md#check-it) and a commit.
  • A row in that page's Where do I start? table: the shape a stack is in before the rung, a file signature that tells that shape apart, the release to walk with, and the link.

The release a rung walks with is the one whose generator produces the rung's end state: its scripts perform the rung, and its reference stack (see Checking the whole stack against a reference on that page) differs from an upgraded stack only where the stack owner's own changes do. It is always a software release (v…): the dated template-skill-* rolling builds are pruned after ten newer ones, so a rung that names one breaks. Usually it is the minor release that ships the change (step 4 above).

items.title: When the end state falls between releases
items.text:
If main has moved on to the next shape before the release is cut, cut a pre-release from the commit that completes the rung's end state. vX.YbN names it, where X.Y is the next minor release and N counts the pre-releases cut ahead of it, so it sorts before vX.Y:

  1. Branch from that commit, in a new worktree:

    # from `main` worktree
git worktree add -b vX.YbN ../vX.YbN <sha>

  2. Bump the package version in pyproject.toml from the X.Ydev0 spelling to X.YbN, and change nothing else. Publishing any release runs pypi.yaml from the tagged commit, which would otherwise upload the X.Y.dev0 wheel:

    uv sync --all-groups
git commit pyproject.toml uv.lock -m "chore: prep 'vX.YbN' release"

  3. Draft the changelog from the commits since the previous release's branch point, and say that this is a synthetic, out-of-order release cut for the rung, linking the rung's page.

  4. Tag, push the tag, and publish the GitHub release from it, marked as a pre-release:

    git tag -s -F ../../release-notes/soliplex-template-vX.YbN.txt vX.YbN
git push origin vX.YbN

  5. Check the result:

    git diff --quiet <sha> vX.YbN -- skills/ && echo "skill unchanged"
uv run skills/soliplex-template/scripts/skill_versions.py list --kind release

    The release carries soliplex-template-skill.tar.gz, .zip, and version.json; list shows vX.YbN; PyPI has X.YbN.

items.title: Backporting a fix
items.text:
Backports are cherry-picks of the merge commit from main onto the most recent minor branch, in that branch's worktree:

git cherry-pick <pr-squash-merge-sha>

Then a follow the same flow as the minor release above: - fresh changelog draft based on the most recent tag on the branch - version bump in pyproject.toml and uv sync --all-groups - commit - signed tag - push tag - GitHub release

items.title: Agent guidance (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md)
items.text: The repo's root CLAUDE.md is a thin stub that imports AGENTS.md; in a generated stack that resolves to the stack's own agent guidance (rendered from AGENTS.md.mako). In a worktree of this repo there is no such AGENTS.md — the agent guidance for working on this repo is this page plus the container-level AGENTS.md (which also describes the worktree container layout). Keep the stub as-is: it is shipped deliberately.

items.title: Generate a project
items.text:
You don't run this template repository directly — you generate your own Soliplex stack from it, then run and operate that generated project. A generated project gets its own project name, host ports, model choices, auth mode, and an installable Python package wired into the backend.

There are two ways to generate, both driven by the same generator (skills/soliplex-template/scripts/generate_soliplex_project.py, which renders the embedded Mako template under skills/soliplex-template/assets/template/ into a fresh, runnable directory):

items.title: With the Agent Skill (usual path)
items.text: In an agent that has the soliplex-template skill available, ask it to create a stack — e.g. "generate a new Soliplex stack". The skill prompts for the parameters it needs (at minimum your Ollama URL) and runs the generator for you. See Working with the skill below for answering its questions up front, what it checks, and what it asks you to decide; once the stack exists, Using the skill covers what else it can do.

items.title: By hand
items.text:
You can also run the generator directly:

# Show every parameter and its default:
uv run skills/soliplex-template/scripts/generate_soliplex_project.py --print-defaults

# Generate into a new directory from a params file:
uv run skills/soliplex-template/scripts/generate_soliplex_project.py \
    --out ../my-stack --params params.json

# Or create it inside a directory that collects your stacks; the project
# directory is named for project_name:
uv run skills/soliplex-template/scripts/generate_soliplex_project.py \
    --parent ~/stacks --params params.json

ollama_base_url is the only value with no usable default; everything else falls back to a sensible default. Useful flags:

  • --interactive — prompt for each parameter on stdin.
  • --no-generate-secrets — skip generating the stack's Docker secrets (generation runs generate_secrets.py by default).
  • --no-git — skip the initial git commit.
  • --parent DIR — create the project inside DIR rather than treating the target as the project directory itself. Mutually exclusive with --out.
  • --force — allow writing into a non-empty target directory (with --parent, that means the project directory, not the parent).

items.title: What the generated project adds
items.text:
Beyond the stack itself, a generated project ships an installable Python library of its own, as a project directory under src/:

src/
  <package_name>/         # this project
    pyproject.toml
    src/<package_name>/   # a demo tools.greeting and views.router
    tests/unit/

Every entry under src/ has that shape, so cd src/<X> && uv sync && uv run pytest works the same for this project and for any repo the stack owner later clones alongside it (the soliplex checkout, a third-party dependency). The backend mounts the whole src/ tree read-only and puts this project's package directory on PYTHONPATH, and the Soliplex config references it by dotted name — so you have a ready place to add custom tools, routers, and configuration.

An existing stack generated before this layout is converted by the skill's scripts/migrate_layout.py: see Move to the src/ project layout, rung 0 of Upgrading an existing stack.

items.title: Working with the skill
items.text: Asked for a new stack, the agent interviews you, grouping related settings into one question each: location, project name, Ollama URL, host ports, auth mode, models, frontend and backend versions, the optional Gitea service, the optional code-execution sandbox, and whether to generate secrets and make an initial git commit.

items.title: Answering up front
items.text:
To skip questions, put the answers on the command that invokes the skill:

/soliplex-template in=~/stacks project=acme ollama=http://192.168.1.20:11434 ports=default models=default
  • key=value sets one setting. key is a generator parameter name (see references/PARAMETERS.md) or one of the shorter aliases listed below.
  • where=DIR makes DIR the project directory, like --out; in=DIR creates the project inside DIR, like --parent. Use one or the other.
  • ports=default or models=default accepts the defaults for that whole group and skips its question.
  • force, git=no, and secrets=no are the --force, --no-git, and --no-generate-secrets flags.

A fully specified command runs without questions; a bare /soliplex-template asks them all. The agent asks about any token it does not recognize rather than guessing.

The full alias and group vocabulary 
{
  "_comment": "Shortcut spellings for `/soliplex-template` generation (issue #92). Single source of truth for the alias/group vocabulary; read by the skill when resolving inline `key=value` tokens, NOT consumed by generate_soliplex_project.py. `aliases` map a friendly token to a generator parameter, with two special routing tokens that are NOT params.json entries: `where`/`output_dir` routes to `--out` (the project directory itself) and `in`/`parent_dir` routes to `--parent` (the directory to create the project in). `groups` name a set of parameters that a `<group>=default` token skips at their defaults. There are no secret parameters. Guarded against drift from the generator's DEFAULTS by tests/unit/scripts/test_aliases_manifest.py.",
  "aliases": {
    "where": "output_dir",
    "in": "parent_dir",
    "project": "project_name",
    "ollama": "ollama_base_url",
    "auth": "auth_mode",
    "gitea": "include_gitea",
    "sandbox": "enable_sandbox",
    "frontend": "frontend_version",
    "soliplex": "soliplex_image_tag"
  },
  "groups": {
    "ports": [
      "nginx_http",
      "nginx_https",
      "ingester_port",
      "docling_port",
      "postgres_port",
      "backend_port",
      "gitea_http_port",
      "gitea_ssh_port"
    ],
    "models": [
      "chat_model",
      "chat_model_alt",
      "title_model",
      "rag_embed_model",
      "rag_embed_dim",
      "rag_qa_model",
      "chunk_size"
    ]
  }
}

items.title: What it checks before writing anything
items.text:
• Models. The agent lists the models your Ollama server actually has and offers those, then sends each chosen model a one-token request, even with models=default. A model that is missing or won't load is caught here, and the agent offers to switch to another or pull it.
  • A loopback-only Ollama. If your Ollama URL names localhost or 127.0.0.1, the containers will not be able to reach it, even though the model checks pass from the host. The agent explains your options (a relay container, rebinding Ollama to the Docker bridge, or another server); see Local Ollama.
  • Versions. It lists the published frontend and backend image tags and asks for each separately; any frontend version works with any backend version.
  • The project name. soliplex is reserved (in any capitalization); the agent suggests the default soliplex-dojo instead.

If you then ask it to bring the stack up, it builds the images, starts the services, waits for them to report healthy, and re-checks the models from inside the stack against the full resolved configuration.

items.title: Decisions it leaves to you
items.text:
• Secrets. No setting is a secret; the stack's secrets are generated into .secrets/. If you type something secret-looking on the command line, the agent treats it as a mistake, not as input.
  • Exposing Ollama. It will not suggest binding Ollama to 0.0.0.0, which would publish an unauthenticated model server to every network the host is on, and it will not rewrite your Ollama URL without asking.

items.title: Where to look
items.text:
• Parameters, defaults, and validation: references/PARAMETERS.md
  • Skill instructions: SKILL.md

Once generated, follow Installation from the secrets step onward to bring your new stack up.

items.title: Using the skill
items.text:
The soliplex-template Agent Skill does more than generate a project: once a stack exists, a coding agent (e.g. Claude Code) can use the skill to inspect it, extend it, and keep it current. You describe what you want in plain language; the agent asks for whatever it still needs, runs the skill's scripts, and reports back.

This page is for the person working with that agent: what you can ask for, what the agent will ask you, and which decisions it leaves to you. Every task is also a script you can run yourself; each section links to the page that covers the manual route.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Start the agent in the stack's directory, or tell it where the stack is.
  • Most tasks run a one-off container from the stack's backend image, so build the images first (docker compose build). Adding a room and migrating the layout touch only files.
  • Provisioning a room for a user needs the stack running.
  • In the "by hand" commands below, <skill> is wherever the skill is installed, e.g. ~/.claude/skills/soliplex-template.

items.title: Inspect a running stack's configuration
items.text:
"Which rooms does this stack load?", "What is room_paths set to?", "Show me the chat room's config."

The agent asks the backend for its resolved configuration (soliplex-cli config), after defaults, secret and environment substitution, and room_paths are applied. The answer reflects what the backend actually runs, not what the files under backend/environment/ appear to say.

By hand: uv run <skill>/scripts/soliplex_config.py show (or get <path>, rooms, room <room_id>) from the stack directory. See Backend configuration.

items.title: Check the Ollama models
items.text:
"Are all the models this stack uses available?"

The agent runs the backend's own audit, which checks every model the resolved configuration names against the Ollama server it resolves to, and has each one answer a request. Use it after changing OLLAMA_BASE_URL in .env, or when requests start failing because the server lost a model. The agent offers to pull any that are missing.

By hand: soliplex-cli audit ollama --check-responsive and soliplex-cli ollama pull in a backend container; see Local Ollama for reaching a server on the Docker host.

items.title: Build a separate RAG database
items.text:
"Build a RAG database called handbook from rag/docs/handbook/." "Add this URL to the handbook database."

The stack's ingester maintains one database continuously. For a separate, mostly static corpus, the agent builds a second database under rag/db/<name>.lancedb with the stack's own haiku-rag image and settings, so it never collides with the ingester. Sources can be a path under rag/docs/, a URL or S3 URI, or any local path. It can also add documents to, re-index, or remove documents from a database built this way.

A new database is not used by any room until you wire it into one; the agent offers to do that next.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/rag_db.py create / update; see RAG pipeline.

items.title: Point rooms at a RAG database
items.text:
"Point the chat room at the handbook database."

The agent lists the rooms the stack loads, with their names and descriptions, and lets you pick one or more. It then edits each room's room_config.yaml in place (comments kept) to read the database. A room that has a skills: block without the RAG skill in it is reported rather than edited, for you to wire by hand.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/rag_db.py add-rag-to-room; see Separate RAG database.

items.title: Add a room
items.text:
"Add a search room for the handbook."

The agent offers the skill's room templates (chat, search, minimal, and sandbox) and asks for the room id, name, description, agent template, system prompt, and (for templates that search) the RAG database to read. It shows you a dry run before writing anything, then tells the running backend to reload its rooms and confirms the new room loads. The sandbox template is offered only for a stack generated with the sandbox enabled.

The new room_config.yaml includes commented-out examples of custom tools and skills, for you to uncomment later.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/add_room.py list / add; see Backend configuration.

items.title: Provision a private room for a user
items.text:
"Provision a room called Q3 Plans for alice."

The agent creates a private RAG room on that user's behalf: its own database fed from the room's uploads, access for that user alone, and its config committed to the stack's src/rooms-provisioned repository. It asks for the user's username (plus email and display name if known) and the room's name; the room id becomes <username>:<slug>.

The provisioner needs an admin_users entry, which the stack's stack-init adds. If the entry is missing, the agent says so and offers to run stack-init.

It leaves one thing to you: leftovers from a room removed by hand. If an earlier room with the same id left its database, uploads, or authorization policy behind, provisioning refuses and the agent lists what is left. It does not delete them to get past the error.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/provision_room.py; see Room provisioning.

items.title: Work on another project alongside the stack
items.text:
"Clone the soliplex repo into this stack."

The agent clones the project into src/, puts its package on the backend's PYTHONPATH, and has the backend restart when its files change. It then checks the project's dependencies against what the backend image has installed and reports:

  • Missing packages — add them to backend/requirements.txt and rebuild the backend; restarting alone will not fix the import error.
  • Conflicting versions — the project wants versions the image does not have. The agent offers the fixes (adapt the project, pick a different soliplex image, or customize backend/Dockerfile) and lets you choose.
  • Changed dev dependencies — the project's test dependencies are added to the soliplex-dev image; rebuild it and commit soliplex-dev/requirements-dev.txt.

If your backend runs without --reload, the agent leaves it that way.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py clone / add / remove / list; see Custom Python package.

items.title: Migrate databases after a version bump
items.text:
"I bumped soliplex; do the databases need migrating?" "I bumped haiku.rag; do the RAG stores need migrating?"

Most bumps need no migration: the backend migrates its own databases on startup, and most haiku.rag releases leave the store format alone. The exceptions are a stack whose databases were created by soliplex 0.81 or earlier, and a haiku.rag bump that crosses a store upgrade. The agent asks which case yours is rather than guessing, then runs a read-only check.

To apply a migration, the backend (for the soliplex databases) or the ingester (for the RAG stores) has to be stopped; the scripts refuse otherwise. The agent suggests a backup first (pg_dump, or a copy of rag/db/). When you change the haiku.rag version, it also checks that the new version is one the stack's soliplex release accepts.

By hand: the stack's own scripts/migrate_soliplex_dbs.py and scripts/migrate_rag_dbs.py, each with --check; see Database migrations.

items.title: Move an older stack to the src/ layout
items.text:
"Migrate this stack to the src/ layout."

Stacks generated before v0.16 keep their package directly under src/. The agent shows a dry run of the conversion, then applies it; the stack must be a clean git checkout, so the result is reviewable as a diff. If a file has drifted from what the script expects, nothing is changed and the error points at the manual steps for that file.

By hand: <skill>/scripts/migrate_layout.py; see Move to the src/ project layout.

items.title: Manage the skill's version
items.text:
"Is there a newer soliplex-template skill?"

The skill can list, diff, and upgrade itself against its published builds:

uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py list          # published versions, newest first
uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py diff [TAG]    # installed copy vs a published build
uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py upgrade [TAG] # install a published build in place

Release builds (v…) are attached to tagged releases; rolling builds (template-skill-YYYY.MM.DD-<sha>) track the main branch, and latest (the default TAG) means the newest rolling build. Pass a v… tag to stay on releases. Setting GITHUB_TOKEN raises the GitHub API rate limit.

items.title: Where to look
items.text: The agent's own instructions are in SKILL.md. They are written for the agent rather than for you, but they are the exact text the agent follows.

items.title: First steps
items.text: A guided walkthrough for someone new to Soliplex: install the skills, generate a stack, bring it up, and exercise the demo tool in the custom room.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A coding agent that supports filesystem Agent Skills (e.g. Claude Code).
  • On the machine the agent drives: Docker (with the Compose plugin), uv, and an Ollama server reachable from the containers that serves the models the stack will reference.

items.title: 1. Install the skills
items.text:
Install two skills into your agent. Both are listed at https://agentskills.io/; each is also published as a rolling latest release you can install from directly:

  • soliplex-template — generates and configures a stack (this template).
  • soliplex-docs — Soliplex's documentation, so the agent can answer setup and usage questions as you go.

items.title: 2. Generate a stack
items.text:
Ask the agent to generate one — e.g. "generate a new Soliplex stack". The soliplex-template skill prompts for what it needs (at minimum your Ollama URL), scaffolds a fresh project directory, and generates its secrets.

(To drive the generator by hand instead, see Generate a project.)

items.title: 3. Bring it up
items.text:
From the generated project directory, prepare the databases, then start the stack:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init
docker compose up

The first run builds the images and initializes Postgres, so it takes a few minutes. Once it settles, the web frontend is at http://localhost:9000. The stack starts with no OIDC provider, so authentication is off and there is no login step.

items.title: 4. Visit the custom room
items.text: Open http://localhost:9000 and select the Custom Tool Demo room. Every generated stack ships it to demonstrate a tool provided by the project's own Python package (src/<package>/src/<package>/tools.py).

items.title: 5. Exercise the greeting tool
items.text:
Ask the room to greet someone:

Please greet Ada.

The room's agent calls the package's greeting tool and replies with something like:

Hello, Ada! This greeting came from your own package's tool.

That round-trip — your prompt, the agent calling a tool defined in your package, and the result coming back — shows the stack already running your own code, not just stock Soliplex.

items.title: Where next
items.text: The next tutorial, Populate RAG, feeds a document set into the stack and asks questions grounded in it.

items.title: Populate RAG
items.text: Feed a set of documents into a stack and ask questions grounded in them. This continues from First steps.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A generated stack, with the soliplex-template and soliplex-docs skills installed in your agent (see First steps).
  • Your Ollama server must serve the embedding model the stack uses (qwen3-embedding:4b by default) — ingestion embeds every chunk with it.

items.title: 1. Bring the stack up
items.text:
From the generated project directory, prepare the databases once (if you haven't yet), then start the stack:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init
docker compose up

items.title: 2. Add a document set
items.text:
The haiku-ingester service watches rag/docs/ (a filesystem source). Drop Markdown files there; it hands them to docling-serve for conversion, chunks and embeds them, and writes the stack's main RAG database, rag/db/haiku.rag.lancedb.

Any Markdown works — the Soliplex documentation is a convenient corpus. If you have a checkout of it:

rsync -rv ~/projects/soliplex/docs/ rag/docs/

Watch progress on the ingester dashboard:

  • Stacks with no OIDC provider (the default) serve it at http://localhost:9000/ingester/ with the bearer injected at the proxy — nothing to type;

  • Stacks with a provider serve it (gated on the soliplex admin check) at https://localhost:9443/ingester/ and redirect to sign-in first.

Once /stats shows the documents processed and the job queue drained, the corpus is searchable.

items.title: 3. Wire the corpus into the custom room
items.text:
A freshly generated stack's custom room has only the greeting tool — no RAG. Ask your agent to wire the ingested database into it (the soliplex-template skill has a helper for exactly this). It adds a RAG skill to the room's backend/environment/rooms/custom/room_config.yaml:

skills:
  skill_configs:
    - kind: "haiku.rag.skills.rag"
      rag_lancedb_stem: "haiku.rag"

The stem haiku.rag is the ingester's database. The backend runs with --reload=config, so it picks the change up without a restart.

items.title: 4. Ask a grounded question
items.text:
Open the Custom Tool Demo room and ask something the corpus can answer, e.g.:

What secret sources does Soliplex support?

The room's agent calls its search_documents tool, retrieves the matching chunks, and answers from them, citing the source documents.

To require citing rather than leave it to the model, add the haiku.rag.skills.citation_policy skill alongside the RAG skill: it makes an answer register the evidence grounding it, or declare that nothing does. Its companion, haiku.rag.skills.evidence_compaction, must not be configured on its own — compaction builds its capsule only from what was cited, so without the policy the evidence for any uncited question is dropped. Configure both, or neither.

items.title: Where next
items.text:
The next tutorial, Add a custom tool, extends the stack with a tool of your own, exercised in a room and covered by a test.

Related: to build a second, independent knowledge base — a one-off database you create and point a room at — see Separate RAG database.

items.title: Add a custom tool
items.text: Extend a running stack with your own tool: add it to the project's Python package, wire it into a room, exercise it, and cover it with a test. This continues from First steps.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A generated stack, brought up (see First steps).
  • git and uv.
  • A stack generated by soliplex-template v0.16 or later. Earlier stacks put the package directly at src/<package>/ with its tests at the stack root, so none of the paths below will match; convert one with Move to the src/ project layout.

items.title: 1. Add a tool
items.text:
Your project is an installable Python package living in its own project directory under src/; tools live in src/<package>/src/<package>/tools.py (the greeting tool from First steps is there). Add a sibling:

# src/<package>/src/<package>/tools.py
def farewell(name: str) -> str:
    """Return a friendly farewell for ``name``."""
    return f"Goodbye, {name}! Come back soon."

The docstring matters: the LLM uses it as the tool's description.

items.title: 2. Wire it into the custom room
items.text:
Add the new tool to backend/environment/rooms/custom/room_config.yaml:

tools:
  - tool_name: "<package>.tools.greeting"
  - tool_name: "<package>.tools.farewell"

The backend watches both its config (--reload=config) and your package (a --reload-dirs flag on its serve command), so saving either file restarts it, picking up farewell. (If it doesn't appear, docker compose restart backend. A stack generated before the backend watched its package needs uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py add <package> once to start.)

items.title: 3. Test it in the room
items.text:
Open the Custom Tool Demo room and ask:

Please say farewell to Ada.

The agent calls your new tool and replies:

Goodbye, Ada! Come back soon.

items.title: 4. Add a unit test
items.text:
The generated project is also a normal Python package with a test suite already wired up: src/<package>/tests/unit/test_tools.py covers greeting. Add a case for farewell beside it (tools is already imported at the top of that file):

# src/<package>/tests/unit/test_tools.py
def test_farewell_includes_name():
    result = tools.farewell("Ada")

    assert "Ada" in result

Create the dev environment once, then run the suite:

cd src/<package>
uv sync          # installs the dev dependencies, incl. pytest
uv run pytest

No setup is needed: the project's own pyproject.toml already declares pytest, puts its src/ on the path, and points testpaths at tests/unit/, so your new test is collected and passes. (Run these from the project directory, not the stack root — the root pyproject.toml is for stack tooling.)

That run uses the project's own lock file, not the versions the backend has. To run the same tests against what the backend actually imports your code with, run them in the dev-mode soliplex-dev service, which carries your project's dev dependencies on top of the backend's image:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -w /app/src/<package> soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/python -m pytest

(The first run builds soliplex-dev.) See Running its tests there.

items.title: 5. Commit it
items.text:
From the stack root again:

cd ../..            # back to the stack root from src/<package>
git add src/<package>/src/<package>/tools.py \
    src/<package>/tests/unit/test_tools.py \
    backend/environment/rooms/custom/room_config.yaml
git commit -m "Add a farewell tool (with a test) to the custom room"

items.title: Where next
items.text:
That completes the core series: Next steps collects the optional walkthroughs you can take from here.

Related: Work with Gitea ships a change like the one you just made through a pull request hosted by the stack's own Gitea.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
You've finished the core walkthroughs — First steps, Populate RAG, and Add a custom tool. The walkthroughs below are independent; pick whichever fits what you're building.

  • Separate RAG database — build a second, independent knowledge base and point a room at it (extends Populate RAG).
  • Work with Gitea — ship a code change through a pull request hosted by the stack's own Gitea (extends Add a custom tool).
  • Hack on the backend — run the stack against a checkout of Soliplex itself, so backend edits reload live.
  • Concierge room — add an about-<project> room where users request new rooms that land as Gitea issues (builds on Work with Gitea).
  • Resolve room requests — the administrator side: review the request issues, create the room, and close them (builds on Concierge room).

items.title: Hack on the backend
items.text: Run your stack against a checkout of Soliplex itself instead of the pinned release, so an edit to the backend source restarts the server the way an edit to your own package or under backend/environment/ already does. This builds on the core walkthroughs — First steps through Add a custom tool — so have a stack you have brought up at least once.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A generated stack, up and working (the three core tutorials).

  • A soliplex-template skill build of v0.16 or later — that release introduced both the src/ project layout and src_projects.py — and recent enough to watch every project on the path: its src_projects.py list shows a watched column. Ask your agent to upgrade it, or:

    uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py list
uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py upgrade

  • A stack in the v0.16 src/ project layout. If you generated yours by following an earlier version of these tutorials, convert it first — see Move to the src/ project layout. This is not optional, and nothing will stop you: an older stack has PYTHONPATH: /app/src, which src_projects.py happily appends to, leaving the mount point itself an import root. src/ is then a sys.path entry, so the checkout's repo root joins soliplex.__path__ ahead of the real package — soliplex.alembic and soliplex.tests become importable, and the package you meant to edit is the second portion, not the first.

    list is the cheap pre-flight check; run it before step 1:

    uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py list

    A converted stack names each project and shows your own marked * and on the path. An unconverted one gives itself away with a (no such directory) /app/src yes row.

  • A stack whose own project is not named soliplex. Its project directory would be src/soliplex/ — exactly where the checkout goes. The generator defaults to soliplex-dojo for this reason; if you named yours soliplex, generate a fresh one for this walkthrough.

items.title: 1. Clone Soliplex into src/
items.text:
Every entry under a stack's src/ is a project directory, and the checkout becomes a sibling of your own project. Ask your agent to "clone the soliplex backend into this stack's src/". The skill runs:

uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py clone https://github.com/soliplex/soliplex

That does three things: clones the repo to src/soliplex/, appends /app/src/soliplex/src to the backend's PYTHONPATH in docker-compose.yml, and adds a matching --reload-dirs=/app/src/soliplex/src to the backend's serve command. It reports what it did:

cloned https://github.com/soliplex/soliplex into src/soliplex
added: /app/src/soliplex/src
  dependencies: every runtime dependency src/soliplex declares is already
                in the backend image.
  reload: watching /app/src/soliplex/src ('--reload-dirs')

Every project on the backend's path is watched the same way, your own package from the start, so nothing here is specific to Soliplex. On an older stack it also settles the reload mode: --reload=both becomes --reload=config, since the checkout's --reload-dirs now does what both added; --reload=python stays, being what turns reload on without watching the config, and the script notes that --reload=config would work as well.

Nothing is needed for git: .gitignore already ignores everything under src/ except the stack's own project, so the checkout stays part of its own repo.

items.title: 2. Restart the backend
items.text:
Editing docker-compose.yml is a compose change, which --reload=config does not pick up:

docker compose up -d backend

items.title: 3. Confirm the checkout is what's running
items.text:
PYTHONPATH is searched before site-packages, so the checkout's modules win over the installed release. Check it from inside the container with the soliplex-dev service, which mirrors the backend's PYTHONPATH exactly:

docker compose run --rm soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/python -c "import soliplex; print(soliplex.__path__)"

['/app/src/soliplex/src/soliplex', '/app/.venv/lib/.../site-packages/soliplex']

soliplex is a namespace package, so those two directories merge rather than one shadowing the other: every module the checkout has wins, and the installed release fills the gaps. Two consequences worth knowing —

  • a module the checkout deletes or renames stays importable from the installed copy, so a clean-looking run may still be executing old code;
  • nothing was installed, so the distribution metadata still reports the pinned version. Anything that reads it — pip list, the admin /v1/installation/versions view — shows the release, not the checkout.

items.title: 4. Watch an edit take effect
items.text:
Follow the backend's log in one terminal:

docker compose logs -f backend

Then edit any module under src/soliplex/src/soliplex/ on the host. The reloader, watching the checkout through its --reload-dirs, notices the change and restarts the server, and the next request runs your edited code — no rebuild, no docker compose up.

The mount is read-only for the backend and the container runs as the PUID:PGID from .env, so edit on the host; the backend only reads.

items.title: 5. Run backend tasks against the stack
items.text:
soliplex-dev is a one-shot task runner (held out of docker compose up by profiles: ["devmode"]) built on the backend's image, with the stack's config, secrets and databases — and src/ mounted read-write. Validate the installation the backend actually serves:

docker compose run --rm soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli audit /environment

A checkout of main is usually ahead of the pinned release, so its database schema may be too. The backend applies the checkout's revisions itself when it restarts, since it migrates on startup; to apply them first, where you can see them, run soliplex-cli database in the same environment:

docker compose run --rm soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment

(database status in place of upgrade reports without changing anything.)

soliplex-dev also carries every src/ project's dev dependency group, so the checkout's own test suite runs against the backend's versions. Cloning it added its group to soliplex-dev/requirements-dev.txt; rebuild, then run it from the checkout's root:

docker compose build soliplex-dev
docker compose run --rm --no-deps -w /app/src/soliplex soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/python -m pytest

A dev requirement that needs a different version of something the image has fails that build, the same conflict step 6 describes, met in the dev group. Generate new revisions with alembic itself, from the checkout's own root (alembic writes into versions/ and prepends . to sys.path, so the -w matters):

docker compose run --rm -w /app/src/soliplex soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/alembic -x soliplex.installation_path=/environment \
    revision --autogenerate -m "add a column"

items.title: 6. When you need a rebuild
items.text:
PYTHONPATH makes source importable; it does not install anything. If the checkout imports a distribution the backend image lacks, the import fails at runtime and docker compose up -d backend will not fix it. clone/add check each requirement the checkout declares inside the backend image, and report it as satisfied, MISSING (not installed), or CONFLICT (installed, at a version the checkout rejects); without Docker, or before the image is built, they say they could not check.

A missing distribution goes in backend/requirements.txt, then

docker compose build backend
docker compose up -d backend

A conflict cannot be fixed that way: the build freezes the image's own versions as constraints, and fails rather than move one. A checkout of main that has moved a dependency ahead of the latest release is the usual case. In order of preference:

  1. adapt the checkout to the image's versions — relax its requirement, and port any code that needs the newer one; you cloned it to work on it;
  2. pick a soliplex image tag (the FROM line in backend/Dockerfile) whose release has versions it accepts;
  3. customize backend/Dockerfile.

See Backend image & dependencies.

The check covers the checkout's direct requirements only. To catch a problem deeper in its tree, import it in the backend's environment:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/python -c "import soliplex.main"

An ImportError names what the image lacks or has at the wrong version; see Checking it in the backend's environment.

items.title: 7. Going back to the release
items.text:
Take the checkout off the import path and the watch list — it leaves the clone itself untouched:

uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py remove soliplex

Then docker compose up -d backend. At any point, src_projects.py list shows which projects are under src/, which are on the path, and which are watched.

items.title: Where next
items.text: The same mechanism works for any repo, not just Soliplex — a library you depend on, a tool you are patching — hot reload included. See Custom Python package for that, and Next steps for the other walkthroughs.

items.title: Resolve room requests
items.text: The administrator's side of the concierge: review the room requests filed as Gitea issues, create the requested room, and close the request. Start with Concierge room so you have a request to resolve.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A stack with the concierge installed and at least one open request (see Concierge room).
  • The soliplex-template skill, plus the soliplex-concierge-admin skill, installed in your agent.
  • Access to the tracking repo with a token that can comment on and close issues (typically more privileged than the room's issue-filing token).

items.title: 1. Install the admin skill
items.text: Install the soliplex-concierge-admin skill into your agent. It drives gitea_issues.py — the installer dropped a copy at scripts/gitea_issues.py in your stack, so the same CLI runs from the stack directory, configured with your Gitea host and admin token (via flags or GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN).

items.title: 2. Review the open requests
items.text:
Ask your agent — using the soliplex-concierge-admin skill — to list the open requests:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py list --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

The research request from Concierge room appears, tagged new-room. Read its details — name, purpose, knowledge sources, access — with:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py show <number> --owner <owner> --repo <repo>

(If the request labels were never created, run gitea_issues.py init once; it is idempotent.)

items.title: 3. Create the requested room
items.text:
Ask your agent — using the soliplex-template skill — to create the room the issue describes: its name, prompt, and any requested tools, plus a RAG database if knowledge sources were named. Then commit the new room to main and push it to Gitea:

git add backend/environment/rooms/research/
git commit -m "Add the 'research' room (concierge request #<number>)"
git push

Unlike the developer pull-request flow, an administrator fulfilling a request commits straight to main.1

items.title: 4. Resolve the request
items.text:
Once the room is live, ask your agent (admin skill) to record the outcome and close the issue:

uv run scripts/gitea_issues.py close <number> --owner <owner> --repo <repo> \
    --body "Created the 'research' room and pushed it to main."

The requester sees the new room in their room list, and the issue closes with a note of what was done.

items.title: Where next
items.text:
The admin skill also resolves private-room access requests — granting or denying a user access to an existing room — which work the same way: review, act, and close.

Back to Next steps.

  1. You can let the push close the request instead of doing step 4: add a closing keyword to the commit message — e.g. a Closes #<number> line — and Gitea closes the referenced issue when the commit lands on main. The skill's explicit close is still worth it when you want to record an outcome comment alongside the closure. ↩

items.title: Concierge room
items.text: Add self-service room requests to a stack: an about-<project> room where users ask for new rooms, and each request is filed as a Gitea issue for an administrator to act on. This builds on Work with Gitea — you need the in-stack Gitea provisioned.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A stack with Gitea provisioned (see Work with Gitea), including the tracking repo and an access token.1
  • The soliplex-template skill installed in your agent (see First steps).

items.title: 1. Install the concierge extension
items.text: Install the soliplex-concierge-installer skill into your agent. (When you run it in the next step, it also fetches the soliplex-concierge-room and soliplex-docs skills it depends on.)

items.title: 2. Add the about-<project> room
items.text: Ask your agent — using the soliplex-concierge-installer skill — to wire concierge into your stack, pointed at your Gitea owner and repo. The skill runs its bundled apply.py (previewing with a dry run, then applying), which creates the about-<project> room — hosting a create_gitea_issue tool and the soliplex-concierge-room skill — and merges the matching installation.yaml entries.

items.title: 3. Rebuild the backend
items.text:
apply.py edits backend/pyproject.toml, backend/Dockerfile, .env, and backend/environment/, so rebuild and restart the backend to pick up the new dependency and configuration:

docker compose up -d --build backend

The about-<project> room then appears in the room list.

items.title: 4. Request a room
items.text:
Open the about-<project> room and ask for a new one, e.g.:

Please open a room called "research" for the research team.

The room's agent calls its create_gitea_issue tool and files the request.

items.title: 5. Confirm the request in Gitea
items.text: In the Gitea web UI, open the tracking repo's Issues — your request is there, labelled new-room, ready for an administrator to act on.

items.title: Where next
items.text:
An administrator reviews these requests, creates the room with the soliplex-template skill, and resolves the issue — using the soliplex-concierge-admin skill. See Resolve room requests.

Back to Next steps.

  1. The concierge can file against any Gitea repository, so your stack need not run its own gitea service at all. If you use an external Gitea repository, ensure the token you supply has Write access to the repo: a read-only token can open issues but Gitea silently drops their labels, so requests would arrive untagged. ↩

items.title: Separate RAG database
items.text: Build a second, independent knowledge base — a one-off database you create and point a room at — alongside the ingester's continuously-updated one. This builds on Populate RAG, so do that first (it covers ingesting a corpus and querying it from a room).

items.title: 1. Build a separate, static database
items.text: The haiku-ingester service maintains one continuously-updated database (rag/db/haiku.rag.lancedb). For a separate corpus you build once, ask the agent to create a standalone database — say a handbook from another directory of Markdown. The skill builds rag/db/handbook.lancedb as a one-off, independent of the ingester's database (and it refuses to overwrite the ingester's own database while that service is running).

items.title: 2. Point a cloned room at it
items.text:
Ask the agent

Ask the agent to clone the custom room under a new id — say handbook — and wire that copy to the new database (rag_lancedb_stem: "handbook") instead of the ingester's. Open the new room and ask a question answerable from the handbook corpus: it answers from that database, while the custom room still uses the ingester's.

A room is not limited to one: list both under rag_databases and a single search covers them together. See Searching several databases at once.

items.title: Where next
items.text: Back to Next steps for the other optional walkthroughs.

items.title: Work with Gitea
items.text: Ship a change through a pull request — hosted by the Gitea that runs inside the stack itself. This builds on Add a custom tool.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The soliplex-template skill installed in your agent (see First steps).
  • git and an SSH key available (in your ssh-agent, or ~/.ssh/*.pub) — --push-to-gitea registers it and pushes over SSH.

items.title: 1. Generate a stack with Gitea
items.text:
Ask your agent to generate a stack with the Gitea service included (include_gitea). Then bring it up from the project directory:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init
docker compose up

items.title: 2. Provision Gitea and back the repo
items.text:
With the stack up, provision Gitea and point the project's git at it:

uv run scripts/init_gitea.py --admin-user yourname --push-to-gitea

This creates a web-UI admin user yourname (prompting for its password), registers your SSH key, creates a repo, sets the project's git origin to it, and pushes the initial commit. nginx serves the Gitea web UI at /gitea/ on the HTTPS port.

items.title: 3. Make a change on a branch
items.text:
Work on a branch so the change can land through review:

git checkout -b add-farewell

Now make a change following Add a custom tool: add the farewell tool, wire it into the custom room, test it, and commit. That commit lands on this branch.

items.title: 4. Push the branch
items.text:
git push -u origin add-farewell

The push goes to the in-stack Gitea over SSH (the remote init_gitea.py set).

items.title: 5. Open a pull request
items.text: Sign in to the Gitea web UI (the /gitea/ path on the HTTPS port) as the admin user from step 2. Gitea shows the freshly pushed add-farewell branch and offers to open a pull request against main; create it.

items.title: 6. Merge it
items.text: Review the diff in Gitea and merge the pull request from the web UI. Back in the project, git checkout main && git pull brings the merged change down — your stack now runs code you shipped through its own review workflow.

items.title: Where next
items.text: The Concierge room walkthrough builds on this one — adding an about-<project> room where users request new rooms that land as Gitea issues. See also the other Next steps.

items.title: Upgrading an existing stack
items.text: A generated stack belongs to you. Regenerating it would throw away your rooms, prompts and configuration, and nothing yet updates one in place, so bringing an older stack up to the current template is a by-hand job. This page lists the changes in order, grouped by the template release that introduced them: find the section your stack is at, and work forward from there.

items.title: Where do I start?
items.text:
Your stack What its files show Skill release to walk with Start at generated before soliplex-template v0.16 the package sits directly under src/ (src/<package>/tools.py), with tests/ at the stack root v0.16.2 0 soliplex 0.84 or earlier backend/constraints.txt pins below 0.85 v0.18b1 1 soliplex 0.85, built from PyPI backend/Dockerfile runs uv add … soliplex v0.18 2 on the 0.85 release images backend/Dockerfile builds FROM ghcr.io/soliplex/soliplex-postgres:0.85 v0.19b1 3 soliplex 0.86.1 backend/Dockerfile builds FROM ghcr.io/soliplex/soliplex-postgres:0.86.1 v0.19b2 4 soliplex 0.87 nginx/nginx.conf rewrites other cookies' SameSite via a catch-all proxy_cookie_flags; the ingester bearer rides an INGESTER_TOKEN compose environment entry v0.19 5 soliplex 0.87, serving through nginx nginx/nginx.conf routes /ingester/; docker-compose.yml has no soliplex-provisioner service v0.20 6 soliplex 0.89, provisioning rooms docker-compose.yml has a soliplex-provisioner service but no stack-init one; nginx/nginx.conf includes nothing from conf.d/ v0.21b1 7 soliplex 0.89, with stack-init docker-compose.yml's soliplex-provisioner runs soliplex_template.provision_service:create_app v0.21 8 soliplex 0.89, with the provisioner on concierge docker-compose.yml's soliplex-provisioner runs soliplex_template.provisioner.wiring:create_app v0.22 9 soliplex 0.89, through rung 9 backend/Dockerfile builds FROM ghcr.io/soliplex/soliplex-postgres:0.89 v0.24 10

Releases without rungs

The v0.23 template introduces no rung: nothing in the generated skeleton changed, so a stack through rung 9 is current — no migration to apply. What it adds to an existing stack:

  • the opt-in in-stack Authelia provider. Install it with skills/soliplex-template/scripts/install_authelia.py: the script splices its compose.authelia.yaml include: into docker-compose.yml and writes the nginx/conf.d/authelia.conf fragment itself. It relies on the conf.d fragment directory and a stack-init service, both in place after rung 7. Manage the users it creates with skills/soliplex-template/scripts/authelia_users.py.
  • refreshed doc pointers: the generated AGENTS.md and docker-compose.yml comments name the room-provisioning docs as a directory (docs/operations/room-provisioning/service.md), where older stacks still carry the single room-provisioning.md page. Cosmetic — refresh the stack's own agent-facing docs with the next upgrade (Afterwards), or by hand.

The [tool.soliplex-template] manifest at the end of the stack's pyproject.toml records the skill commit (skill_source_commit) and date (skill_generated) that generated it, and the parameters it was generated with. (skill_version may be empty.)

Compare against a fresh stack

Each step names what the current template has. To see it in place, generate a throwaway stack with the skill release the rung walks with (see Before you start #1) and your own parameters, and diff the two; see Checking the whole stack against a reference.

Which haiku.rag pairs with which soliplex?

The two pins are not a free pair: the ingester writes the LanceDB the backend reads, so its haiku.rag-slim release must stay inside the range the pinned soliplex release declares — including for --params overrides. Every rung below names its pair; the full generated table sits in the appendix at the end of this page.

items.title: How an upgrade runs
items.text:
Every upgrade on this page should follow this phased process:

  1. Prepare — "Before you start": the new skill, a clean branch, the stack stopped, the state recorded and backed up.
  2. Run the rung — the numbered section Where do I start? named for your stack's state.
  3. Check it — the shared verification checklist: the audit's database lines and a room's ask.
  4. Afterwards — restore dev mode, refresh the stack's own agent-facing docs. Still on the rung's branch.
  5. Roll out — merge the branch to main and bring the live stack up on the merged state. main carries the files; the migration steps the rung rehearsed (the queue migration, the LanceDB store upgrades, the Alembic head) run live, against the deployment's own stores and databases, in the rollout's stop-apply-restart order.

Each phase completes before the next begins: a rung is not done until it has passed Check it and its commit exists, and no rung starts with the previous one unfinished.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
1. Upgrade the soliplex-template skill in your harness, then pick the release that matches the rung being walked: the rung's steps run the skill's scripts (src_projects.py), and its generator renders the reference stack the rung compares against. The release this page describes is the right one for the newest rung (10); earlier rungs walk with the release that generated the shape the rung lands on — the stack's own manifest (skill_source_commit in [tool.soliplex-template]) names the release that generated it, the one the rung moving from it needs.

    Every rung names a software release (v…). A rung whose end state fell between two regular releases has a pre-release cut for it (e.g. v0.18b1).

    For instance, upgrade rung #1 above specifies the v0.18b1 skill release. If that is your rung, ask your agent, e.g.:

    Set the installed soliplex-template skill to the `v0.18b1` release.

    or run its helper yourself (list shows the published releases, diff what a move would change; upgrade installs whichever release it is given, older or newer than the installed one — no need to pass through the newest release first):

    uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py list
uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py upgrade v0.18b1   # e.g. rung 1
