  • in stacks with Gitea, scripts/init_gitea.py creates the tracking repository's provision-status labels (provision-start, provision-complete, provision-incomplete, provision-failed); the provisioner files new-room issues tagged provision-start, and tags one of the others when the provision resolves or fails (see Room provisioning)

Where a step differs, it says which kind of stack it means:

  • a stack with provisions has directories under src/rooms-provisioned/
  • a stack with the concierge has a soliplex-concierge line in backend/requirements.txt, and an about-<project> room
  • a stack with Gitea has GITEA_HOST set in .env

Skip the steps that do not apply. Each names what the current template has; compare against a stack the rung's release generates.

  1. Stop the stack with docker compose down. This rung changes no database, so no backup is needed beyond your usual one.

  2. In a stack with provisions, choose the room id form. Listing the clone shows which forms a stack's rooms live in:

ls src/rooms-provisioned/

Rooms provisioned before rung 8 are in the : form; rooms provisioned under it follow the framework's default, --. In .env, set the form the stack keeps:

# Keep the room ids' legacy ':' form
PROVISIONER_ROOM_ID_SEPARATOR=:

Stacks whose rooms are all ---form, or that provisioned none, leave it unset: -- is the default everywhere. A clone holding both forms: set the form new provisions should file, and reconcile reads the rooms that match; rooms in the other form keep working as rooms, but after a docker compose down -v their stored authz.yaml records must be replayed by hand, room-authz from-yaml per room from each clone directory. There is no rename tool yet.

  1. In a stack with the concierge, raise its pin to 0.15. In backend/requirements.txt, change the soliplex-concierge line's version (for example soliplex-concierge[truststore]==0.14 to ==0.15). soliplex-dev installs soliplex-template 0.22 with the backend image's versions as constraints, so an older concierge pin makes its build fail.

  2. Install soliplex-template 0.22 in soliplex-dev. In soliplex-dev/Dockerfile, change the SOLIPLEX_TEMPLATE default:

    ARG SOLIPLEX_TEMPLATE="soliplex-template[provisioner]>=0.22"

  3. Rebuild and start. The backend image rebuilds in a stack with the concierge, for its new pin; soliplex-dev and soliplex-provisioner rebuild in every stack:

docker compose build backend soliplex-dev soliplex-provisioner
docker compose up -d
  1. In a stack with Gitea, create the labels. Run the stack's Gitea setup again: it is idempotent, and it now also creates the tracking repository's provision-status labels. Until it runs, a provision cannot file: the provisioner tags the issue as it files, and the labels do not exist yet. It rotates the service account's token, so recreate the services that read .env afterwards:
uv run scripts/init_gitea.py
docker compose up -d backend soliplex-provisioner
  1. Reconcile, to see where the clone stands. Rooms whose ids parse the configured form are named in the report; rooms without an authz.yaml are reported, and their policies left alone:
docker compose run --rm --quiet-build soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-provision-room --reconcile

  1. Check it.

    Then check that the provisioner service answers (GET /ok through the compose network, or docker compose ps soliplex-provisioner reporting it healthy).

    Commit.
path: Room id forms and tracker labels

items.title: Serve through nginx
items.text:
Part of Upgrading an existing stack.

Walk this rung with the v0.19 skill release — its generator produces the rung's end state (only nginx published by default; the ingester control plane served behind nginx at /ingester/; its bearer token a file-backed Docker secret). The stack being upgraded names the release that generated it in its own [tool.soliplex-template] manifest — use that one when climbing from an older shape.

uv run <skill>/scripts/skill_versions.py upgrade v0.19

This rung bumps no releases — soliplex, haiku.rag-slim, docling-serve and the frontend all stay as the stack has them, and it touches no databases or RAG stores, so none of the migration machinery applies. What changes:

  • the edge: by default only nginx is published to the host; every other service's host port becomes opt-in via a *_port parameter;
  • the ingester control plane: always served behind nginx at /ingester/, its bearer token injected by the proxy from the new file-backed Docker secret ingester_bearer — never an environment variable — and, in auth-mode stacks, gated on soliplex admin auth;
  • nginx keeps the soliplex_authn cookie's SameSite=Lax under proxied rewrites of other cookies;
  • the .secrets/.env provisioning scripts gain rotation and recovery features.

Skip the steps that do not apply.

  1. Stop the stack with docker compose down. This rung migrates nothing, so backing up first is optional; the stack stays down until the last step.

  2. Fetch the updated stack scripts. generate_secrets.py (required: it provisions the new ingester_bearer secret, see step 10) and generate_env.py (optional: recreates a fresh clone's missing .env from the manifest, see Installation). Fetch them into the stack's scripts/ directory, the way Before you start describes:

    for s in generate_secrets generate_env; do
    curl -fsSL -o "scripts/$s.py" \
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soliplex/soliplex-template/main/scripts/$s.py"
done

    Both are PEP 723 shims over the soliplex-template package, which uv run provisions on first use: they need soliplex-template 0.19 (or later) published on PyPI, which is the release this rung ships with.

  3. Exempt the authn cookie from the cookie-flags rewrite, in nginx/nginx.conf — above the catch-all

        proxy_cookie_flags ~ HttpOnly Secure SameSite=None;

    (there is normally one, in the TLS server block; check both blocks if the stack customized them), add the no-op flag line for the soliplex authn cookie:

        # SameSite=None is required for federation flows, but must not apply
    # to the soliplex authn cookie: rewriting it to SameSite=None would
    # let other origins carry the session cookie. nginx applies the
    # first matching directive, and this one lists a flag the backend
    # already sets, so the catch-all below never runs for it.
    proxy_cookie_flags soliplex_authn httponly;
    proxy_cookie_flags ~ HttpOnly Secure SameSite=None;

  4. Give the nginx service the ingester bearer and a rendered config. In docker-compose.yml, in the nginx service:

    add haiku-ingester to depends_on (nginx now routes to it, and must not start ahead of it):

        depends_on:
      - backend
      - haiku-ingester

    (keep the stack's existing tui / gitea lines below it), and mount the new secret onto the service and swap the plain command for the wrapper that fails loudly on a missing token and renders it into a copy of the config (nginx cannot read a secret file inside location blocks, nor expand environment references in its configuration). Add both below volumes:, as the template has them:

        secrets:
      - ingester_bearer

    #
    # '$$' is Compose's escape for a literal '$': the container's shell
    # sees '$(cat ...)'.
    #
    # Tokens are generated as [A-Za-z0-9]{32} (scripts/generate_secrets.py),
    # so the sed below cannot trip on metacharacters in its replacement.
    command:
      - sh
      - -ec
      - |
        # Fail loudly on a missing or empty token.
        test -s /run/secrets/ingester_bearer || {
            echo "error: /run/secrets/ingester_bearer missing or empty; run 'uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py'" >&2
            exit 1
        }
        # nginx cannot read a secret file inside 'location' blocks, nor
        # environment references in its configuration: substitute the
        # ingester bearer into a copy of the config instead.
        sed "s|@@INGESTER_BEARER@@|$$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_bearer)|g" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf > /tmp/nginx.conf
        exec nginx -c /tmp/nginx.conf -g 'daemon off;'

  5. Point the ingester service at the shared bearer. In the haiku-ingester service:

    replace its command: with the block below — it adds the INGESTER_TOKEN export (the shared haiku.rag.yaml interpolates the token, so the ingester needs it in the environment) and the --root-path /ingester serve flag that mounts the API and the dashboard's <base href> under the public prefix, so nginx's /ingester/ locations (step 8) can strip it before proxying:

        command:
      - sh
      - -ec
      - |
        # haiku.rag interpolates environment references in its own config
        # (0.57+), so the ingester reads the bind-mounted yaml directly -- no
        # rendered copy. Pending a possible direct read (ggozad/haiku-rag#749),
        # read secrets files into the environment variables expected by its
        # interpolation.
        # - queue password:
        export INGESTER_DB_PASSWORD="$$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_db_password)"
        # - control plane bearer token:
        export INGESTER_TOKEN="$$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_bearer)"
        # The queue role owns its schema; prepare it before serving.
        haiku-ingester --config /app/haiku.rag.yaml queue migrate
        # '--root-path /ingester' mounts the API (and the dashboard's
        # <base href>) under the public prefix so nginx's '/ingester/'
        # locations strip it before proxying.
        exec haiku-ingester --config /app/haiku.rag.yaml serve --root-path /ingester

    delete the INGESTER_TOKEN entry from its environment: block (and its three comment lines) — the token is a secret file now, not an environment variable:

        # delete these three comment lines and the entry:
    #  # Bearer token clients must send to /jobs, /sources, /dlq, etc.
    #  # Override in '.env'; the default 'secret' is intentionally weak
    #  # so unhardened deployments fail an obvious security review.
    #  INGESTER_TOKEN: ${INGESTER_TOKEN:-secret}

    add the secret to its secrets: list:

        secrets:
      - ingester_db_password
      - ingester_bearer

  6. Give the one-shot CLI the bearer too. In the haiku-rag service, the shared haiku.rag.yaml interpolates INGESTER_TOKEN, so its entrypoint must export it as well — and it takes the second secret on its secrets: list:

        entrypoint:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |
        export INGESTER_DB_PASSWORD="$$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_db_password)"
        # The shared haiku.rag.yaml interpolates INGESTER_TOKEN as well (it
        # describes the 'haiku-ingester' service's API), so the CLI needs it
        # in the environment even though it never calls the API itself.
        export INGESTER_TOKEN="$$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_bearer)"
        exec haiku-rag --config /app/haiku.rag.yaml "$$@"
      - haiku-rag

    secrets:
      - ingester_db_password
      - ingester_bearer

  7. Declare the secret at the top level of docker-compose.yml, beside the other *.gen files:

        secrets:
        ingester_db_password:
            file: ./.secrets/ingester_db_password.gen
        ingester_bearer:
            file: ./.secrets/ingester_bearer.gen
        postgres_password:
            file: ./.secrets/postgres_password.gen
        # ... the stack's remaining secrets unchanged

  8. Route /ingester/ through nginx, in nginx/nginx.conf. In each server { block (both listen 9000 and listen 9443):

    teach the backend-down handler the new prefix, so control-plane outages get the JSON error for API clients — add |ingester to the handler's if regex:

        location @backend_down {
        default_type application/json;
        if ($uri ~ ^/(api|mcp|ingester)/) {
            return 503 '{"error": "service_unavailable", "message": "Backend is temporarily unavailable"}';
        }
        # ...
    }

    Then add the two routing locations (between the versioned assets location and the /tui redirect, as the template has them):

        # Bare /ingester -> the dashboard and <base href> live under the
    # trailing slash.
    location = /ingester {
        return 301 /ingester/;
    }

    location /ingester/ {
        proxy_intercept_errors off;
        error_page 502 503 504 = @backend_down;
        error_page 403 /error-pages/403.html;
        limit_req zone=api burst=100 nodelay;

        # Use variable to force DNS re-resolution via the resolver
        # directive.
        set $backend_ingester "haiku-ingester";
        rewrite ^/ingester/?(.*)$ /$1 break;

        proxy_pass http://$backend_ingester:8765;

        proxy_no_cache 1;
        proxy_cache_bypass 1;
        proxy_cache off;
        proxy_set_header Host $host$host_port;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $backend_port;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $backend_proto;
        proxy_set_header Authorization "Bearer @@INGESTER_BEARER@@";
        proxy_connect_timeout 10;
        proxy_send_timeout 60;
        proxy_read_timeout 600;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;
        chunked_transfer_encoding off;
    }

    (X-Forwarded-Proto spells $backend_proto in the HTTP server and the literal https in the TLS one, matching how the block already proxies /api/.)

    Stacks whose backend runs with auth — no --no-auth-mode in the backend service's command: — also gate the surface on soliplex admin auth, in both server blocks and once at http scope:

    # at http scope, above the first server block:
# '/ingester/' gate: a 401 redirects the browser's top-level navigations
# to sign-in, while the dashboard's own polling fetch()es must get a
# plain 401. Any 'Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate' request is a browser
# navigation.
map $http_sec_fetch_mode $soliplex_navigate {
    default 0;
    navigate 1;
}

    # inside each server block, beside the other named locations:
# Named location for the '/ingester/' gate's 401: navigations to
# sign-in, everything else a plain JSON 401 (see the map above).
# '$request_uri' is still the original request's URI, so the
# sign-in flow returns the browser to the page it wanted.
location @ingester_signin {
    if ($soliplex_navigate) {
        # delivery=cookie makes the login set the authn cookie the
        # check (and its callers) read; the provider id matches the
        # auth_systems entry in 'oidc/config.yaml' -- keep the two in
        # step when editing that config.
        return 302 "/api/login/keycloak?delivery=cookie&return_to=$request_uri";
    }
    return 401 '{"error": "signin_required", "message": "Sign in with an admin account to use the ingester control plane"}';
}

# Internal auth_request target for the '/ingester/' gate:
# - 204 lets the request proceed
# - 401 lands in @ingester_signin
# - 403 gets the stack's error
location = /_authz_check {
    internal;
    set $backend_authz "backend";
    proxy_pass http://$backend_authz:8000/api/v1/authz/check/ingester;
    proxy_pass_request_body off;
    proxy_set_header Content-Length "";
}

    With those in place, the gate itself goes into the location /ingester/ routing block added above, in two spots, in both server blocks. Above the limit_req zone=api burst=100 nodelay; line (directly after the existing error_page 403 ... line):

            # The gate (auth-mode stacks): an admin's authn cookie passes
        # the check; anything else 401s into @ingester_signin (401) or
        # the stack's 403 page. In no-auth stacks the backend check
        # would answer 204 for everyone, so the gate is omitted.
        auth_request /_authz_check;
        auth_request_set $soliplex_user $upstream_http_x_soliplex_user;
        error_page 401 = @ingester_signin;

    and directly above the `proxy_set_header Authorization "Bearer ..." line:

            # Set by the auth_request above ('X-Soliplex-User'); names the
        # caller for the control plane's logs.
        proxy_set_header X-Soliplex-User $soliplex_user;

    (the provider id keycloak in the sign-in redirect matches the auth_systems entry in the stack's backend/environment/oidc/config.yaml — use the stack's own id there.)

  9. Decide which host ports stay published. The current template publishes only nginx (9000, 9443): every other service is opt-in via a *_port parameter, recorded in the manifest's [tool.soliplex-template.params] table and baked into the compose file as a literal host port at generation time. Nothing ports-related lives in .env. For each service with a published port today, either:

    • Adopt the default and unpublish it — delete its ports: block from docker-compose.yml (8000:8000 on backend, 8765:8765 on haiku-ingester, 5001:5001 on docling-serve, 5432:5432 on postgres, 3000:3000 / 2222:2222 on gitea), and delete the matching keys from the manifest (ingester_port, docling_port, postgres_port, plus backend_port, gitea_http_port, gitea_ssh_port where present).

    • Keep it published — the compose mapping is already a literal host port and needs no change; just make the manifest agree: keep ingester_port, docling_port, postgres_port; add backend_port = 8000 if the backend stays directly reachable, and gitea_http_port = 3000 / gitea_ssh_port = 2222 in gitea stacks. (gitea_ssh_port is the only way to keep git-over-SSH clones from the host working; web use needs nothing — nginx serves the forge at /gitea/.)

    Per-service choices are fine. A stack which keeps the ingester or backend direct still gets the new nginx route: the control plane is served either way, and the /ingester/ route is the browser-dashboard path.

  10. Provision the bearer, then bring the stack up. With the updated generate_secrets.py from step 2:

    uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py

    It provisions only the secrets whose .gen files are missing — this rung's only new one is .secrets/ingester_bearer.gen (32 alphanumeric characters, the spelling the nginx wrapper's sed expects) — leaving every existing secret untouched. If .env carries an INGESTER_TOKEN line (older stacks could set it as an override), delete it: the token is a secret file now and the compose no longer reads it from the environment.

    Then rebuild nothing (the nginx config is bind-mounted and the scripts are not baked into any image) and start the stack:

    docker compose up -d
docker compose logs nginx | head      # started clean: no 'sed' or bearer errors

    Open http://localhost:9000/ingester/ — the dashboard loads, and in auth-mode stacks the browser first runs the admin sign-in. If the stack kept a direct published port, its bearer-authed API answers without nginx:

    curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat .secrets/ingester_bearer.gen)" \
    http://localhost:8765/stats

    Then Check it, and commit.

    Afterwards, refresh the stack's agent-facing docs from a reference stack as usual — this rung rewrites the ports paragraph, the "Ingester control plane auth" section and the haiku-ingester / haiku-rag service descriptions in AGENTS.md, and the corresponding pages under docs/.

items.title: ${project_name}
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

A Soliplex Docker Compose stack — nginx + Soliplex backend + Flutter frontend + haiku-ingester + Postgres, plus docling-serve and a TUI — scaffolded from the soliplex-template generator.

This site documents this project. The quickest path to a running stack is the README.md at the project root; for the full walkthrough see Installation.

items.title: Services
items.text:
• nginx — serves the Flutter web frontend and reverse-proxies the API.
  • backend — the Soliplex server (soliplex-cli serve).
  • haiku-ingester — the document-pipeline writer for the RAG vector store.
  • docling-serve — stateless document converter.
  • postgres — thread persistence and authorization policy.

items.title: Exposed ports
items.text:
Only nginx is published by default; every other service binds only the compose network — set a *_port parameter (ingester_port, docling_port, postgres_port, backend_port, gitea_http_port, gitea_ssh_port) to publish one.

Service Host port (published) nginx (HTTP) ${nginx_http} nginx (HTTPS) ${nginx_https}

| haiku-ingester | ${ingester_port} (opt-in) |

| docling-serve | ${docling_port} (opt-in) |

| postgres | ${postgres_port} (opt-in) |

items.title: Documentation map
items.text:
• Installation — generate secrets, confirm OLLAMA_BASE_URL, bring the stack up.
  • Service graph — what each container does and how they connect.
  • Backend configuration — the backend/environment/ layout and the sandbox.
  • Backend image & dependencies — building the backend image and adding dependencies.
  • Secrets — file-based vs env-var secret modes.
  • RAG pipeline — the vector store, the ingester, and adding documents.
  • Ingester control plane — the control-plane API and its auth token.
  • Custom Python package — the installable src/${package_name} project, and how to clone others alongside it.

items.title: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider
items.text:
The stack starts with no OIDC provider, and so without authentication: anyone who can reach nginx uses it as Soliplex's fixed no-auth user. That is fine on a workstation. To require sign-in, add a provider — either one the stack runs itself, or one operated elsewhere. Both are added after the stack is generated, by scripts the soliplex-template skill bundles; the backend picks up a change by itself (--reload=config), and the scripts keep nginx's /ingester/ sign-in in step.

Choice Provider runs Fit No sign-in — workstation use; add one before exposing the stack In-stack Authelia inside the stack one place to give accounts to; no IdP operator to deal with External provider Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID, ... users already live there; your org runs it
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: Staying without sign-in
items.text: With no auth_systems entry in backend/environment/oidc/config.yaml, the backend treats every request as the fixed no-auth user, and stack-init makes that user an admin (only while no provider is configured), so admin-only routes such as /ingester/ keep working. If you later add and then remove all providers, re-run stack-init to hand the no-auth user its admin rights back.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: In-stack Authelia
items.text: Authelia (pinned image) lives inside the stack, is reverse-proxied at /authelia/, and stores its users and state in the stack's Postgres (soliplex_authelia database). The stack owns both ends of the sign-in exchange, so nothing has to be registered with an outside operator; the backend already trusts the provider's own TLS certificate.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: Installing
items.text:
From the stack directory, after docker compose build:

python3 <skill>/scripts/install_authelia.py \
    --project-dir <stack> --admin-email <you>@<domain>

The script is idempotent. It writes compose.authelia.yaml (pulled in by a top-level include: in docker-compose.yml), authelia/configuration.yml, and nginx/conf.d/authelia.conf; generates and — on later runs — preserves the Authelia secrets and the OIDC issuer key in .secrets/; registers the soliplex OIDC client (public, PKCE, RS256 access tokens); creates the soliplex_authelia role and database; starts Authelia; and creates the first admin user. Its --no-up flag writes the configuration and stops before touching Docker, for stacks not yet up. Finish then with stack-init, docker compose up -d, and authelia_users.py add --admin --email <you>@<domain> — the script prints the commands.

The admin password is generated randomly and written to .secrets/authelia_user_<email>.gen (mode 0600); hand its contents to the user out of band and change it in the portal afterward.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: Managing users
items.text:
python3 <skill>/scripts/authelia_users.py --project-dir <stack> \
    add --email <user>@<domain>            # [--admin] also a soliplex admin
python3 <skill>/scripts/authelia_users.py --project-dir <stack> list
python3 <skill>/scripts/authelia_users.py --project-dir <stack> \
    reset <user>@<domain>                  # new password file
python3 <skill>/scripts/authelia_users.py --project-dir <stack> \
    remove <user>@<domain>                 # also drops a soliplex admin entry

Users change their own passwords in the Authelia portal: they confirm their identity with a one-time validation link, which the operator relays — with the filesystem notifier it lands in authelia/notification.txt, and

python3 <skill>/scripts/authelia_users.py --project-dir <stack> code

prints the latest notification for relaying. Each notification overwrites the whole file, so two requests raised at the same moment keep only the later one; a stack with the SMTP notifier (a configuration change) mails notifications out and no file is written.

An admin user's rights in soliplex follow their Authelia sign-in, so removing an admin's user entry also removes their admin_users entry. For the provisioner, add its own service subject instead — see Room provisioning.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: Key rotation
items.text: Authelia's OIDC signing key and the server certificate are generated once and preserved across re-runs of install_authelia.py. To replace the signing key, delete .secrets/authelia_oidc_issuer_private_key.gen and .secrets/authelia_oidc_issuer_certificate.pem and re-run the install: it re-registers the provider entry and refreshes the backend's trust list. The server certificate is valid for a year; rotate it the same way, deleting .secrets/authelia_tls_certificate.pem and .secrets/authelia_tls_key.gen.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: External provider
items.text:
For a provider your organization already runs, use the skill's scripts/oidc_providers.py:

python3 <skill>/scripts/oidc_providers.py add --id <id> \
    --title "<button label>" --server-url <issuer URL> \
    --client-id <client id> --pem-file <token-signing public key, PEM>

The script writes a public client (no client secret; soliplex always sends PKCE), so the provider just needs the callback registered: https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/api/auth/<id>.

Registering the client is done with whoever runs the IdP; the flow is scripted end to end only from the provider's side. Soliplex requires the provider to issue RS256 access tokens; until soliplex's web client stops expecting a refresh token (soliplex/frontend#671), a provider that sends none ends the session a few minutes before the access token expires.

If a provider rotates its signing key, soliplex never fetches keys itself: fetch the new signing key and run oidc_providers.py add again with the same id and the new PEM, or remove and re-add it (--signin-successor names the provider that takes over the /ingester/ sign-in while others remain).
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: How the pieces fit
items.text:
• backend/environment/oidc/config.yaml — the auth_systems entries. With none, Soliplex runs the fixed no-auth user; the first entry turns authentication on. The backend reloads this file by itself.
  • nginx/conf.d/signin-provider.conf — names the one provider the /ingester/ gate sends browsers to. nginx reads fragments at start only: after a change, docker compose restart nginx.
  • backend/environment/oidc/cacert.pem — the backend's extra trust list; the provider's certificate is appended when its TLS is self-signed (as the in-stack Authelia's is).
  • Provider ids appear in the login and callback URLs: lowercase letters, digits, _ and -. ${server_name}:${nginx_https} on this page are this stack's resolved values on its generated copy.
path: Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider

items.title: Custom Python package
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

Every entry under src/ is a self-contained project directory: a pyproject.toml, an src/ package inside it, and its own tests. This project's own is src/${package_name}/:

src/
  ${package_name}/
    pyproject.toml
    src/${package_name}/
    tests/unit/
  <other>/

src/${package_name}/ is the project directory; src/${package_name}/src/${package_name}/ is the importable package inside it. <other>/ is whatever else you clone — same shape, no special handling.

Work in it the way you would work in any checkout:

cd src/${package_name}
uv sync                 # create/refresh the dev environment (installs pytest)
uv run pytest           # run the project's tests
uv pip install -e .     # or a plain editable install into another environment

The stack root has its own pyproject.toml, but it is a tooling environment (soliplex-cli, the docs site) rather than a library — the importable code all lives under src/.

items.title: How it reaches the backend
items.text:
The Soliplex backend bind-mounts ./src (read-only) into its container as /app/src and puts this project's package directory on PYTHONPATH as /app/src/${package_name}/src (see docker-compose.yml), so anything you define here is importable by dotted name from the Soliplex config under backend/environment/ — no image rebuild needed to edit your code. The backend watches it too: its serve command carries --reload-dirs=/app/src/${package_name}/src, so saving a change to your code restarts the server.

Because only the package directories named in PYTHONPATH are import roots, /app/src itself is not one: a repo you clone next to this project is visible to the container but contributes nothing to the import namespace until you add its own src/ to PYTHONPATH.

items.title: What ships wired up
items.text:
Two examples are referenced from the config so you can see the pattern:

  • a tool, ${package_name}.tools.greeting, referenced from backend/environment/rooms/custom/room_config.yaml;
  • a FastAPI router, ${package_name}.views.router, registered via app_router_operations in backend/environment/installation.yaml.

Dotted names into this package can equally be used in the installation.yaml meta: section (tool/agent/skill config classes, MCP wrappers, secret sources) — see the commented ${package_name}.* examples there.

items.title: Making it your own
items.text: Add modules under src/${package_name}/src/${package_name}/, reference them by dotted name from the config, and add tests under src/${package_name}/tests/unit/. Delete the demonstration custom room once you have your own.

items.title: Adding a second project
items.text:
Ask the agent

src/ is where you clone any other repo you want to work on alongside this one — the soliplex backend itself, a library you depend on, a tool you are patching.

items.title: 1. Clone it
items.text:
The soliplex-template skill does the clone and the wiring below in one step, which is the recommended route:

uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py clone <url>
uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py list     # what is there, what is on the path

By hand it is just:

git clone <url> src/<other>

Nothing to do for git either way: .gitignore ignores everything under src/ except this project's own directory, so the clone stays part of its own repo and never shows up in this stack's git status. That is a rule, not a list — a third and fourth clone need no further edits.

items.title: 2. Work on it
items.text:
Each project directory carries its own environment, so treat it as the standalone checkout it is:

cd src/<other>
uv sync
uv run pytest

Its .venv is its own; nothing is shared with this project's, or with the stack root's.

items.title: 3. Make it importable by the backend (optional)
items.text:
Only needed if the backend should run that checkout's code. The ./src bind mount already carries it into the container at /app/src/<other>; what it lacks is a place on the import path.

src_projects.py clone does this automatically, and src_projects.py add <other> does it for a checkout you cloned by hand. Either way it also checks the checkout's declared dependencies against the backend image and tells you whether a rebuild is needed — see What PYTHONPATH does and does not do below for why that matters.

By hand, append its package directory to the backend's PYTHONPATH in docker-compose.yml:

      PYTHONPATH: /app/src/${package_name}/src:/app/src/<other>/src

and, so edits to it restart the server, a matching --reload-dirs line to the backend's serve command, after this project's own:

      --reload=config
      --reload-dirs=/app/src/${package_name}/src
      --reload-dirs=/app/src/<other>/src

The trailing /src is right for a checkout that uses a src/ layout (most modern projects, including this one). For a flat-layout repo — packages sitting at the repo root — use /app/src/<other> instead. Point at the directory that contains the importable package, never at the package itself, and never at /app/src: making the mount point an import root is what this layout exists to avoid.

Then restart the backend. This is a compose change, so the --reload=config flag does not pick it up:

docker compose up -d backend

items.title: What PYTHONPATH does and does not do
items.text:
• It shadows installed distributions. PYTHONPATH is searched before site-packages, so a soliplex checkout listed there wins over the soliplex installed in the image. That is what makes a backend dev-mode checkout work — and what makes an accidental name collision confusing.
  • Every project on it is watched. The backend's serve command carries one --reload-dirs per PYTHONPATH entry, which src_projects.py keeps in step, so editing any of them restarts the server: a soliplex checkout is no special case. src_projects.py list shows which are watched.
  • It does not install anything. The checkout's own dependencies are not resolved: only its source becomes importable. If it imports a third-party package the backend image does not already have, the import fails at runtime — and docker compose up -d backend will not fix it, because the dependency has to be baked into the image. Add it to backend/requirements.txt, then docker compose build backend; see Backend image & dependencies. src_projects.py checks the project's direct requirements for you, reporting each as satisfied, MISSING, or CONFLICT: installed, at a version the project rejects. requirements.txt cannot fix a conflict, since the image's own versions are frozen as constraints; adapt the project to the image's versions, pick a soliplex image tag that has versions it accepts, or customize backend/Dockerfile. For what lies deeper than the direct requirements, see Checking it in the backend's environment.
  • The mount is read-only, and the container runs as the PUID:PGID from .env. Edit the checkout on the host; the backend only reads it.

items.title: Checking it in the backend's environment
items.text:
uv run pytest in a project directory runs against that project's own uv.lock, which is not what the backend has: the backend imports the project's code alongside the soliplex image's own versions. When src_projects.py adds a project, it checks the direct requirements in its pyproject.toml against the image, but not the requirements of those requirements.

To check the code itself against the image, import it in the dev-mode soliplex-dev service, which runs the backend's image with the very same PYTHONPATH (--no-deps: the check needs no database):

docker compose run --rm --no-deps soliplex-dev /app/.venv/bin/python -c "import ${package_name}.tools, ${package_name}.views"

For another project on the path, import its own package instead. A silent exit means everything its modules import is there; an ImportError, or a version error raised on import, names what the image lacks or has at the wrong version, however deep in the tree. It does not run the project's tests, so code that imports cleanly but needs a newer API still fails only when it runs — which is what the tests are for.

items.title: Running its tests there
items.text:
soliplex-dev is built with every src/ project's dev dependency group (pytest and the like) installed on top of the backend's image, with the image's own versions frozen, so a project's tests run there against the very versions the backend imports it with:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps -w /app/src/${package_name} soliplex-dev /app/.venv/bin/python -m pytest

For another project, pass its own directory to -w. The dev groups are listed in soliplex-dev/requirements-dev.txt, which src_projects.py regenerates whenever it adds or clones a project. Every project directory under src/ contributes, whether or not it is on PYTHONPATH, so taking one off the path (src_projects.py remove) leaves the file as it is. After changing a project's dev group yourself, or deleting a project's directory from src/, regenerate the file and rebuild:

uv run <skill>/scripts/src_projects.py dev-requirements
docker compose build soliplex-dev

Commit the regenerated file: a change to it is a change to what the tests run against. A dev requirement that needs a different version of something the backend image has fails that build, as one in backend/requirements.txt does; adapt the project's dev group to the image's versions.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

This project was scaffolded by the soliplex-template generator, so most setup is already done. Bringing the stack up takes three steps.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Docker with the Compose plugin (docker compose version).
  • An Ollama server reachable from the containers, serving the models named in backend/environment/installation.yaml. Its URL is recorded in .env as OLLAMA_BASE_URL (see step 2).
  • uv to run the secrets script (scripts/generate_secrets.py).

items.title: 1. Generate secrets
items.text:
The Postgres roles and the backend read their credentials from Docker secrets. Generate them before the first up:

uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py   # populates .secrets/*.gen (gitignored)

Don't hand-edit .secrets/*.gen

The script only fills missing files by default; it never rewrites an existing one. Deleting one after the Postgres volume already exists breaks the backend's auth to the database -- rotate the credential with --rotate instead. See Secrets.

The generated .env records PUID / PGID — the uid/gid the containers run as and that owns these secret files (defaulted to the operator who scaffolded the project). If you run services as a different account, set them explicitly and rebuild; see Secrets.

Just clone this stack from another one?

.env and the .secrets/*.gen files are gitignored, so a fresh clone of this project (a checkout made later, run as another stack) starts without both.

Recreate them with the generator pair as described in the project README's "First-time setup":

uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py
then 
uv run scripts/generate_env.py

items.title: 2. Confirm OLLAMA_BASE_URL
items.text: The generator wrote .env with the OLLAMA_BASE_URL you supplied. Confirm it points at your Ollama server and adjust if needed.

items.title: 3. Decide whether to require sign-in
items.text:
The stack starts with no OIDC provider, and so without authentication: anyone who can reach nginx uses it as Soliplex's fixed no-auth user. That is fine on a workstation; before you expose the stack, add a provider. The two ways:

  • an in-stack Authelia provider, which the skill's scripts/install_authelia.py installs — see Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider;
  • an external provider registered with whoever runs your IdP:
python3 <skill>/scripts/oidc_providers.py add --id <id> --title "<label>" \
    --server-url <issuer URL> --client-id <client id> \
    --pem-file <the provider's token-signing public key>

Adding the first provider turns authentication on; the script then prints the command that gives your own account admin rights. Adding one before the next step means the no-auth user never becomes an admin. See Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider.

items.title: 4. Prepare the databases
items.text:
docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init

stack-init brings the Soliplex databases to their current schema, then runs the setup steps in stack-init/init.d/ (see stack-init/README.md). Every step is safe to re-run.

items.title: 5. Bring the stack up
items.text:
docker compose up        # foreground
docker compose up -d     # detached

The first run builds the nginx and backend images and initializes Postgres; it takes a few minutes. Subsequent runs are fast.

items.title: Exposed ports
items.text:
Port Service Purpose ${nginx_http} nginx HTTP — the web frontend ${nginx_https} nginx HTTPS (self-signed cert)

Only nginx is published by default. Every other service binds only the compose network; set its *_port parameter (ingester_port, docling_port, postgres_port, backend_port, gitea_http_port, gitea_ssh_port) to publish a host port for it.

The direct-access rows below render only for ports you published:

| ${backend_port} | backend | Soliplex backend, direct |

| ${ingester_port} | haiku-ingester | Control plane + dashboard (direct: bearer required) |

| ${docling_port} | docling-serve | Document converter |

| ${postgres_port} | postgres | Database |

| ${gitea_http_port} | gitea | Gitea HTTP (direct) -- nginx already serves the forge at /gitea/ |

| ${gitea_ssh_port} | gitea | Gitea SSH (for git-over-SSH clones from the host) |

(Container-internal ports are fixed; these are the host-published sides.)

items.title: Sign-in and admins
items.text:
Authentication follows backend/environment/oidc/config.yaml. With no auth_systems there, the backend runs without authentication, and treats every request as Soliplex's no-auth user (phreddy@example.com). stack-init makes that user an admin while there is no provider, so admin-only routes such as /ingester/ admit it.

Providers come in two sorts, both added from the soliplex-template skill: an in-stack Authelia installed with scripts/install_authelia.py and managed day to day with scripts/authelia_users.py, or external IdPs managed by the scripts/oidc_providers.py below. See Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider for the commands and what they print.

scripts/oidc_providers.py (in the soliplex-template skill) manages the external providers:

  • list shows them, marking the one /ingester/ signs in with.
  • add adds one. The first turns authentication on: give real accounts admin rights with the soliplex-cli admin-users add command it prints.
  • remove removes one. Removing the last turns authentication off: re-run stack-init to make the no-auth user an admin again.
  • signin chooses the provider /ingester/ signs in with.

The backend picks up a change by itself. nginx reads its sign-in fragment (nginx/conf.d/signin-provider.conf) only at start, so restart it when the script says so:

docker compose restart nginx

items.title: Verify the stack
items.text:
docker compose ps
<!-- ifp:ingester_port -->
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat .secrets/ingester_bearer.gen)" \
  http://localhost:${ingester_port}/ingester/health
<!-- endif -->
docker compose logs -f backend

Then open http://localhost:${nginx_http} for the web frontend.

items.title: Provision Gitea
items.text:
This stack includes a local Gitea, reverse-proxied at /gitea/. After the stack is up, provision it:

uv run scripts/init_gitea.py

This creates a rotating service account (its password is never persisted), and writes GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN into .env. It also creates the tracking repository's provision-status labels (provision-start, provision-complete, provision-incomplete, provision-failed; see Room provisioning). It reaches Gitea through nginx's /gitea/, trusting only the stack's own certificate (or through gitea_http_port, when that is set). Then recreate the services that read .env:

docker compose up -d backend soliplex-provisioner

Useful flags:

  • --admin-user NAME — also create a distinct web-UI admin login (you are prompted for its password).
  • --push-to-gitea — register your SSH key(s), create a repo, set this stack's git origin to it, and push the initial commit. It pushes over Gitea's SSH, so it needs the stack generated with gitea_ssh_port.

Open Gitea at https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/gitea/.

items.title: Using the TUI
items.text:
Soliplex includes an interactive terminal client. The backend image bundles it, so you can run it against the running stack without installing anything on the host:

docker compose exec backend soliplex-tui --url http://localhost:8000

This stack also serves the same client as a web app via the tui service; nginx proxies it at https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/tui/.

items.title: Everyday commands
items.text:
docker compose build <service>   # rebuild one image (backend, nginx, …)
docker compose down              # stop (keeps the postgres_data volume)
docker compose down -v           # stop AND wipe the postgres volume

down -v is destructive

docker compose down -v drops the postgres_data volume — chat threads, authorization grants, and the ingester's job queue (now its own Postgres database) all go with it. The RAG vector store and your documents live under rag/db/ (a bind mount), so they survive a down -v.

items.title: Backend image & dependencies
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The backend service image is built from backend/Dockerfile, on top of the published soliplex release image:

FROM ghcr.io/soliplex/soliplex-postgres:${soliplex_image_tag}

That image already holds soliplex and its PostgreSQL driver (psycopg, over the system libpq5) in /app/.venv. The Dockerfile adds only what is particular to this stack:

  • bwrap (bubblewrap), for the bubble-sandbox skill;
  • the extra PyPI packages listed in backend/requirements.txt;
  • the sandbox environments under backend/sandbox/environments/;
  • the service user, from PUID / PGID in .env.

The image carries no uv, curl, git, or compiler. uv is mounted only into the build steps that need it, and never lands in the image.

Because everything is baked in at build time, changing any of it requires a rebuild:

docker compose build backend
docker compose up -d backend

The dev-mode soliplex-dev service builds on this image, adding the src/ projects' dev dependencies, so rebuild it too if you use it (docker compose build backend soliplex-dev).

items.title: Choosing the soliplex release
items.text:
The tag on the FROM line picks the release:

Tag Meaning 0.85 moving: the newest 0.85.x patch release 0.85.3 exact: that one release latest moving: the newest release of any series

Docker keeps using its local copy of a moving tag until it is told to look again, so pass --pull to pick up a new patch release:

docker compose build --pull backend
docker compose up -d backend

To see which tags are published:

TOKEN=$(curl -s "https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:soliplex/soliplex-postgres:pull" | jq -r .token)
TAGS=https://ghcr.io/v2/soliplex/soliplex-postgres/tags/list
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$TAGS" | jq -r '.tags[]' | sort -V

Moving to a new series (say 0.85 to 0.86) is an upgrade, not a rebuild:

  • check the release notes, and Database migrations for the databases and RAG stores it may need to migrate;
  • raise the soliplex requirement in pyproject.toml and src/<package>/pyproject.toml to match, so host-side work runs the same release the backend does;
  • check the haiku.rag-slim tag in docker-compose.yml (the &haiku_rag_image anchor) against the haiku.rag-slim range the new release requires: the ingester writes the LanceDB the backend reads.

The TUI's tui/Dockerfile builds on ghcr.io/soliplex/soliplex-tui at the same tag. Change the two together, and rebuild tui as well.

items.title: Adding a third-party dependency (from PyPI)
items.text:
1. Add one requirement per line to backend/requirements.txt:

    httpx2-kerberos >= 2.1.1

  2. Rebuild and restart the service (see above).

The build freezes every package the soliplex image already holds as a constraint, and resolves the new requirements around them. An extra can add packages, but one that needs a different version of a package the soliplex release pinned fails the build with a resolver error rather than quietly moving it. Pick a compatible version of the extra, or a soliplex release whose pins suit it.

items.title: Adding a local Python dependency
items.text:
"Local" means a package whose source lives on your machine. The build context of the backend image is the backend/ directory, so anything the Dockerfile COPYs must live inside backend/. Place the source under backend/vendor/<pkgname>/, copy it in just before the requirements.txt install step in backend/Dockerfile:

COPY --link vendor /vendor

and list it in backend/requirements.txt by path (/vendor/<pkgname>). Its own dependencies are resolved against the same frozen constraints as any other extra.

Your own code does not need this

For code that belongs to this project, use its own project directory under src/ instead — it is bind-mounted onto the backend's PYTHONPATH with no rebuild. See Custom Python package.

items.title: Gotchas
items.text:
• While backend/requirements.txt holds only comments and blank lines, the install step is skipped entirely.
  • The install layer is cached on requirements.txt and the soliplex image it builds on. A --pull that fetches a newer image re-runs it, against that release's versions, so an extra that fit the old release can fail on the new one.
  • requirements.txt should be bind-mounted into the install step, not copied into the image. Older stacks COPY --link it into /tmp, which can fail the build under newer Docker.

Check a built image with:

```bash
docker compose run --rm --no-deps --entrypoint stat backend -c %a /tmp
```

1777 is fine.

Otherwise, replace the COPY --link lines in backend/Dockerfile and soliplex-dev/Dockerfile with a --mount=type=bind,... on the RUN that reads the file, then rebuild both backend and soliplex-dev.

  • Sandbox environments under backend/sandbox/environments/<name>/ are separate uv projects, with their own locked dependencies; a package the sandboxed code needs belongs there, not in requirements.txt.

items.title: Backend configuration
items.text:
Ask the agent

About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The backend's behavior is driven by the files under backend/environment/, bind-mounted into the container at /environment. Because the backend runs with --reload=config, edits here take effect without a rebuild.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• installation.yaml — the top-level install config: agents, secrets, env vars, room list, skills, DB URIs, paths. Start here.
  • rooms/<name>/room_config.yaml — per-room agent prompts, tools, and skills.
  • skills/<name>/ — filesystem skills discovered via filesystem_skills_paths.
  • logging.yaml, haiku.rag.yaml — logging and RAG configuration.

installation.yaml is heavily commented with pointers to the Soliplex config docs. Those comments describe defaults — so a section being empty or absent is not the same as being unconfigured.

items.title: Sign-in configuration
items.text:
Authentication lives off installation.yaml, in its own files:

  • oidc/config.yaml — the auth_systems entries. With none, the backend runs without authentication; the first turns it on. Written by the skill's scripts/oidc_providers.py and scripts/install_authelia.py (see Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider); the backend reloads it by itself.
  • oidc/cacert.pem — the backend's extra trust list for issuer certificates it would not otherwise trust (the in-stack Authelia's self-signed certificate); scripts append to it.
  • nginx/conf.d/ — nginx fragments, read at start only: one names the provider the /ingester/ gate signs in with, and an Authelia-installed stack gains a route for /authelia/.
  • authelia/configuration.yml (in Authelia stacks) — the provider-side configuration: server, storage, notifier, and the registered soliplex client.

Two sources of truth to remember

  • room_paths in installation.yaml lists the directories rooms load from. It points at ./rooms, so every rooms/<name>/room_config.yaml is loaded; to leave a room out, remove its directory or replace ./rooms with an explicit list. It also lists /app/src/rooms-provisioned (src/rooms-provisioned/ on the host): rooms created on request by the provisioner, a git clone of its own that the provisioner alone writes.
  • A filesystem skill must be both present under a filesystem_skills_paths directory and declared in skill_configs to be enabled.

items.title: Sandbox (code execution for agents)
items.text:
• backend/sandbox/environments/<name>/pyproject.toml — each subdirectory is a uv project. The backend Dockerfile runs uv sync --frozen on each at build time, so adding or changing one requires docker compose build backend.
  • backend/sandbox/workdirs/ — per-run working directories created by agents at runtime (gitignored).

Dependencies needed by agent-executed sandbox code belong in the relevant sandbox environment, not in the backend image's top-level dependency list (see Backend image & dependencies).

Running sandbox code is opt-in, chosen when the stack is generated (enable_sandbox). The backend image includes bwrap (bubblewrap), but inside a container bwrap needs user namespaces and a fresh /proc. Docker's default seccomp profile, AppArmor profile and /proc masking each block one of those, so all three have to be lifted. A stack generated with enable_sandbox: true carries this security_opt block on the backend service in docker-compose.yml (and the matching line on soliplex-dev); one generated without it carries the same lines commented out. To opt in later, uncomment both and recreate the containers:

    security_opt: &sandbox_security_opt
      - seccomp=unconfined
      - apparmor=unconfined
      - systempaths=unconfined

That relaxes the backend container's own hardening, in exchange for bwrap isolating each execution inside it. Without it, a room that configures the bubble-sandbox skill fails when used, with "Sandbox unavailable": soliplex checks that bwrap can run before it hands the room the skill. The skill's add_room.py checks the same security_opt block, and refuses to add such a room (the sandbox template) to a stack without it.

items.title: Service graph
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The stack is defined in docker-compose.yml. Browsers reach every service through nginx, which routes each path prefix to the service behind it. In the diagrams, dashed outlines mark what is not always a stack service: Authelia exists only once installed, and Ollama runs outside the stack.

The TUI and Gitea are dashed too: a project includes each only when generated with it.

flowchart LR
  browser([Browser]) -->|"${nginx_http} / ${nginx_https}"| nginx
  nginx -->|"/api/ /mcp/"| backend
  nginx -->|"/ingester/"| ingester[haiku-ingester]
  nginx -.->|"/authelia/"| authelia["authelia<br/>(if installed)"]
  %% if:tui
  nginx -->|"/tui/"| tui
  tui -->|API| backend
  %% endif
  %% if:gitea
  nginx -->|"/gitea/"| gitea
  %% endif
  classDef optional stroke-dasharray: 5 5
  class authelia optional
  %% site-only
  class tui,gitea optional
  %% endsite-only

Behind nginx, the services share Postgres (each with its own database) and two stores on disk: the backend reads the RAG vector store the ingester writes, and the ingester reads the room fragments the provisioner commits. Both the backend and the ingester reach Ollama at OLLAMA_BASE_URL.

flowchart TB
  authelia["authelia<br/>(if installed)"]
  backend
  ingester[haiku-ingester]
  provisioner[soliplex-provisioner]

  backend -.->|OIDC| authelia
  backend -->|LLM + embed| ollama{{"Ollama<br/>(external)"}}
  ingester -->|embed| ollama
  backend -->|reads| ragdb[("rag/db<br/>(LanceDB)")]
  ingester -->|writes| ragdb
  ingester --> docling[docling-serve]
  ingester --> rooms[("provisioned rooms<br/>(src/ clone)")]
  provisioner -->|commits| rooms
  %% if:gitea
  provisioner --> gitea
  backend --> gitea
  %% endif

  authelia -.-> postgres[(postgres)]
  backend --> postgres
  ingester --> postgres
  provisioner --> postgres
  %% if:gitea
  gitea --> postgres
  %% endif

  classDef optional stroke-dasharray: 5 5
  class authelia,ollama optional
  %% site-only
  class gitea optional
  %% endsite-only

items.title: nginx
items.text:
• Serves the Flutter web frontend.

  • Reverse-proxies /api/ and /mcp/ to backend:8000.

  • Reverse-proxies /ingester/ to haiku-ingester:8765 (see Ingester control plane).

  • An installed Authelia provider is reverse-proxied at /authelia/ (see Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider).

  • The web client is copied in nginx/Dockerfile from the published ghcr.io/soliplex/frontend-web image, whose tag picks the release

  • Its assets sit under a v<release-tag>/ directory, which nginx/nginx.conf caches for a year

  • index.html is never cached, so a new release reaches browsers on their next load.

  • Terminates TLS on host port ${nginx_https} with a self-signed cert.

  • Both servers include every nginx/conf.d/*.conf fragment, which skill scripts add and remove (see nginx/conf.d/README.md). nginx reads them only at start: docker compose restart nginx after a change.

items.title: backend
items.text: Runs soliplex-cli serve /environment, from an image built on the published soliplex release image (see Backend image & dependencies). Authentication follows backend/environment/oidc/config.yaml: with no OIDC provider there, the backend runs without authentication (see Sign-in and admins). The --reload=config flag means edits under backend/environment/ take effect without a rebuild, and one --reload-dirs flag per project on its PYTHONPATH (this project's own package, plus any added with src_projects.py) restarts it when their code changes.

items.title: soliplex-dev
items.text:
A one-shot task runner, not a long-running service: profiles: ["devmode"] keeps it out of docker compose up. It exists for commands that need the stack's config, secrets and databases and write access to the project directories under src/.

It is built on the backend's own image (soliplex-dev/Dockerfile, with compose passing the backend's image in as service:backend), plus every src/ project's dev dependency group, so a project's tests run here against the backend's versions (see Custom Python package). It mirrors the backend's secrets, mounts and environment — the same /app/src paths, and the very same PYTHONPATH (a YAML alias, so the two cannot drift). So an audit run here sees exactly what the backend sees:

docker compose run --rm soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli audit /environment

The one difference is that src/ is mounted read-write (the backend mounts the same tree read-only). Pass -w /app/src/<project> for anything that must run from a project's own root — alembic writes into its versions/ directory and prepends . to sys.path:

docker compose run --rm -w /app/src/soliplex soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/alembic -x soliplex.installation_path=/environment \
    revision --autogenerate -m "add a column"

Any project directory under src/ works, not just a soliplex checkout.

items.title: soliplex-provisioner
items.text:
The room provisioner's HTTP service (see Room provisioning): it creates rooms on a requester's behalf, for callers holding the stack's url_safe_token_secret. It runs with docker compose up, listening on the compose network only, at http://soliplex-provisioner:8090.

It shares soliplex-dev's image, secrets, environment and mounts (YAML aliases in docker-compose.yml), including its read-write src/, where the provisioner commits each room and its database fragment to the provisioned-rooms clone. The ingester mounts that clone read-only, and its config includes the fragments.

items.title: stack-init
items.text:
A one-shot setup run, held out of docker compose up by profiles: ["init"]. Run it before the stack first comes up, and again after adding a part of the stack that brings its own setup step:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init

It shares soliplex-dev's image, secrets and environment. stack-init/run.sh brings the Soliplex databases to their current schema (soliplex-cli database upgrade), then runs every step in stack-init/init.d/, in name order. Each step is safe to re-run.

items.title: authelia
items.text: The in-stack OIDC provider, installed after generation with scripts/install_authelia.py and absent from stacks that never installed it (see Sign-in: choosing and running an identity provider). The pinned Authelia image serves its own TLS on the HTTPS port at /authelia/, with a network alias so the backend reaches the issuer URL directly; nginx reverse-proxies the same path for browsers. Its state lives in the soliplex_authelia Postgres database; its configuration is bind-mounted from authelia/ (configuration.yml, the gitignored users.yml and notification.txt, and the committed identifiers.yml). The service and its secrets live in a separate fragment, compose.authelia.yaml, pulled in by a top-level include: in docker-compose.yml.

items.title: haiku-ingester
items.text:
The writer for the LanceDB at rag/db/.

Runs haiku-ingester serve --root-path /ingester with a Postgres-backed job queue (its own soliplex_ingester database), an async worker pool, retries + a dead-letter queue, and an HTTP control plane.

Secrets handling:

  • The service entrypoint exports INGESTER_DB_PASSWORD and INGESTER_TOKEN from Docker secrets files;

  • The haiku-rag config machinery interpolates them into haiku.rag.yaml

There is a single-writer constraint: only one ingester per LanceDB. Reads are safe while the stack is up; writing a store the ingester owns needs docker compose stop haiku-ingester first.

The backend reads the same store through a bind mount. See RAG pipeline and Ingester control plane.

items.title: haiku-rag
items.text:
A one-shot runner for the haiku-rag CLI, held out of docker compose up by profiles: ["tools"] (docker compose run enables the profile itself). It shares the ingester's image, mounts, environment and queue-password secret, and passes whatever follows the service name straight to the CLI:

docker compose run --rm haiku-rag info --db /data/haiku.rag.lancedb

Uses the same secrets interpolation as haiku-ingester.

items.title: docling-serve
items.text: A stateless document converter. Runs the upstream -cpu image directly; its variant/version are chosen at generation and baked into docker-compose.yml — re-point by editing that line and committing (see the stack's docling-serve/README.md for the variants, the tagging policy, and a local-build recipe).

items.title: tui
items.text: Soliplex's Textual terminal client, served as a web app over textual-serve; nginx proxies it at /tui/, so open https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/tui/. The same client is bundled in the backend image — to run it from the command line, see Using the TUI.

items.title: postgres
items.text:
Creates the stack's databases on first boot via postgres/config/init.sh:

  • ${agui_db} (thread persistence)
  • ${authz_db} (authorization policy)

  • soliplex_ingester (the haiku-ingester job queue)

  • soliplex_gitea (Gitea's backing store)

Each gets a dedicated low-privilege role whose password is a Docker secret.

Init runs only on an empty data volume; to re-run it, docker compose down -v first.

items.title: gitea
items.text:
A local Gitea instance (rootless image), backed by the soliplex_gitea Postgres database. nginx reverse-proxies it under /gitea/ on the HTTPS port — open https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/gitea/. Its built-in SSH and HTTP are unpublished by default; set gitea_ssh_port (git-over-SSH clones from the host) or gitea_http_port (direct web/HTTP) to publish. State lives in the gitea_data / gitea_config named volumes. Provision it after first boot with scripts/init_gitea.py — see Provision Gitea.

Two of its settings serve the concierge's tracking issues:

  • it accepts YAML attachments, beside Gitea's stock types: each requester's profile is attached as user-profile.yaml
  • it builds links from its public URL, whichever host a request came through: the backend and the room provisioner call it at http://gitea:3000, and the issue links they show users point at /gitea/

items.title: Ingester control plane
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

haiku-ingester binds its control plane on 0.0.0.0:8765, reachable only from the stack network: nginx is its public face at /ingester/, and the control plane's host port is unpublished unless ingester_port was set at generation. With a non-loopback bind, haiku.rag requires a bearer token (ingester.api.auth_token); otherwise anyone who can reach the port could cancel jobs, retry from the dead-letter queue, and trigger source refreshes.

items.title: How the token gets in
items.text:
1. The service interpolates the ${INGESTER_TOKEN} value into haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml from the environment, not files. Each service exports the value from the secret file into the environment before the config loads.

  2. nginx does not read the token from the environment at all. Its command reads the value from the secret file and renders it via sed into a writable copy of /etc/nginx.conf at /tmp at container start.

  3. The proxy also gates /ingester/ on the backend's admin check via an auth_request against /_authz_check: signed-in admins get through, anonymous requests are redirected to sign-in, and non-admins get the stack's error page. In a stack with no OIDC provider, every request is the no-auth user, which stack-init makes an admin, so the gate lets it through.

items.title: Reaching it
items.text:
Via nginx — the normal route. In a stack with no OIDC provider, open http://localhost:${nginx_http}/ingester/ and you're done (the token is injected at the proxy). If that answers with the "access denied" page, the no-auth user is not an admin: run docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init. In a stack with a provider, open https://${server_name}:${nginx_https}/ingester/: not signed in → sign-in page; signed in as an admin → the dashboard; signed in as a non-admin → the stack's "access denied" page.

Direct (the stack's ${ingester_port} mapping) — for scripts and debugging; pass the token yourself:

curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat .secrets/ingester_bearer.gen)" \
  http://localhost:${ingester_port}/stats

items.title: Choosing a token
items.text: Tokens are generated as 32 alphanumeric characters by scripts/generate_secrets.py when ingester_bearer.gen is missing -- the script never rewrites an existing file. Rotate the token with uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py --rotate ingester_bearer, then restart haiku-ingester and nginx (the token is rendered into nginx's running config).

items.title: Database migrations
items.text:
Ask the agent

About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

Upgrading across template releases

These migrations are one step of bringing an older stack up to date; Upgrading an existing stack lists the by-hand changes to its files that go with them.

items.title: The Soliplex databases (Postgres)
items.text:
The backend keeps two databases, soliplex_agui (thread persistence) and soliplex_authz (authorization policy), and tracks their schema with Alembic. In this stack each application role owns its own schema, so the backend migrates both databases itself, on startup: a soliplex bump that adds a revision needs nothing more than a rebuild and a restart.

The one exception is a stack whose databases were created by soliplex 0.81 or earlier. Those releases recorded no Alembic revision, and from 0.82 on the backend refuses to start against such a database rather than guess its schema:

soliplex.alembic_migrations.UnstampedDatabase: agui: tables are present but
alembic_version is empty, so this database was created by soliplex 0.81 or
earlier. ...

Stamping them is a one-time step, after which the backend migrates them like any other. A stack first brought up on 0.82 or later is stamped when its databases are created, and never needs it.

items.title: Ask, rather than assume
items.text:
scripts/migrate_soliplex_dbs.py puts the question to the backend image, so raise the soliplex image tag in backend/Dockerfile and rebuild first — the script refuses an image too old to answer:

docker compose build --pull backend
uv run scripts/migrate_soliplex_dbs.py --check

A stack with nothing owed reports:

soliplex 0.82; head b7e2f41c9d05
✓ agui: at head
✓ authz: at head

A database behind head is listed with the revisions it would apply, and an unstamped one with the revision its schema matches — here, a stack created by soliplex 0.79:

soliplex 0.82; head b7e2f41c9d05
! agui: unstamped, created by soliplex 0.81 or earlier (would stamp 63edaa5987f6)
! authz: unstamped, created by soliplex 0.81 or earlier (would stamp 63edaa5987f6)

Checking only reads, so it is safe while the stack is up, and it exits non-zero when anything is owed — or when a database cannot be migrated as it stands, most often because postgres is not running.

items.title: Apply them
items.text:
Migrating changes the schema under the backend, so the script refuses while the backend is running:

docker compose stop backend
uv run scripts/migrate_soliplex_dbs.py
docker compose start backend

It stamps any unstamped database first, with soliplex's one-time scripts/bootstrap_alembic_version.py, fetched at the tag matching the soliplex in the backend image. That writes the alembic_version row and nothing else, detecting the revision by fingerprinting the live schema. Then it runs soliplex-cli database upgrade, which brings both databases to head in one run, committing them together. Re-running on a stack with nothing owed reports Nothing to migrate. and changes nothing.

Starting the backend would apply the pending revisions too, once the databases are stamped; running the script first reports them where you can see them.

Back the databases up first if their threads matter. A dump taken as the postgres superuser, inside its own container:

docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c \
    'PGPASSWORD=$(cat /run/secrets/postgres_password) \
     pg_dump -h localhost -U postgres -Fc soliplex_agui' > soliplex_agui.dump

and the same for soliplex_authz.

items.title: Driving the CLI directly
items.text:
The script is a wrapper over commands the backend image already has, each run with docker compose run --rm --no-deps backend:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps backend \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli database status /environment
docker compose run --rm --no-deps backend \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli database upgrade /environment

status lists each database's applied and pending revisions, and exits non-zero for a database which cannot be migrated as it stands (unstamped, unreachable, or stamped by a newer release); soliplex-cli audit databases /environment gives the same verdict in one line per database. The bootstrap script is not part of the installed package, so it is fetched and run in one throwaway container. Use the tag matching the image's soliplex, and drop --dry-run to write the stamp:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps backend sh -c '
  curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soliplex/soliplex/v0.82/scripts/bootstrap_alembic_version.py \
    -o /tmp/bootstrap.py &&
  /app/.venv/bin/python /tmp/bootstrap.py --installation-path /environment --dry-run'

items.title: The ingester's job queue
items.text:
soliplex_ingester, the haiku-ingester's job queue, is not an Alembic database. The Compose startup command runs haiku-ingester queue migrate before serve, using the queue's schema-owning role. It creates the schema on a fresh database and applies pending migrations on an existing one; failure prevents the ingester from serving.

The queue uses the namespace soliplex. When upgrading from haiku.rag before 0.97, assign existing rows to this namespace before starting the upgraded ingester. Back up soliplex_ingester first, then:

docker compose stop haiku-ingester
docker compose build --pull haiku-ingester
docker compose run --rm --no-deps haiku-ingester sh -ec '
  export INGESTER_DB_PASSWORD="$(cat /run/secrets/ingester_db_password)"
  exec haiku-ingester --config /app/haiku.rag.yaml queue migrate'
docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c '
  export PGPASSWORD="$(cat /run/secrets/postgres_password)"
  exec psql -U postgres -d soliplex_ingester -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1' <<'SQL'
BEGIN;
UPDATE jobs SET namespace = 'soliplex' WHERE namespace = '';
UPDATE sync_state SET namespace = 'soliplex' WHERE namespace = '';
COMMIT;
SQL
docker compose up -d haiku-ingester

This preserves queued jobs and source sync state. Keep the namespace stable after migration. For a shared queue, stop all its ingesters and assign rows by source id to each ingester's namespace instead of using the blanket updates above. Fresh installations need no manual queue setup.

items.title: The RAG vector store (LanceDB)
items.text:
Each LanceDB under rag/db/ records the haiku.rag version that last wrote it, and haiku.rag ships an upgrade only for those few releases that changed the store layout. Opening a store checks it against that set of upgrades rather than against the release number, so most haiku.rag-slim bumps need nothing — including bumps that skip several releases, as long as they cross none of those upgrades.

When a bump does step over one, every store written before it has to be migrated, and until that happens the pipeline is down rather than degraded: the ingester crash-loops at startup and every read fails, the backend's included, so rooms lose RAG search. Opening a store written by 0.56.0 with 0.82.1 — which crosses three upgrades — reports:

Error: Database requires migration from 0.56.0 to 0.82.1.
3 migration(s) pending. Run 'haiku-rag migrate' to upgrade.

A store created by the pinned image is current by definition, so a stack that has only ever run one release has nothing to migrate.

items.title: Ask, rather than assume
items.text:
scripts/migrate_rag_dbs.py puts the question to the pinned image's haiku-rag CLI for every *.lancedb under rag/db/. So bump the tag first — the &haiku_rag_image anchor in docker-compose.yml — and then ask what it would demand:

uv run scripts/migrate_rag_dbs.py --check

The answer for most bumps, and the one worth confirming rather than guessing:

✓ haiku.rag.lancedb: up to date
✓ handbook.lancedb: up to date

When a bump does cross an upgrade, each store reports what it needs, in haiku.rag's own words, one line per pending upgrade:

! haiku.rag.lancedb: 3 migration(s) pending
    0.58.0: Move mutable document attributes into the document_meta table
    0.64.0: Rename the document_meta identity column document_id to id
    0.75.0: Index documents.id, chunks.id, chunks.document_id and …
✓ handbook.lancedb: up to date

Checking only reads, so it is safe while the stack is up, and it exits non-zero when any store is behind — enough to gate a deployment or a CI job.

items.title: Apply them
items.text:
Migrating writes, and LanceDB allows a single writer, so the ingester has to be out of the way. The script refuses while it is running rather than risking the store:

docker compose stop haiku-ingester
uv run scripts/migrate_rag_dbs.py
docker compose start haiku-ingester

It migrates every store it finds; pass --db-name (repeatable) to select stores by stem, e.g. --db-name handbook for rag/db/handbook.lancedb. Migrating is idempotent — a store that needs nothing reports No migrations pending and is left alone — so re-running after a partial failure is safe, as is running it on a stack that turned out not to need it.

Back the stores up first if the corpus is expensive to rebuild. They are a bind mount, not a volume, so a plain copy taken while the ingester is stopped is enough:

docker compose stop haiku-ingester
cp -a rag/db rag/db.backup

items.title: Driving the CLI directly
items.text:
The script is a loop over two haiku-rag subcommands, either of which can be run by hand on the haiku-rag service:

docker compose run --rm haiku-rag info --db /data/haiku.rag.lancedb
docker compose run --rm haiku-rag migrate --db /data/haiku.rag.lancedb

info is the one command a store awaiting migration still answers. It reports the version that last wrote the store (haiku.rag version (db)) and either Database is up to date. or the pending upgrades. Note that it exits 0 in both cases — that is why --check reads its output rather than its status.

items.title: Converter bumps (docling-serve)
items.text:
Bumping docling-serve — the image: line in docker-compose.yml, baked in at generation — never needs a migration: the store layout belongs to haiku.rag, and migrate_rag_dbs.py --check has nothing to say about the converter. What a bump can change is the conversion output itself, and so where chunks begin and end.

The docling-serve release pairs with the pinned haiku.rag-slim.

Changes which have affected soliplex:

  • docling-serve v1.32.0 (docling 2.124.0, pinned by haiku.rag 0.83)

Adjacent text items merge after the bump, so chunk boundaries shift. Existing stores stayed readable and their chunks were left as they are; nothing changes until a document is re-ingested. A re-ingested document gets new chunks with new chunk ids, so anything that kept an id from before — a saved citation, an external index — no longer resolves. A store that mixes documents ingested on either side of the bump works, but chunks them differently; re-ingest the whole corpus if consistent chunking matters.

items.title: Local Ollama
items.text:
Ask the agent

About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

Every model this stack names — the chat models, the title model, the RAG question-answering model, and the embedding model — resolves through the Ollama server at OLLAMA_BASE_URL in .env. When that server runs on the Docker host rather than another machine, it usually is not reachable from the containers, and the fix is less obvious than it looks.

items.title: Why the default install is unreachable
items.text:
A local Ollama install binds to 127.0.0.1:11434. Each container has its own network namespace, so localhost inside backend is the backend container, not the host — and the host's loopback interface is not routable from any container at all. OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434 therefore fails from backend and haiku-ingester no matter what else is configured.

Confirm what your server is bound to:

ss -ltn | grep 11434
#  LISTEN 0 4096 127.0.0.1:11434 0.0.0.0:*   <- loopback only, unreachable
#  LISTEN 0 4096   0.0.0.0:11434 0.0.0.0:*   <- all interfaces, incl. the LAN
