Binding to 0.0.0.0 does make Ollama reachable, but it also publishes an unauthenticated model server to every network the host is attached to. The options below keep it off the network while still reaching the containers.

items.title: Address Ollama by IP, never by hostname
items.text:
A friendly hostname will return 403

Ollama has a DNS-rebinding guard that rejects any request whose Host header is neither localhost nor an IP literal. Give OLLAMA_BASE_URL a name — say by adding an extra_hosts alias so services can use http://ollama:11434 — and every request is answered 403 with an empty body.

This is worth internalising before trying any option below, because the failure does not look like a networking problem. It surfaces in the backend log as a model error:

Stream error: status_code: 403, model_name: <model>, body:

Reproduce the rule directly against the server:

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: ollama:11434' \
  http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags      # 403
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Host: 172.17.0.1:11434' \
  http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags      # 200

A TCP relay cannot paper over this: it forwards bytes and never sees the HTTP header. So OLLAMA_BASE_URL must carry a bare IP address.

OLLAMA_ORIGINS is a different setting

OLLAMA_ORIGINS controls CORS — the browser's Origin header. It has no effect on the Host check described here.

items.title: Option 1 — relay the host's Ollama (recommended)
items.text:
Leave Ollama bound to 127.0.0.1 and add a small proxy service which republishes it on the Docker bridge gateway, 172.17.0.1. Containers can route to that address; no other machine can.

Add the service to docker-compose.yml:

  ollama-relay:

    image: alpine/socat:latest

    # Required: only a container sharing the host's network namespace can
    # connect to the host's 127.0.0.1. Incompatible with 'ports:'/'networks:'.
    network_mode: host

    command:
      - "TCP-LISTEN:11434,bind=${OLLAMA_RELAY_BIND:-172.17.0.1},fork,reuseaddr"
      - "TCP:127.0.0.1:11434"

    restart: unless-stopped

Point the stack at it in .env:

OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://172.17.0.1:11434
OLLAMA_RELAY_BIND=172.17.0.1

Optionally add ollama-relay to the depends_on of backend and haiku-ingester so it starts first.

Confirm your bridge gateway

172.17.0.1 is the conventional docker0 address, but it is a daemon-level detail. Check with ip -4 addr show docker0 and adjust both values if your host differs.

This option changes nothing about how Ollama itself is installed or supervised, which makes it the least invasive choice for a systemd-managed install.

items.title: Option 2 — rebind Ollama to the bridge gateway
items.text:
The same reachability without a proxy service: tell Ollama to listen on the bridge gateway instead of loopback.

sudo systemctl edit ollama

[Service]
Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=172.17.0.1:11434"

sudo systemctl restart ollama

Then set OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://172.17.0.1:11434 in .env.

The trade-off is on the host side: the ollama CLI defaults to 127.0.0.1:11434 and will no longer find the server, so you must export OLLAMA_HOST=172.17.0.1:11434 in your shell to use ollama list, ollama pull, and friends.

items.title: Option 3 — run Ollama inside the stack
items.text:
The strongest isolation. Ollama joins the Compose network as an ordinary service with no ports: mapping, so it is reachable from the stack and from nowhere else — not from the host's LAN interfaces, and not from containers outside this project.

Stop the host service first, so the two do not compete for the same model store and GPU:

sudo systemctl disable --now ollama

  ollama:

    image: ollama/ollama:latest

    # Deliberately no 'ports:' -- reachable only on the Compose network.

    volumes:
      - ollama_models:/root/.ollama

    restart: unless-stopped

Add ollama_models: to the top-level volumes: block, and set OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434 in .env.

The hostname works here — and only here

This is the one option where a name is correct rather than a 403. The official image sets OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0, which lifts the Host check described above. Inside the container that is not an exposure, because the port is never published.

Two things to plan for:

  • Existing models. A fresh volume starts empty and every model re-downloads. To reuse what the host already pulled, find the store with systemctl show ollama -p Environment | tr ' ' '\n' | grep OLLAMA_MODELS (commonly /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models) and bind-mount it instead of using a named volume. Run the container as the owning uid:gid so new pulls do not leave root-owned blobs behind.
  • GPU access. A containerized Ollama does not inherit the host's GPU. NVIDIA hosts need the Container Toolkit plus a device reservation; AMD/ROCm hosts need the ollama/ollama:rocm image with /dev/kfd and /dev/dri passed through and the video/render groups added. On a CPU-only host the plain image is sufficient and no extra wiring is needed. Check which case you are in with journalctl -u ollama | grep -i 'inference compute' before you migrate.

items.title: What not to do: network_mode: host on the stack's services
items.text:
It looks like the obvious fix — put backend in the host's namespace and let it reach 127.0.0.1 — and it does technically work, but it is the wrong lever:

  • network_mode: host is mutually exclusive with ports:, which every published service in this stack uses.
  • A host-mode service leaves the Compose network and loses its DNS entry. nginx resolves the backend by name (proxy_pass http://$backend_soliplex:8000), and Gitea reaches Postgres at postgres:5432; both break as soon as their target moves.

Fixing the cascade means moving nginx, backend, and haiku-ingester all into host mode, rewriting every service name to 127.0.0.1, deleting the ports: blocks, and managing port collisions directly on the host. Host mode belongs on the one-line proxy service (Option 1), not on the application services.

items.title: Verify
items.text:
The authoritative check runs against the resolved installation, so it covers every model named in every referenced YAML file — not just the ones set during generation:

docker compose run --rm backend \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli audit ollama --check-responsive /environment

It reports reachable / MISSING / OK per configured URL and exits non-zero on failure.

--check-responsive flags the embedding model

The responsiveness probe sends a chat-completion request to every configured model, including rag_embed_model. An embedding model correctly rejects that with 400 Bad Request, so it is reported UNRESPONSIVE and the command exits non-zero even when the model is healthy. Read the chat-model results as valid, and check an embedding model by hand against /v1/embeddings instead. Tracked in soliplex#1356.

Pull anything it reports missing:

docker compose run --rm backend \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli ollama pull /environment   # -n to preview

To test the transport by itself, bypassing the installation config:

docker compose exec backend \
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://172.17.0.1:11434/api/tags

HTTP 200 means the address and the Host header are both acceptable. 403 means the URL uses a hostname — see Address Ollama by IP. A connection failure means the relay or bind address is wrong.

Restart after editing .env

OLLAMA_BASE_URL is read into the container environment at creation, so docker compose up -d backend haiku-ingester is needed to pick up a change. Confirm with docker compose exec backend printenv OLLAMA_BASE_URL.

items.title: A note on model sizes
items.text: Reachability is not the only thing that makes a local Ollama feel broken. A large chat model on a CPU-only host answers at low single-digit tokens per second, and embedding a corpus for RAG slows to a crawl. If the stack responds but does so very slowly, the model choice matters more than the networking — see Configuration for where the model names are set.

items.title: RAG pipeline
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

rag/db/ is the single source of truth for vector data. It is mounted by two services:

  • haiku-ingester is the writer (/data); its job queue is a Postgres database (soliplex_ingester), not a file under rag/db/.
  • backend reads it via the haiku.rag.skills.rag skill.

Only one ingester may write a given LanceDB (the single-writer constraint).

items.title: Adding documents
items.text:
Drop files into ${docs_dir}/. The filesystem source in haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml picks them up on its next poll, and docling-serve converts and chunks them.

To ingest only part of what lands there, set ignore_patterns / include_patterns (gitignore-style) on that source. Note that a non-empty include_patterns is exclusive — anything it does not match is skipped.

items.title: Adding other sources
items.text:
To pull from S3, HTTP, WebDAV, and the like, append entries under the ingester.databases entry keyed haiku.rag, in haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml, and restart the ingester:

docker compose restart haiku-ingester

items.title: A separate, static database
items.text:
Ask the agent

For a separate, mostly-static corpus, build a standalone database with the haiku-rag CLI through the haiku-rag service — the stack's one-shot CLI runner, which shares the ingester's image, its rag/db and rag/docs mounts, its OLLAMA_BASE_URL and its haiku.rag.yaml. Point it at a different --db so it never collides with haiku.rag.lancedb:

docker compose run --rm --no-TTY haiku-rag init --db /data/handbook.lancedb
docker compose run --rm --no-TTY haiku-rag add-src /docs/handbook/ \
    --db /data/handbook.lancedb

Everything after the service name goes to haiku-rag. Do not run the CLI on the haiku-ingester service instead: docker compose run replaces that service's command, which is the only thing that exports the queue password haiku.rag.yaml interpolates, and the config then fails to load before the subcommand runs.

add-src also takes a URL or s3:// URI; for a local path outside ${docs_dir}/, add -v /abs/path:/src:ro and point add-src at /src. Use rebuild to re-index and delete <id> to remove a document. The database lands at rag/db/handbook.lancedb, which the backend already reads through its rag/db mount. Wire a room to it with rag_lancedb_stem: "handbook" in that room's room_config.yaml.

items.title: Ingesting multiple databases
items.text:
One ingester can maintain several databases with the same queue and control plane. In haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml, list their locations under lancedb.databases and their sources under ingester.databases. Keep the default database in both maps when adding another. (Provisioned rooms' databases are not listed here: each is in a fragment of its own, which the file's databases_include merges in; see Room provisioning.)

lancedb:
  databases:
    haiku.rag: /data/haiku.rag.lancedb
    handbook: /data/handbook.lancedb

ingester:
  # Keep the existing queue and api sections here.
  databases:
    haiku.rag:
      sources:
        - type: fs
          id: local-docs
          root: /docs
          ignore_patterns: ["handbook/**"]
          delete_orphans: true
    handbook:
      sources:
        - type: fs
          id: handbook-docs
          root: /docs/handbook
          delete_orphans: true

Source ids must be unique across databases. Each database must have only one writer. Point a room at handbook with rag_lancedb_stem: "handbook". Moving a source does not remove documents already stored in another database.

Apply database and source changes without restarting the other databases:

docker compose kill -s SIGHUP haiku-ingester

POST /reload is the HTTP equivalent. GET /databases/{name} reports a database's details. Changes outside lancedb.databases and ingester.databases, such as embeddings or queue settings, require a restart.

items.title: Migrating a store
items.text: Most haiku.rag-slim bumps need nothing, but a release that changed the store layout leaves every LanceDB written before it needing a one-off upgrade before haiku.rag will open it. See Database migrations for how to ask which case a bump is.

items.title: Changing the embedding model
items.text:
The embedding model is set in two files, and they must agree: haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml configures the ingester (and the one-shot haiku-rag service), and backend/environment/haiku.rag.yaml configures the backend. Both open the same LanceDB, and a store records the vector dimension it was written with, so it refuses to open under a different one:

Database configuration is incompatible with current settings:
  - Stored (db) embedding vector dimension 2560 -> Environment
    (current) embedding vector dimension 1024

When that check fails, the ingester crash-loops. Stacks generated before soliplex-template#218 was fixed are affected even if the model was never changed. In those stacks the ingester's file has no embeddings: section, so it fell back to haiku.rag's default (qwen3-embedding:4b, 2560 dimensions), whatever rag_embed_model said.

To switch models, or to repair one of those stacks:

  1. Set the same embeddings: block in both files:

    embeddings:
  model:
    name: qwen3-embedding:0.6b
    provider: ollama
    vector_dim: 1024

  2. Stop the writer: docker compose stop haiku-ingester.

  3. Bring the store in line with the new model. Check whether it holds any documents (info reports the row count of each table):

    docker compose run --rm --no-TTY haiku-rag info \
    --db /data/haiku.rag.lancedb

    An empty store can just be moved aside, and the ingester creates a fresh one on start: mv rag/db/haiku.rag.lancedb rag/db/haiku.rag.lancedb.old.

    A store holding documents needs its existing chunks re-embedded with the new model. This drops and recreates the chunks table at the new dimension, and does not re-convert the source documents:

    docker compose run --rm --no-TTY haiku-rag rebuild --embed-only \
    --db /data/haiku.rag.lancedb

    Do the same for every other store under rag/db/ that a room reads: one query is embedded once, with one model.

  4. Restart: docker compose start haiku-ingester, then docker compose restart backend.

  5. Jobs that failed under the old configuration, for example with a 404 for a model the Ollama server doesn't have, sit in the dead-letter queue. List them with GET /dlq, then retry each one with POST /dlq/{id}/retry, or let the next source sweep queue them again. Both calls need the bearer token; see Ingester control plane.

items.title: Searching several databases at once
items.text:
A room's RAG skill or search_documents tool can name more than one database under rag_databases, and a search then covers them as one set:

rag_databases:
  - rag_lancedb_stem: "haiku.rag"
  - rag_lancedb_stem: "handbook"

Each entry carries exactly one of rag_lancedb_stem or rag_lancedb_override_path, plus an optional name — the identity reported in search results, documents and citations, defaulting to the stem that placed it. Names must be unique, and every database in the list must have been written with the same embedding model, since one query is embedded once for all of them. A bare rag_lancedb_stem on the skill is shorthand for a one-entry list.

items.title: Operating the pipeline
items.text: The ingester exposes a dashboard and control plane API behind nginx at /ingester/. All requests under that path require the bearer token.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The Postgres roles and the Soliplex backend read their credentials from secrets. There are two modes, both documented at the bottom of docker-compose.yml.

items.title: File-based (active by default)
items.text:
scripts/generate_secrets.py writes .secrets/*.gen files, which Compose mounts as Docker secrets at /run/secrets/*. .secrets/ is gitignored, so the initial commit never captures secrets.

uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py

By default the script only generates secrets whose .gen files are missing; existing files are left untouched, so it is safe to re-run at any time -- e.g. after adopting a stack feature that declares new secrets.

Don't hand-edit .secrets/*.gen

Deleting one after the Postgres volume already exists breaks the backend's auth to the database -- rotate the credential with --rotate instead, or docker compose down -v and re-init (see the caveat below).

items.title: Rotating secrets
items.text:
Pass secret names (the .gen suffix is optional) to replace specific credentials:

uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py --rotate ingester_bearer

--rotate-all replaces every declared secret. Bare --rotate (no names) replaces nothing: it prints a preview of what --rotate-all would do.

Rotation of a secret that feeds a Postgres role password needs one extra step, and the script prints it after regenerating: role passwords are read only at initdb, so once the postgres_data volume exists its roles still hold the old passwords. The script prints a ready-to-paste ALTER ROLE command per affected role (the role names are joined from the compose wiring and the postgres/config init scripts), or docker compose down -v as the wipe-everything alternative (see the caveat below).

--dry-run turns any invocation into a preview: it prints what the run would write and touches nothing.

items.title: File ownership (PUID / PGID)
items.text:
The secret files are mode 0600 (owner-only). For an in-container service (e.g. Postgres) to read one, the file's owner must match the uid the container runs as. The stack ties both ends to PUID / PGID in .env:

  • every built image runs as PUID:PGID (Compose build.args), and
  • scripts/generate_secrets.py ensures the .secrets/*.gen files end up owned by PUID:PGID.

The generator defaults PUID / PGID to the host operator who scaffolded the project, so on a single-developer machine this is automatic. On a deploy host whose login uid differs from the runtime service account, set PUID / PGID explicitly (and rebuild — see below); generate_secrets.py then re-owns the secret files to that uid/gid via a throwaway container (it needs Docker for that step).

Changing PUID / PGID needs a rebuild

The uid is baked into the images at build time, so after editing PUID / PGID in .env you must docker compose build (and re-run uv run scripts/generate_secrets.py so the secret files are re-owned to match).

Override uid: who owns the secret files

When PUID differs from your login uid, the .secrets/*.gen files are owned by PUID, so reading or deleting them from the host needs that uid (or sudo). This is expected — it is what lets the container read them at mode 0600.

items.title: Env-var (commented alternative)
items.text: Uncomment the env-var secret blocks in docker-compose.yml and set the corresponding SOLIPLEX_* environment variables instead of using files.

items.title: The down -v caveat
items.text: docker compose down -v drops the postgres_data volume — chat threads, authorization grants, and the ingester's job queue (its own soliplex_ingester database) all go with it. The RAG vector store under rag/db/ (a bind mount) is separate, so a down -v does not touch it.

items.title: Room provisioning
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The room provisioner creates a private RAG room for a requester in one step: the room's config, its own database, ingestion from the room's uploads, and access for its owner alone: the requester, unless an admin names another (see Rooms for someone else).

A room is requested in one of two ways:

  • a user asks the concierge's about room, whose request_room tool calls the provisioner service on their behalf
  • an operator runs the provisioner from the command line, naming the requester

items.title: A request, end to end
items.text:
A user asking the concierge's about room for a room, with the provisioner service's default settings:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as User
    participant A as backend :8000<br/>(agent + concierge tools)
    participant P as soliplex-provisioner<br/>:8090
    participant Z as postgres<br/>(authz)
    participant F as Stack files<br/>src/rooms-provisioned,<br/>uploads/rooms, rag/db
    participant G as Gitea
    participant I as haiku-ingester<br/>:8765

    U->>A: "Make me a room called Q3 plans"
    A->>A: request_room: mint a short-lived service token<br/>with the user's claims (url_safe_token_secret)
    A->>P: POST /rooms {name, slug?, description?}<br/>Bearer service token
    P->>Z: Admission: admin, or WRITE on __provision__?
    alt not admitted
        P-->>A: 403
        A-->>U: Files a "new-room" issue instead
    end
    P->>P: plan_room: owner from preferred_username,<br/>slug from the name -> alice--q3-plans
    P->>A: Check the backend admits the provisioner<br/>(its own service token)
    P->>F: Take the lock, check the room id is free:<br/>room dir, fragment, database, uploads
    P->>Z: Check the room id is free: no policy
    P->>G: File the tracking issue (provision-start)
    P-->>A: 202 {room_id, issue_url}
    A-->>U: "alice--q3-plans is being created"

    Note over P,I: Background: create the room, holding the lock
    P->>F: Write room_config.yaml, REQUEST.md, provision.yaml<br/>to src/rooms-provisioned/alice--q3-plans/
    P->>F: mkdir uploads/rooms/alice--q3-plans
    P->>F: Write databases.d/alice--q3-plans.yaml
    P->>I: Reload the config
    I->>F: Create rag/db/alice--q3-plans.lancedb
    P->>Z: soliplex-cli room-authz: grant the owner, audit the rooms
    P->>F: git commit (the requester as author)
    alt a step before the commit fails
        P->>F: Undo this run's steps, newest first
        P->>G: Report the failure on the issue (provision-failed)
    end
    P->>G: git push the clone
    P->>A: POST /api/v1/installation/reload/rooms:<br/>the room is in the delta
    P->>G: Tag (provision-complete), comment on, and close the issue

    U->>A: "Is it ready?"
    A->>P: GET /rooms/alice--q3-plans
    P-->>A: live / pending / incomplete / failed
    A-->>U: "Ready: refresh your room list"

    U->>A: Upload documents to the room
    A->>F: uploads/rooms/alice--q3-plans/
    I->>F: Its fs source picks up the files
    I->>F: Convert, chunk, embed, store in the room's database

items.text:

items.title: From the command line
items.text:
Ask the agent

About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The provisioner also runs from the command line, in a one-off soliplex-dev container, which carries git and the provisioner (soliplex-provision-room). It needs the stack to be up; with OIDC on, the backend must admit the provisioner (see With OIDC on).

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-provision-room \
    --claims '{"preferred_username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "name": "Alice Example"}' \
    --name "Q3 Plans"

The room's id is <owner>--<slug>1: the owner comes from the requester's preferred_username claim, the slug from the room's name (q3-plans), or --slug. --description defaults to the name. The soliplex-template skill's provision_room.py runs the same command, taking --username / --email / --display-name as an alternative to --claims.

It exits 0 when the room is live, 1 when steps after its commit remain (each is printed), and 2 on an error.

  1. In general, a room's id is <owner><separator><slug>, where the separator defaults to --. Set PROVISIONER_ROOM_ID_SEPARATOR in the stack's .env to change it, for instance to keep the legacy form (<owner>:<slug>):

    PROVISIONER_ROOM_ID_SEPARATOR=:

    See Settings. ↩

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The provisioner's settings, what it needs from the backend with OIDC on, how it commits, and the agent its rooms use.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
The provisioner reads these from the stack's .env:

Variable Meaning PROVISIONER_SERVICE_SUBJECT The subject (sub claim) of the provisioner's service tokens (default soliplex-provisioner); the admin_users entry above must match it, as stack-init makes it do. PROVISIONER_OWNER_CLAIM The claim a room's owner comes from (default preferred_username). PROVISIONER_FLATTEN_OWNER true to turn @ into _ in the owner, for email-shaped claims. PROVISIONER_LOWERCASE_OWNER false to keep the owner part's case from the claim (default true: lowercased). PROVISIONER_ROOM_ID_SEPARATOR What joins the owner part and the slug in a room id (default --, the concierge's; : keeps the legacy form). GITEA_HOST / GITEA_ACCESS_TOKEN The Gitea for tracking issues and the provisioned-rooms repository; unset means none. scripts/init_gitea.py sets both for the stack's own Gitea. GITEA_OWNER / GITEA_REPO The tracking-issue repository (default soliplex-admin/soliplex-requests, the concierge's). GITEA_ROOMS_REPO The provisioned-rooms repository, under GITEA_OWNER (default rooms-provisioned).

For the stack's own Gitea, scripts/init_gitea.py creates both repositories. On a Gitea hosted elsewhere, create the provisioned-rooms repository before the first run; until then, each run reports the push as a step to finish.

items.title: With OIDC on
items.text:
The provisioner authenticates to the backend with service tokens it mints for itself (soliplex-cli service-token mint, signed with the stack's url_safe_token_secret): a fresh one for each call, valid for five minutes, with the subject soliplex-provisioner. Nothing is stored. The backend admits those tokens as an admin's through an admin_users entry matching their subject, which stack-init adds (its init.d/20-provisioner-admin.py step):

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build stack-init

Without the entry, the provisioner stops before changing anything, naming the entry it needs, and the soliplex-provisioner service reports itself unhealthy (docker compose ps): its log, and its /ok, name the entry too. It keeps checking, so running stack-init is enough. To add the entry by hand instead:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli admin-users add /environment \
    --json-path '$[?$.sub == "soliplex-provisioner"]'

A stack with no OIDC provider runs without authentication: it treats the provisioner's calls as its no-auth user, which stack-init also makes an admin.

items.title: Git policy
items.text: The provisioner commits with the requester as author. The committer is the git configuration's user.name / user.email, falling back to Soliplex provisioner <provisioner@soliplex.invalid>. To set a committer identity, hooks or signing, mount a git config file into soliplex-dev (the commented line in docker-compose.yml) and set GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/etc/provisioner/gitconfig in .env. Signing needs its tools in the image: it has no gpg.

items.title: The provisioned rooms' agent
items.text: Every provisioned room uses the provisioned_rag agent config from backend/environment/installation.yaml as its agent's template, adding no prompt of its own. Edit that entry's model_name or system_prompt to change the agent of every provisioned room at once. Without the entry, provisioning fails its rooms audit and rolls back.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The provisioner is the template's own adapters (its room config, records, ingester fragments and advice) over soliplex-concierge's provisioner framework, which runs the steps below and serves the HTTP API.

Holding a lock (src/.rooms-provisioned.lock) through step 8, the provisioner:

  1. refuses a room id that anything already uses (see Before anything changes)
  2. files a new-room tracking issue tagged provision-start, when a Gitea is configured and the concierge extension is installed
  3. writes room_config.yaml, REQUEST.md (who asked for what, and what is set up) and provision.yaml (the same, as data) into src/rooms-provisioned/<room-id>/
  4. creates the room's uploads directory, uploads/rooms/<room-id>/
  5. registers the room's database with the ingester, in a fragment of its own, src/rooms-provisioned/databases.d/<room-id>.yaml (an fs source over the room's uploads, and its place in lancedb.databases), then has the ingester reload its config, which creates the database
  6. makes the room private, granting READ and WRITE to its owner: by default, users whose preferred_username (PROVISIONER_OWNER_CLAIM) is the requester's; the policy is also recorded as the room's authz.yaml
  7. audits the installation's rooms
  8. commits the room (its directory, with all three records) and its fragment in src/rooms-provisioned (the requester as author), and pushes it when a Gitea is configured
  9. has the backend reload its room configs, which makes the room live
  10. tags the tracking issue provision-complete, or provision-incomplete when the steps after the commit left work for an operator (listed in the comment), then comments on and closes it

A failure before the commit undoes what the run itself created, and only that (and tags the issue provision-failed, comments on it, and leaves it open). After the commit, the room is valid as committed: a step that fails there is reported, with how to finish it.

Two steps have time limits:

  • the ingester's reload (120 seconds): one that times out may still apply after the run has undone its changes, so the failure says to reload the ingester again once it answers, and to remove the room's database directory if one appears
  • the push (60 seconds): one that times out is reported as a step to finish

src/rooms-provisioned is a git repository of its own (the stack's src/* rule ignores it), listed in room_paths as /app/src/rooms-provisioned. The backend reads it through its read-only src/ mount, outside its config watch.

items.title: Before anything changes
items.text:
The provisioner refuses a room id when any resource named for it already exists:

  • its directory in the clone
  • its database directory (rag/db/<room-id>.lancedb)
  • its fragment in the clone (databases.d/<room-id>.yaml)
  • an entry for it in either map of haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml or of a fragment (or another database placed at its location)

It also refuses to start when haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml cannot take the fragments:

  • its databases_include must name rooms-provisioned/databases.d, where the ingester mounts the clone's fragments
  • every database in its ingester.databases must be placed in its lancedb.databases, as haiku.rag requires once fragments place theirs
  • a non-empty uploads directory
  • a room authorization policy

The refusal names each one found, and changes nothing: remove them, or choose another name.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• The lock serializes provisioner runs only. Hand edits of haiku.rag/haiku.rag.yaml, or rag_db.py / add_room.py runs, are not serialized with it; an ingester reload applies whatever the file says then.
  • Every room the provisioner creates is a conversational RAG room over its own database; suggestions are left out, for an edit once documents are ingested.

items.title: Reconciling the stack with the clone
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The clone records everything provisioning sets up for each room: its config, its database's fragment (databases.d/<room-id>.yaml), and its policy (<room-id>/authz.yaml). The policies themselves live in the Postgres authz database, and the ingester's view of its databases in its own process, so either can drift from the clone. Reconcile replays the records:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-provision-room --reconcile

Holding the provisioner's lock, it:

  1. applies each provisioned room's authz.yaml, where the stored policy differs, and creates its uploads directory where it is missing
  2. has the ingester reload its config, which opens the database of each room whose fragment is in databases.d/
  3. has the backend reload its room configs, which loads each room in the clone

It prints each change, and exits 0 when nothing needed changing, 1 when it changed something, and 2 on an error. A second run changes nothing.

After docker compose down -v

down -v deletes the authz database's volume, and with it every provisioned room's policy: a room with no policy is open to every user for READ. Run reconcile before letting users back in; the same goes for restoring the Postgres databases from a backup.

Rooms provisioned before the clone recorded policies (by template 0.20 or 0.21b1) have no authz.yaml. Reconcile names them, and leaves their policies as they are.

Reconcile does not deprovision rooms. A room that is no longer in the clone (its commit reverted, or its directory removed) is not reconciled: reconcile leaves its policy, its database directory under rag/db/ and its uploads in place. Its reloads still follow the clone, though:

  • the ingester retires the room's database, when its fragment is gone from databases.d/
  • the backend stops serving the room, when its directory is gone

The policy left behind shows as stale in soliplex-cli audit room-authz, and makes the provisioner refuse that room id until it is removed.
path: Reconciling the stack with the clone

items.title: The provisioner service
items.text:
About this page

This documents a stack generated from soliplex-template. A generated project ships its own copy of this page without this note.

The soliplex-provisioner service runs the provisioner over HTTP, on a user's behalf. It starts with docker compose up, and listens on the compose network only, at http://soliplex-provisioner:8090:

  • POST /rooms, with {"name": ..., "description": ..., "slug": ..., "owner": ...} (all but the name optional), answers 202 with {"room_id": ..., "issue_url": ...} once the request is admitted, its id is free, and its tracking issue is filed; it then creates the room in the background
  • GET /ok answers 200 once the backend admits the provisioner, and 503, saying why, until then
  • GET /rooms/{room_id} answers the request's state: pending, live, incomplete (with the steps still to do) or failed (with the error)

Refusals:

  • 400: an unusable name, slug or owner, or an owner's predicate the installation does not register
  • 401: a missing or invalid token
  • 403: a requester who is not admitted, or who names an owner without being an admin
  • 404: a GET for a request that is not the caller's (unless they are an admin), or that the service does not know
  • 409: a room id already taken, or with a request already pending; the body names the room, {"detail": ..., "room_id": ...}
  • 422: a body that is not a request, for instance an owner in neither form below
  • 500: a check or the provisioner failed; the service's log has the detail

Every answer carries X-Soliplex-Provisioner-API: 1, the version of the API it serves.

A caller authenticates as the requester: its bearer token is a service token carrying the requester's claims, signed with the stack's url_safe_token_secret (code in the backend can mint one with soliplex.token_mint.mint_service_token). Keep its lifetime short: the backend accepts the same token as that user.

A requester is admitted when they are an admin, or hold WRITE on the reserved room id __provision__. With no policy for that id, only admins are admitted. To admit every signed-in user:

docker compose run --rm --quiet-build --no-TTY soliplex-dev \
    /app/.venv/bin/soliplex-cli room-authz from-yaml /environment \
    __provision__ <<'EOF'
room_id: "__provision__"
default_allow_deny: DENY
acl_entries:
  - allow_deny: ALLOW
    permission: WRITE
    authenticated: true
EOF

The service keeps request state in memory: a restart loses it, while the tracking issue remains the record. The service needs the same admin entry as the command line (see With OIDC on).

A request, end to end follows one request through the service, step by step.

items.title: Rooms for someone else
items.text:
An admin may request a room owned by someone other than themselves, with an owner in one of two forms:

  • one person, by a claim and its exact value:

    {"name": "Q3 Plans",
 "owner": {"owner": "bharney", "claim": "email",
           "value": "bharney@example.com"}}

  • everyone a predicate recognizes: a function the installation registers under meta.jsonpath_functions in backend/environment/installation.yaml, applied to a user's claims as a whole:

    {"name": "Quarry Notes",
 "owner": {"owner": "foremen", "predicate": "is_foreman"}}

owner.owner is the room id's owner part (foremen--quarry-notes). The provisioner builds the room's access rule from the form; no caller writes a JSONPath, and it refuses a predicate the installation does not register. The requester is still recorded as the one who asked, and may see the request.

The concierge's about room asks for such rooms on an admin's behalf. A stack whose about room was installed before soliplex-concierge's installer skill 0.7.0 gets that only by reinstalling the room (install_concierge.py … --force); a reinstalled room's room_config.yaml starts with an # Installed by soliplex-concierge-installer <version> line.
